Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That, in pursuance of the Directions of an Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to repeal so much of Two Acts, made in the " Tenth and Fifteenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, as authorizes the Speaker of the House of Commons to issue his Warrants, to the Clerk of w the Crown, for making out Writs for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament, in the Manner " therein mentioned, and for substituting other Provivisions for the like Purposes," he had ilftied his Warrants to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out new Writs for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the following Places j viz. for the Borough of Higham Ferrers, in the County of Northampton in the room of James Adair, Esquire, deceased; for the County of Lei-

cejier, in the room of William , Esquire, deceased;

and for the Borough of Ripon, in the County of York, in the room of William Lawrence, Esquire, deceased.

A Member present, and several Members returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and Cub feribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for _ those Purposes; and such of the said Members as are by Law required to deliver in, to the Clerk of this House, an Account of their Qualification, and to take and subscribe the Oath of Qualification, delivered in such Account, and took and subscribed the said Oath accordingly.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended His Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had,-to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

1

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Events which have taken place in the Course of the present Year, and the lignal Success which, by the Blelfing of Providence, has attended My Arms, have been productive of the happielt Consequences, and have essentially promoted the Prolperity and Glory of Our Country.

The unexampled Series of Our Naval Triumphs has received fresh Splendour from the memorable and deci-five Action, in which a Detachment of My Fleet, under the Command of Rear Admiral Lord attacked,

and almost totally destroyed, a superior Force of the Enemy, strengthened by every Advantage of Situation: By this great and brilliant Victory, an Enterprize, of which the Injustice, Perfidy, and Extravagance, had fixed the Attention of the World, and which was peculiarly directed against some of the most valuable Interests of the British Empire, has, in the first Instance, been

turned to the Confusion of its Authors; and the Blow thus given to the Power and Influence of France has afforded an Opening, which, if improved by suitable Exertions on the Part of other Powers, may lead to the general Deliverance of Europe.

The Wisdom and Magnanimity so eminently dif-played at this Conjuncture by the Emperor of and the Decision and Vigour of the Ottoman Porte, have shewn that those Powers are impressed with a just Sense of the present Crisis; and their Example, joined to the Disposition manifested almost univerlally in the different Countries struggling under the Yoke of , must be a powerful Encouragement to other States to adopt that vigorous Line of Conduct, which Experience has proved to be alone consistent with Security or Honour.

The Extent of Otir Preparations at Home, and the Demonstrations of Zeal and Spirit among all Ranks of

My Subjects, have deterred the Enemy from attempt ing to execute their vain Threat of invading the Coults of this Kingdom.

In Ireland the Rebellion which they had instigated has been curbed and repjeffed; the Troops which they landed for its Support have beehi compelled to surrender; and the Armaments since destined for the same Purpose have, by the Vigilance and Activity of My Squadrons, been captured or dispersed.

I'he Views and Principles of those who, in Concert with Our inveterate Enemy, have long planned the Subversion of Our Constitution, have been fully detected and exposed, and their Treasons made manifest to the World. Those whom they had milled or fe-duced mull now be awakened to their Duty; and a just Sense of the Miseries and Horrors which these traitorous Designs have produced, must impress on the Minds of all My faithful Subjects the NccciTity of continuing to repel with Firmness every Attack on the Laws and established Government of their Country.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

Under the unavoidable Pressure of protracted War, it is a great Satisfaction to me to observe, that the Produce of the Public Revenue has proved fully adequate to the Encrease of our permanent Expenditure; that the National Credit has been maintained and improved; and that the Commerce and Industry of My Subjects have continued to encrease and flourish in a Degree hitherto unknown.

The Situation in which We are placed, unhappily renders the Continuance of heavy Expences indispensable for the Public Safety. But the State of Our Resources, and the good Sense and Public Spirit which prevail through every Part of My Kingdom, will, I trust, enable you to provide the necessary Supplies, without etrential Inconvenience to My People, and with as little Addition as possible to the permanent Burdens of the State. The Progress made towards such a System, by the Measures adopted in the last Session, and the Aid given to Public Credit by the Pian for the Redemption of the Land Tax, have been attended with the most beneficial Effects, which you will, I am persuaded, omit no Opportunity to, confirm and improve.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I rely with Confidence, on the Continuance of your Exertions to enable Me ultimately to conduct the great Contest in which We are engaged to a' safe and honourable Conclusion.

We have surmounted many and great Difficulties. Our Perseverance in a just Caule has been rewarded with distinguished Succels; and our present Situation, compared with that of other Countries, sufficiently proves how much, in a Period of general Danger and Calamity, the Security and Ilappiness of the Nation have

depended (under the Blessing of Providence) on its own Constancy, its Energy, and its Virtue.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High Crime-and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence,- in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting of losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Poll Office to this House, or some other Person, to be appointed by the Postmaster General, do for the future, every Day during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the least immediately after the Riling of the House; and also from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters, and take Care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others, bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered, and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours' aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Postmaster General.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjecb, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty the Thanks of this House, for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne; and to congratulate Your Majesty on the signal Succels which, by the Blessing of Providence, has attended Your Majesty's Arms, particularly on the memorable and decisive Action in which a Detachment erf Your Majesty's Fleet, under the Command of Rear Admiral Lord Nelson, attacked, and almost totally destroyed, a superior Force of the Enemy, strength^ned by every Advantage of Situation.

It is with just Pride and Exultation that we observe, that, by this great and brilliant Victory, an Enterprise, of which the Injustice, Perfidy, and Extravagance, had fixed the Attention of the World, and which was peculiarly directed against some of the most valuable Interests of the Briti/k Empire, has, in the first Instance, been turned to the Confusion of its Authors; and we entertain an earnest Hope, that the Blow thus given to the Power and Influence of France, the laudable Example held out by the Emperor of and The Ottoman. Porte, and the Disposition manifested in the different Countries struggling under the Yoke of France, may encourage other Powers to adopt that vigorous Line of Conduct, which Experience has shewn to be alone consistent with the Security and Honour of independent States, and which, if generally adopted, may lead to the Deliverance of Europe.

We are fully sensible of the peculiar Advantage *

derived

derived to this Kingdom from the Extent of our Preparations at Home, and from the general Demonstrations of Zeal and Spirit among all Ranks of Your Majesty's Subjects; arid we have ieen, with the greatest Satisfaction, the Effect of the Measures adopted in Ireland for repressing a Rebellion instigated by our inveterate ' Enemy; the Surrender of the French Troops landed for _ its Support; and the fuccelsful Vigilance and Activity of Your Majesty's Squadrons in capturing or dispersing the Armaments since destined for the same Purpose.

We are anxious to testify to Your Majesty the Abhorrence and Indignation with which we have observed the desperate Principles and Practices of those who have long planned the Subversion of our Constitution, which have now been fully detected and made manifest to the World; and we cannot but express our firm Persuasion, . that those who have been milled or seduced mull now be awakened to their Duty, and that a just Sense of the Mileries and Horrors Which these traitorous Designs have produced, must impress on the Minds of all Your Majesty's faithful Subjects the Necessity of continuing to repel with Firinness every Attack on the Laws and established Government of their Country.

We shall not fail diligently to apply ourselves to the - Consideration of such Measures as may provide the necessary Supplies with as little Inconvenience to Your People, and as little Addition to the permanent Burdens of the State, as the Circumstances will admit; and, under the unavoidable Pressure of protracted War, while we join with Your Majesty in regretting the indispensable Necessity of heavy Expences, we shall derive the greatest Satisfaction and Confidence from the productive State of the Revenue, the Maintenance and Improvement of Public Credit, and the Extent and Prosperity of the Commerce and Industry of Your Majesty's Subjects; and that we shall eagerly avail ourselves of every Opportunity to cultivate and improve Advantages lb important to the Public Safety and Welfare.

surest Support (under the Blessing of Providence) in its own Constancy, its Energy, and its Virtue.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth;

GEORGE R.

His Majesty having taken into His Royal Consideration the signal and glorious Service performed by Rear Admiral Lord Nelson, in the memorable and decisive Victory obtained over a superior French Fleet off the the Mouth of the Nile, in the Month of Augttfi last, not only in the highest Degree honourable to himself, but eminently beneficial to His Majesty's Kingdoms; and being delirous to bestow upon the said Rear Admiral Lord Nelson some considerable and lasting Mark of His Royal Favour, as a Testimony of His Majesty's Approbation of such distinguished Service, and for this Purpose to give and grant unto the said Rear Admiral Lord Nelson, and to the Two next succeeding Heirs Male of the Body of the said Rear Admiral Lord Nelson, to whom the Title of Baron Nelson of the Nile, and of Burnham Thorpe, in the County of Norfolk, shall descend, for and during their Lives, a Net Annuity of Two Thousand Pounds per Annum: But His Majesty, not having it in His Power to grant an Annuity to that Amount, or to extend the Effect of the said Grant beyond the Term of His own Life, recommends it to His faithful Commons to consider of a proper Method of enabling His Majesty to grant the lame, and of extending, securing, and settling, such Annuity to the said Rear Admiral Lord Nelson, and to the Two next Persons on whom the Title of Baron Nelson of the Nile, and of Burnham Thorpe, in the County of Norfolk, shall descend, in such Manner as shall be thought most effectual for the Benefit of the said Rear Admiral Lord Nelson, and his Family.

R.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to take His Majesty's said most Gracious Message into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ, for the electing of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of in the County of

Wilts, in the room of the Right Honourable Sir William Scott, who, since his Election for the said Borough, hath accepted the Office of President and Judge of the High Court of Admiralty of England.

The Order of the Day being read;

The House proceeded to take into Consideration His Majesty's most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament.

And the same was again read by the Speaker.

And a Motion being made, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty;

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of that Motion.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

MR. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty Yesterday, with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most Gracious Answer;

Gentlemen,

I return you My particular Thanks for this loyal and dutiful Address; and receive, with the greatest Satisfaction, your Congratulations on the late glorious Events, and the Declaration of your firm Adherence to those wife and honourable Principles which have uniformly guided your Conduct. The Perseverance and Firmness of Parliament, and the Zeal and Spirit of My People, will give additional Weight to My Exertions in endeavouring to improve the Advantages which this Country and Europe have every Reason to expect from the happy Consequences of the Success of My Arms, and from the present State and Disposition of other Powers.

Mr. John Pitt presented to the House (according to Order) a Bill for naturalizing Charles Fredrick Hennings: And the same was received; and read the First Time. Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

By the Act passed in 178 r, intituled, "An Act for establishing an Agreement with the United Company of " Merchants of England, trading to the East Indies, &c." The East India Company are required to pay a certain Sum of Money, which is specified in the said Act, in proportion to the Number of Troops sent, or to be sent to the East Indies, on the Requisition of the said Company.

This Sum the said Company claim, under the Words of the Act, a Right of paying in the East Indies only; and as it will be necessary to provide for the Subsistence of the Four Recruiting Troops, and Twenty Recruiting Companies remaining in Great Britain, there will be wanting at present for this Purpose, the Sum of £.29,124.3J. 4d. which it will be necessary to vote on Account of the above Estimate.

Ordered, Th.it the said Estimate do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

The House was moved, That an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to continue, " until the Expiration of Thirty Days after the Com-' " mencement of the next Session of Parliament, an " Act, passed in the Session of Parliament of the <s Thirty-lixtii and Thirty-seventh Years of His present Majesty, Chapter One Hundred and Thirty-seven, " videlicet, on the Twentieth of July One thousand " Seven hundred and Ninety-seven,'intituled, An Act " to continue an Act, made in this present Sdlion of " Parliament, intituled, An Act to revive and continue, for a limited Time, and amend an Act, passed " in the present Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act' " to allow the Banks, and certain Banking Companies ' in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, to issue " Notes for Sums under a certain Amount, for a Umited Time, and for indemnifying all Persons who " have issued Notes for small Sums of Money in that " Part of the United Kingdom, for a limited Time," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to continue the said Act, for a Time to be limited: And that Mr. William Dundas, Mr. Hope, and Mr. Pringle, do

prepare, and bring in, the lame.

The Order of the Day being read;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Hobart took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Hobart reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the -Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Mr. Hobart also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move. That they may have Leave to lit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the

whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Parts adjacent, the different legal Quays and Wharfs on the River Thames, and those used by Sufferance as Wharfs and Quays, are found inadequate to the Accommodation of the Shipping, which has been in a State of Increase during the last Hundred Years, and to the Purposes of Landing and Shipping of Goods and Merchandize, and, from the crouded State of the River, the Navigation is much impeded, and many Inconveniencies. Delays, and Accidents, as well as Lolles and Damages, are occasioned to the Trade and Commerce of the Port of London; and that, by Reason of the increased Navigation of the said River, great Damages and Delays are sustained by the Owners of, and Persons interested in, Ships and Vessels resorting to the said

Anno 39° Georgii 3 " Regis, 1798. Prayers.

APETITIO.N of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Trustees for executing Two Acts, the one passed in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and the other in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for amending; widening, and keeping in Repair, the Road leading from the North-east Corner of Nuffield Common, by the Parish Church of Nuffield, otherwise Nuffield, in the County of Oxford, through Wallingford and IVantage, to in the County of Berks, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Trustees, appointed by virtue of the said Acts, have proceeded in the Execution thereof, and have borrowed several Sums of Money on the Credit of the Tolls, which (till remain due; and that the said Roads cannot be completely amended, turned, altered, and kept in Repair, and the said Debts be discharged, unless the Term of the said Acts be continued, and the Powers thereof enlarged: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. George Mr. Wallace,

&c.:‘And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others. Proprietors of several Open Common Fields and Common Meadows, and of Estates claiming Right of Common on certain Commons or Waste Lands, in the several Parillies of Leintwardine, Downton, Aston,

and Elton, in the County of Hereford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the several Parishes aforesaid, several Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, and Waste Lands, which lie intermixed and dispersed in small Parcels, and are, in their present State, of little Value, and incapable of any considerable Improvement; but, if the same were divided into specific Shares, and allotted to the several Persons interested therein in Severalty, and such Allotments inclosed, the same would be more convenient, and for the Benefit and Advantage of all Parties: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the said Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, and Waste Lands, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. John Pitt and Mr. Hobart do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

County of Huntingdon, was preferred to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are, within the said Parish, several Open and Common Fields, Meadows, Commonable Lands, and Waste Grounds, containing in the Whole, by Estimation, i ,000 Acres, or thereabouts; and that the several Properties of the Owners of the said Open and Common Fields and Meadows lie very much intermixed and dispersed in ftnall Parcels, so as to render the Cultivation thereof very inconvenient; but, if the lame, together with the said other Commonable Lands and Waste Grounds, were divided and allotted unto and amongst the several Persons interested therein, according to their several and respective Rights and Interests, and such Allotments inclosed, they would be rendered of greater Value, and might bemuch improved: And therefore praying. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty an Aid and Contribution for the Prosecution " of the War," as charges any Person with an additional Duty in Proportion to the Amount of the Rates or Duties to which, prior to the 5th Day of April11798, such Person was assessed according to any Assessment made in pursuance of any Act of Parliament in Force at the Time of passing the said Act of the last Session, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be charged Annually, during a Term to be limited, the several Rates and Duties following, upon all Income arising from Property in Great Britain, belonging to any of His Majesty's Subjects, although not resident in Great Britain, and upon all Income of every Person residing in Great Britain, and of every Body Politic or Corporate, or Company, Fraternity, or Society of Persons (whether Corporate or not Corporate) in Great Britain, whether any such Income.shall arise from Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, where-soever the same shall be situate, in Great Britain or elsewhere, or from any Kind of Personal Property, or other "Property whatever, or from any Profession, Office, Employment, Trade, or Vocation; that is to say,.

MR. Speaker acquainted the Hoilfe, That he had received, from Sir John Borlafe Warren, the following Letter, in return to the Thanks of this House, of the 21 ft Day of November last, signified to him by Mr. Speaker: -

It is difficult for me to express the Sense I entertain of the high Honour conferred upon me, by so august an Assembly as the House of Commons of Great Britain, by their Vote of Thanks, and their Approval of my Conduct, with that of my Brother Officers Seamen, and Marines, on the 12th of OSlbber last; and which I have, in Obedience to your Commands, communicated this Day to the Officers and several Ships Companies that composed the Squadron.

The greatest Encouragement that an Officer can receive to a faithful Discharge of his Duty, is to obtain the good Opinion of his Country, expressed by their Representatives in Parliament assembled *

I am convinced that the Officers and Men, with whom I acted on the above Day, as well as hiyself, will continue to preserve the most grateful Remembrance of so high a Distinction, to the latest Hour of their Lives; and we rely upon your Goodness to make these Sentiments known to the Honourable House of Commons.

I take the Liberty to return you, Sir, my belt Acknowledgments for the very polite Manner in which you have been pleased to signify to me the Thanks of the House; and also to allure you, that I feel most fen-sibly the favourable Light in which you are pleased to consider those Events of Service in which I have been concerned fihce the Commencement of the War, but more particularly in the Defeat of the Armament commanded by Monsieur Bompard; as it may have been the Means of preserving Ireland from the calamitous Consequences which Foreign Interference and Invasion might have produced in that Country.

I have the Honour to remain, with the utmost Respedi, Sir,

Your most obedient

humble Servant,

John Borlafe Warren,

Sir,

Canada, Bam Pool, 6 December 1798.

I beg Leave to acknowledge the Receipt of your Letter of the 22d of November, inclosing the Resolution of Thanks of the House of Commons.

A Petition of Edward Bancroft, of Francis Street, in the Parish of Saint Pancras, and County of Doctor in Physic, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, an Act was made for vesting in the Petitioner, his Executors, &c. the sole Property of his Invention or Discovery of the Ufeand Application of certain Vegetables, for dying, staining, printing, or painting, certain valuable Colours throughout that Part of His Majesty's Kingdom of Great Britain called England, the Dominion of Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon Tweed, for the Term of Fourteen Years; and the End of this Act, as dated in the Preamble thereof, was, that the Petitioner might be restored to the foil Benefit of certain Letters Patent, bearing Date at Westminster, the 23d of October, in the Fifteenth Year of His Majesty's Reign, and containing His Majesty's Grant to the Petitioner, exclusive iy, of the Benefits of the said Invention, for the like Term of Fourteen Years, of which the Petitioner was, and in the (kid Act is, declared to have been deprived, in consequence of an Act, made in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to prohibit all Trade and inter-course with the then united Colonies of America, and of the succeeding War; and that, at the Time of jJafiing this Act, His Majesty, by his other Letters Patent, under the Seal appointed by the Treaty of Union to be kept and used in Scotla, indead of the Great Seal thereof, bearing Date at Edinburgh, the 4th Day of June, in the Twenty-fifth Year of His Reign, was pleased to make a like Grant to the Petitioner of the exclusive Benefits of his said Invention within that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, during the like Term of Fourteen Years; and that the Vegetables of which the exclusive Use in dying, &c. was granted to the Petitioner by the said Act and Letters Patent, are Two Barks of Trees, which, in the Act of the Thirty-second Year of His present Majesty, Cap. 49, are denominated Quercitron and Red Mangrove Barks, together with the Bark of the American Hiccory Tree; and that though the Petitioner was thusredored to his original Patent Term of Fourteen Years throughout England and Wales, and though he at the same Time acquired a like originalTerra throughout Scotland, he continued liable to be frudrated of the Benefits graciously intended to be thereby secured to him, in all the Ways, and by all the Impediments, which have operated in the Cafes of other Patentees of new Inventions, whose respective Terms have been prolonged by Parliament, in consequence of their having been so frudrated; and that in Fad the Petitioner has greatly fullered in all these Ways, and by all these Means, as well as in other Ways, and by other Means, connected with the particular Nature and C-ircum-dances of his said Invention, as depending on the Rro-dudions of a didant Foreign Country, liable to be affected and obdruded in coming hither, by Events not capable of materially affecting the Use and Exercise of other Inventions; and that for the various heavy Lodes which the Petitioner has thus fudained, he has no Prospect of obtaining any Relief otherwise than by an Application to Parliament; but, in preparing to make such Applicati >n, he finds himself precluded therefrom, during the present Section, by a Standing Order of the House, made on the 1 ft Day of May last, which requires that, before any Petition be presented to this VOL. 54.

extend to Scotland, in the Months of Augv.fi and September, or either of them, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Application is intended to be made; and that this Order, having been so recently made, and never acted upon, did not come to the Knowledge of the Petitioner until the 2d Day of October last, when a Compliance therewith wa s no" longer possible; and that the Petitioner's said restored Term and Patent Term, unless prolonged, will expire in the Month of June next, and therefore his intended Application to Parliament will be too late, if made. after the present Section, and, consequently, the said Standing Order, if it should be rigorously enforced against the Petitioner, iftuft absolutely preclude him from all Possibility of obtaining that Relief which he has otherwise Reason to hope he may be found to have deserved: And therefore praying. That the House, in? Consideration of the Prenmes, and of his otherwise hopeless Situation, will be pleased to allow him to give the proper Notice of his intended Application to Parliament in this present Month of December, or in the Month of January next, or either of them, instead of the Months' of August and September last, or afford him such other Relief as may be found convenient.

Then to prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Walker, being further examined, said, That the Want of Accommodation for the Landing and Shipping of Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, in the Port of London, has for some Years pafl been experienced by all Persons trading to the said Port, and more especiatly the Persons concerned in the India Trade, by reason of the confined and crowded State of the Legal Quays in or belonging to the said Port: That, from the Nature and Value of the Cargoes imported from the West Indies, the Persons concerned in the West India Trade suffer in a highly aggravated Degree, from the heavy Lollies occasioned by Plunder, and from the Delay and increased Expence arising from the above-mentioned Causes attending the Discharge of the Ships and Vessels employed in that Trade, and the Public Revenue is thereby materially diminished: That if good and sufficient Wet Docks and Basons, with proper Cuts, Sluices, and Outlets, were made and established in some Part or Parts of the Isle of Dogs, with Quays, Wharfs, and Warehouses, attached thereto, w here necessary, for the Reception and Discharge of Ships and other Vessels employed in the India Trade, the same would not only be extremely beneficial to all Persons concerned in the said Trade, but advantageous to the Trade in general frequenting the Port of London, by reason of the Room and Accommodation which would necessarily arise from the Removal of the Ships and Vessels employed in the West India Trade out of the River; that, by Plans and Surveys lately made, it appears, that such Wet Docks, Basons, and other Requisites, may be made and constructed in the Isle of Dogs, and that the Petitioners are willing and desirous to make the same at their own Expence: That Application is making to this House by the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of for a

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Vol. 54.

Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue; within tfift Port of London; and Setting forth That the Mayor and Commonalty, and Citizens, of the City of London, by virtue? of, and under divers Charters, recognized and confirmed by divers Acts of Parliament have had and exercised, and ought and have accustomed themselves to have and exercise, the Office of Bailiff and Contervator of the Water of Thames, to be exercised and occupied by tho Mayor of the f ame City for the Time being, during the Time of his Mayoralty, or by his sufficient Deputies, in, upon, and about, the Water of 2(that is., to say) from the Bridge of the Town of , in the County of Middlesex, towards the East unto London. Bridge, and from thence to a certain Place called Kendall, otherwise Tenia nd, otherwise Tenleet, towards the Sea, and East, and in Medway, and in the Port of the City of London aforesaid, and upon whatsoever Bank, and upon every Shore, and upon every Wharf, of the same Water of Thames, within the Limits and Bounds aforesaid, and in, upon, and about, all and every of them, and also, for all the Time aforesaid, heldJurisdiction over the fame, and have had and taken, and ought and have accustomed themselves to have and take, to their own proper Use, by the Mayor of the same City for the Time being, during the Time of his Mayoralty, or his sufficient Deputies, all Wages, Rewards, Fees, and Profits, belonging to the same Office of - Bailiff; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Rights and Privileges of the Petitioners would be invaded, and the Trade and Commerce of the said Port of London, where it has flourished for a. great Length of Time, to the great Benefit and Advantage of the City of London and the Kingdom ir\ general, would, in a very material Degree, be removed to a new Scite, out of the Controul and SupCrintend-ance, as well as out of the Care and Protection, of the Petitioners; and that such Removal would not only be a Violation of the ancient Customs and.Privileges of the Petitioners, but also be productive of the most ruinous and distressing Consequences to divers incorporated Societies and Companies, as well as to great Numbers of Individuals, the Value of whose Property, or the Profits of whose Labour and Industry, in a great Measure, depend on the Trade and Commerce of the City and Port of London being continued to be carried on within the Limits and Jurisdiction of the said City; And that the Petitioners, and their Predecefi'ors, ever careful of the Rights and Welfare of their Fellow Citizens, and anxious to accommodate, promote, and in crease, the Trade and Commerce of the City of London, have from Time to Time devised, and offered to execute, Plans conducive to those Ends; and actuated by these Motives, as well as in consequence of divers Applications made to them in that respect, Plans have been fqrmed for increasing the Accommodation, and so) the more effectually securing the Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, of the Port of London, which, by the Aid and Authority of Parliament, they have Reason to Believe may be carried into Execution, without the Necessity of creating a new Corporation, or other expensive Establishment, without futh an Extent of Injury or Inconvenience to Individuals as the said Bill must nc-ceffarily produce, and without unnccefl'ariiy infringing on the ancient Rights and Privileges of the City of London, or burthening the Trade of the said Port in the Manner and to the Extent propefed by the said Bill; and the Petitioners pledge themselves such Plans will be brought forward, and, if duly encouraged and fanCtioned by the Legislature, carried into Execution; and that, as by carrying such a Plan into Execution, the Public at large would derive such Benefit and Accommodation, as the Commerce of London at present most urgently requires, at a moderate Expence, and perfectly confident with she Safety of its Shipping, and the Security of the Revenue; and as the Petitioners would not thereby take, or do they mean to take, any Emolument or Advantage to themselves, they rely on the Justice

Justice of the House that no new Corporation shall be established as proposed by the said Bill: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for vesting in Edward Bancroft, Doctor in Physic, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, the sole Property of his Invention or Discovery of the Use and Application of certain Vegetables, for dying, staining, printing, and painting, certain valuable Colours, throughout that Part of His Majesty's Kingdom of Great Britain called England, the Dominion of Wales, and Town of Berwick upon Tweed, for a limited Time, was read: And the Specification of the said Invention, duly inrolledin His Majesty's High Court of Chancery, as required by the said Act, was also produced to your Committee, and read: Then Letters Patent, under the Seal appointed by the Treaty of Union for that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, dated at Edinburgh, the 4th Day of June 1785, granting to the Petitioner the exclusive Benefits of his feid Invention for the Term of Fourteen Years; and also the Specification of the said Letters Patent, dated the 22nd of September 1785, were also produced to your Committee, and read:

And,

Mr. Charles Davids, a Cailico Printer, being examined, feid, That lie has uled the Quercitron Dye, invented by the Petitioner, for several Years: That it dyes Yellow and other Colours, and is of general Importance to the Cotton Trade: That in his own Practice he can get Goods ready in One Week with such Dye, which lie could not do in a Month with any other Dye: That he considers its Reputation as yearly increasing with the Use ol it: That there is a Variety of Work and Colours, which could not be any Way accom-plished without the Aid of the Dye extra died from the Quercitron Bark, by the Petitioner: And the Witness further feid. That the Cailico Printers have not yet obtained the full Use and Value of the said Dye; and from his own Experience, he is of Opinion, that it may turn out cf great Advantage in working of Manufactures X yet

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Henry Brown, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Commerce of the said Town has for some Years past progressively and considerably increased, and is likely so to do, and in Proportion to such Increase its Populousness ' has been greatly augmented, and in consequence thereof a great many new made Streets have been laid out, and Buildings have been erc<Tted, and many of the old Streets in the said Town are narrow, dangerous, and inconvenient, and the Levels of many of such new made Streets arc improperly and irregularly laid out, and no common Sewers made through the same; and also, many Windmills, Limekilns, and other Annoyances, are erected too near the Streets and Highways in the said Town: And the Witness further laid. That the Pavement and Common Sewers of the Streets, Lanes, and Public Parfages, within the said Town, are, in many Places, kept in bad Repair, and it would be a great Safety and Convenience not only to the Inhabitants, but to all Persons resorting thereto, if the said Streets , and Public Pali'ages were properly paved, and the said old Streets made wider, more safe, and convenient, and the Levels of fuels new made, or hereafter to be made.

Streets, properly laid out, and common Sewers made, and the Nuisances and Annoyances removed, and prevented.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for taking into further Consideration the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to enlarge the Time limited for the Redemption of the Land Tax, and to explain and amend an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for making perpetual, " subject to Redemption and Purchase, in the Manner therein stated, the several Sums of Money now charged in Great Britain as a Land Tax for One Year, from " the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Seven " hundred and Ninety-eight," was committed, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

The House proceeded to take the said Report into further Consideration.

And the Amendments, made by the Committee to the said Bill, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, with Amendments to several of them, agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for allowing the Sale of Reversionary Estates, by Ecclesiastical Bodies.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for restraining the Sales to the Lessees.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and; upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the1 Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for Application of the Monies arising by Sales.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, declaring that the Land Tax redeemed shall be payable as a Rent Charge, and recoverable as such.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, providing that, in case of Sale, the Purchaser may pay by Instalments.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, directing, that where the Purchase Money shall not exceed a certain Sum, the same may be paid to the Receiver General.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with Blanks; which, being filled up, the said Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, declaring, that Interest shall be paid, where the Money is paid by Instalments, in the same Manner as upon Transfer of Stock.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for Sale of Copyhold Estates.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, declaring, that Fines shall not be paid in Cafes of mortgaging, or otherwise charging Premitfes, for the Purposes of the Act.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed toby the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, declaring, that Registry of Deeds shall be as valid as Inrolment.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, declaring, that the Office of a Commissioner, shall not be deemed a Place of Profit under His Majesty.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Then several Amendments were made, by the House, to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time Tomorrow Morning, if the said Bill shall be then ingrafted.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill to repeal the Duties, imposed by an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, for granting an Aid and Contribution for the Prosecution of the War, and to make more effectual Provision for the like Purpose, by granting certain Duties upon Income, in Lieu of the said Duties, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

A Petition of the Governors and Company of the Waterworks and Water Houses in Shadwell, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are the Proprietors of certain Water Works and Water Houses, established in the Parish of Saint Paul, Shadwell, in the County of Middlesex, which Works have been carried on under the Authority Voi. 54.

of an Act, made in the 3d and 4th Years of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, to the present Time, and the said Parish, and several other neighbouring Parishes, have been supplied with Water from the said Works by the Means of Engines, Pipes, and Cisterns, erected and laid for the Passage and Conveyance of Water, to the great Accommodation of the Inhabitants in the said Parishes, and at the great Expence and Rilk of the Petitioners and their Predecessors; and that the said Works have been found to be of great Public Utility, upon the Success whereof depends the Health and Comfort of many Thousands of the Inhabitants of the Neighbourhood; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is now depending for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, &c. and for other Purposes, in the said Parish of Shadwell, and other Parishes adjoining thereto, and, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners will be very much injured in their Property, their Works destroyed, and the Inhabitants in the Neighbourhood deprived of their Comforts, and be put to the greatest Inconvenience; And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Couniel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Bakers resider.t in the City and Suburbs of Winchef a, and Places adjacent, in the County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners feel themselves much aggrieved for Want of the Magistrates letting the Price of Bread, agreeable to the Table of the 31st Geo. II. availing themselves, under the Third Ciaule of the said Act, and making them (the Bakers) Allowance of Profit much insufficient, on an Average, being only Six Shillings per Sack of Flour, to enable them to live by their Trade, and support themselves and Families; and that the Petitioners have felt the more lcnfibly such Oppression of late Years, in consequence of the great increase of Wages, and every Article of Life, exclusive of the heavy additional Duty on Salt, now so much advanced: And therefore praying for such Relief as to the House shall seem meet, either by amending or explaining the present Act, and the Table for the Assize of Bread therein contained, as the Standard for regulating the Prices, or to cause an additional Assize Table to be added, regulating the Price of Bread agreeable to the Price of Flour, in the' same Manner as hath lately been done for the City of London, thereby making such Allowance to the Trade as may be thought just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England trading into the Levant Seas, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and' read] Setting forth. That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey, has for a long Series of Years been carried on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Chatter, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on this Trade with Safety, and pro-tedl His Majesty's Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it' has been found necessary that an Ambassador or Public Minister should be lent from England to reside at Confiantimple , and that Consuls, Viceconluls, and other Officers and Servants, should be established in other Parts of Turkey, where British Subjects reside, and where English. Merchants carry on Trade, the whole Expence of which has been borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with other Expences incident to carrying on this Trade, have of late: Years amounted to about f.8,000 per Annumand that the

Petitioners acknowledge, with Gratitude, the several Grants they have frequently received from Parliament, which have enabled them to support their Establishments in Turkey, but they are sensible they should not discharge the Duty incumbent on them by. their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public (for. whom they consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not again declare their present Inability to support' their necessary and unavoidable Expences unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take thele Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as may be thought necessary and proper;

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill to repeal the Duties, imposed by an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, for granting an Aid and Contribution for the Prosecutijon of the War, and to make more effectual Provision for the like Purpose, by granting certain Duties upon Income, in Lieu of the said Duties, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

The House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. John Smyth took the Chaff of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. John Smyth reported from the Committee, That they had made a further Progress in the Bill; and that he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

And the House having continued to fit till Half an Hour after Twelve of the Clock on Morning;

Resolved, That this House will, this Day, resolve itself -Into a Committee of the whole House, to consider fun-ther of the said Bill;

A Petition of several of the Owners and Proprietors of the Allotments of the Lands set out by virtue of an Act, passed in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, lor dividing, allotting, and inclosing, a certain Common Moor or Tract of Waste Land called Tynemouth Moor, Shire Moor, Billy Moor, or Billy Mill Moor, within the Manor of

otherwise Tinmouthshire, otherwise Tinmouth with

mouthshire, in the County of Northumberland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in pursuance of the said Act, the Commissioners thereby appointed, divided and allotted the said Tract of Waste Land, and have set out several Roads through or over the lame, but the Commissioners were not by the said Act authorized to ascertain or determine what Parts of the said Roads were to be amended and kept in Repair by the respective Townships wherein the said Moor or Waste Land was situate, or to which Allotments of the said Waste Lands were set out, and therefore Doubts and Disputes have arisen touching the fame, and the said Act is in other Respects defective: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for ascertaining and settling in what Manner, and by whom, the different Parts and Proportions of the said Roads are to be amended and kept in Repair in future, and for otherwise amending the said Act, in such Manner as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Tierney, Mr. Grey, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

The House, according to Order, resumed the adjourned Consideration of the Matter of the Complaint made to the House upon Thursday last, of the printed Newspaper, intituled, " The Times,

" her 26, 1798" — London: — Printed at the Printing Office, in Printing House Square, Blackfriars, by C. Bell, (Brunswick Street) and published by J. (Salisbury

Square) as containing an Account of the Debates, and misrepresenting the Speeches of some. of the Members of this House, in Contempt of the Orders, and in Breach of the Privilege, of this House.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed. That the said Order be discharged;

The said Motion was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

And the said Complaint was also, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

juckheath A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names Petition? arc thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of Lands and Grounds within the Parish of Rack-heath, in the County of Norfolk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the said Parish, certain Commons and Waste Lands, which, in their present State, are incapable of any considerable Improvement, and that, if the same were divided and inclosed, and specific Allotments made to the several Persons interested therein, they would derive great Advantages therefrom; but that the Notices, as required by the Standing Order? of the House, relative to Bills of Inclosure, have not been given, the Petitioners not having resolved to apply for - any Bill for the Inclosure of the said Commons and Waste Lands until this present Month, and that it will be attended with great Loss to the Petitioners, if Leave be not given to bring in a Bill, for the Purposes ' aforesaid, in this present Session of Parliament: And

therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, and that the Petitioners may have Leave to give such Notices in the present Motiths of January and February next ensuing, or either of them.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine. the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. John Pitt, Sir William Toting, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have' Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Record.

appendant or appurtenant Rights of Common over and upon the Commons and Waste Grounds within the said Parish, and also Owners and Proprietors of certain Lands within such Pacts of the Open Fields called Upton Field and Fishley Crofts, as lie in the Parish of in the said County of Norfolk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the said Parish of Upton, fiindry old inclosed Lands, Open Fields, Half Year Lands, Commons, and Waste Grounds, and also certain Open Fields called Upton Field and Fishley Crofts, which lie partly within the said Parish of Upton, and partly within the adjoining Parish of Fishley, and that the greater Part of the said inclosed Lands is inconveniently situated for the respective Owners thereof, the Lands in the said Open Fields belonging ro the respective Owners thereof lie veiy dispersedly, and the said Half Year Lands, Commons, and Waste Grounds, are frequently overflowed with Water, and, in their present State, yield but little Profit to the several Persons inte-Tested therein; and that it would be advantageous to the several Persons entitled to, and interested in, the Premises, if the said old inclosed Lands, Open Fields, Half Year Lands, Commons, and Waste Grounds, were divided, and specific Parts and Shares thereof allotted to the several Persons entitled to, and interested therein, according to their respective Estates, Rights, and Inte-Tests, -and if such Half Year Lands, Commons, and Waste Grounds, were drained: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes above-mentioned, under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Ord and Mr, _ IVUmot:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to repeal the Duties imposed by an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, for granting an Aid and Contribution for the Prosecution of the War, and to make more effectual Provision for the like Purpose, by granting certain Duties upon Income, in lieu of the said Duties; without any Amendment; And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for exempting, during the present War, certain Persons serving in Volunteer Corps from being ballotted for the Supplementary Militia, under certain Conditions; and for making out new Lists of Men liable to serve in the said Militia; with some Amendments; to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The House proceeded to take the said Amendments into Consideration.

And the said Amendments were read, and are as followeth; viz.

peared to the Committee, that the proposed Improvement would be attended with very important Advantages to the Inhabitants of the said Town; and that it would render the Approaches to the Docks and Quays,. which are already made, and to the additional Works, respecting which an Application has been made to the House in this Session of Parliament, more safe and commodious for the Trade and Commerce of the said Town; and that it was not determined to apply to Parliament until the Time for giving the Notices was expired; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Henry Brown, Esquire, being examined, said. That the Commerce of the said Town has for some Years past progressively and considerably increased, and is likely so to do, and in proportion to such Increase its Populousness has been greatly augmented, and in consequence thereof, a great many new made Streets have been laid out, and Buildings have been erected, and many of the old Streets in the said Town are harrow, dangerous, and inconvenient, and the Levels of many of such new made Streets are improperly and irregularly laid out, and no Common Sewers made through the fame, and also many Windmills, Limekilns, and other Annoyances, areerected too near the Streets and Highways Tn the said Town.

And the Witness further said. That the Pavement and Common Sewers of the Streets, Lanes, and Public Passages, within the said Town, are in many Places kept in bad Repair, and- it would be a great Safety and Convenience, not only to the Inhabitants, but to all Persons resorting thereto, if the said Streets and Public Passages were properly paved, and the said old Streets made wider, more safe, and convenient, and the Levels of such new made, or hereafter to be made, Streets, properly laid out, and Common Sewers made, and the Nuisances and Annoyances removed and prevented.'

A Message by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Usher of the Rogrf Assent

Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's. Commission, for declaring His Royal Afi'ent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Duke of Portland, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

A Petition of: several Persons, whose Names are

thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of Estates within the several Parishes of South Brent and

Lympsham, in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the said Parishes, several Moors, Commons, and Waste Lands, the Property of the Petitioners and others, which, in their present Situation, are incapable of any considerable Improvement; and the Petitioners apprehend it would be very advantageous to them, and to all other Persons interested in the said Lands and Grounds, if the same were divided and inclosed, and specific Allotments made to them, according to their respective Shares, Rights, and Interests therein: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Lands and Grounds, tinder such Regulations as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of Thomas Beji, of in the Parish of

Halejoweit, in the County of , and of Ed-

mund Hall, in the University of Oxford, Clerk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Parish of Halesowen, which lies in the Counties of Salop and Worcester, is very extensive, and the Inhabitants thereof are become so numerous, that the present Vicarage Church is too small to contain them; and that there is, within the said Parish, a Hamlet, or District, called Cradley, situate at a great Distance from the said Church, by reason whereof many of the Inhabitants of the said Hamlet are precluded from attending Public Worship in the said Church; and that the Petitioner, and divers other Persons, by or from voluntary Contributions collected for that Purpose, and by Monies raised and borrowed upon their Security, have crected a Church or Chapel within the said Hamlet of Cradley, and have provided a Cemetery adjoining thereto, and to be used therewith; and that such new Church or Chapel, having, with the Consent of the Vicar of the said Parish, and of the Patron thereof, and of the Bishop of the Diocese, been duly consecrated, is now resorted to by the Inhabitants of the said fbunlet for Public Worship; jand that the Fee Simple and Inheritance of the said Church or Chapel, and Cemetery, was, prior to the Consecration thereof, vested in the Petitioner; and it is expedient that the said Church or Chapel should be made a perpetual Cure and Benefice, and that proper and necessary Rules, Orders, and Regulations, should be established, for the Use, Support, and Management; thereof, and that the Right of Patronage or Presentation of or to the same should be settled and permanently fixed: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making the said Church or Chapel a perpetual Cure or Benefice, and for effectingother the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Secretary D uhdasacquainted the House, That he

had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz,

GEORGER.

His Majesty is persuaded that the unremitting Indus-iry, with which our Enemies perseverc in their avowed Design of effecting the Separation of Ireland from this Kingdom, cannot fail to engage the particular Attention of Parliament, and His Majesty recommends it to this House to consider of the most effectual Means of counteracting, and finally defeating, this Design; and He trusts, that a ReView of all the Circumstances which have recently occurred (joined to the Sentiment of mutual Affect ion and common Interest) will dispose the Parliaments of both Kingdoms to provide, in the Man ner which they shall judge most expedient, for settling such a complete and final Adjustment as may belt tend to improve and perpetuate a Connection, essential for their common Security, and to augment and consolidate the Strength, Power, and Resources, of the British Empire.

R.

Ordered, That His Majesty's said most Gracious Message be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning Ten of the Clock.

A Motion was made, and the Question being pro-pol'ed, That no Measures can have a Tendency to improve and perpetuate the Ties of Amity and Connection now existing between Great Britain and Ireland, which have not for their Basis the manifest, fair, and free Consent and Approbation of the Parliaments of the Two Countries; and that whoever shall endeavour to obtain the Appearance of such Consent and Approbation in either Kingdom, by employing the Influence of Government, for the Purposes of Corruption or Intimidation, is an Enemy to His Majesty, and to the Constitution of His Country.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors, Lessees, and Wharfingers, of certain Quays upon the River 'Thames, in the Port of London, known by the Name and Appellation of The Legal Quays, and of certain Warehouses situate thereon, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Ba-fons. Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London; and Setting forth. That the said Quays were established and legalized, by Acts of Parliament, in the Reigns of Queen Elizabeth and King Charles the Second, and by virtue of certain Royal Commissions, proceeding under the Sanction and Authority of those Acts; and that the said Quays, and the Warehouses situated thereon, are of great Value to the Petitioners, many of whom depend entirely upon the Rents thereof, or the Business transacted at them, f(?r the Support of themselves and Families, and they mull, in many Instances, be brought to Poverty and Ruin, and in all Instances very severely injured, if the Business, which has been carried on there, should be removed from thence to And that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the necessary Consequence will be the Removal of the Trade, either wholly, or in a great Degree, from the said Quays and Warehouses of the Petitioners, and the Places where it has heretofore been carried on under the Authority aforesaid: And that the Petitioners Ancestors and Pre-decefl'ors, and they themselves,' have, from Time to Time, laid out large Sums of Money upon the said Quays, and- in erecting and improving the said Warehouses, in the just and reasonable Expectation that the Trade of the City of London would continue to be carried on as heretofore; and the Petitioners have at all Times used their utmost Endeavours to render the said Quays and Warehouses commodious to the Merchants of the City of London, and to the Persons appointed to conduct and manage the Affairs of the Revenue within the Port of London; and that the said Property, thus established by Law, has become at divers Times, and is now, the SubjeCc of Family Settlements, and other Securities; and the Petitioners can only be rendered secure of a Compensation, for the Loss of their present legal Rights and Interests, by a full, sufficient, and adequate Fund being set apart for their Indemnity, by proper Provisions in the said Bill: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves, their Couufel, Agents, and Witnesses, against such Parts of the said

Vol. 54.

i.

Bill as may affect them, and that Provision may be made therein for indemnifying the Petitioners, and all other Persons, being Owners of, or interested in, the Legal Quays and Warehouses aforesaid, for all such Loss, Damage, and Injury, as they may sustain from the Operation and Consequences of the said Bill, or that the Petitioners may have fudh other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall feetti meet.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are "

thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors, Lessees, and Occupiers of Warehouses, situated in the Vicinity of the Legal Quays of the Port of London, and in various other Parts of the City of London, was also presented to the House, and read: likewise taking Notice of the said Bill j and Setting forth. That the aforesaid Legal Quays have been established for a long Period of Years, by vir- ' tue of certain Royal Commissions, proceeding under the Sanction, and by the Authority, of divers Acts of Parliament; and that the Warehouses of the Petitioners have been erected at a very great Expence in the Vicinity of the said Quays, and in various other Parts of the said City, convenient to the Merchants thereof, in Confidence that Parliament would, at all Times, protect the said Quays, which had been established under its own Sanction, and are occupied principally by Goods and Merchandizes landed upon, or shipped from, the said Quays, and have been, and are not only productive of considerable Profit to the Petitioners, but also of great Convenience and Accommodation to the said Merchants, and all Persons concerned in the Importation and Exportation of Goods, at the said Quays; and that the Petitioners have been, for several Years last, continually erecting new and additional Warehouses for the Accommodation of the Merchants, in order to keep Pace with the Increase of the Commerce of the Port of London; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, and the Business now transacted at the said Quays be removed to Wapping, the Warehouses of the Petitioners, will cease to be wanted by Merchants and others, for the Reception of their Goods, and, consequently, will become useless, the Money expended in the Erection of them will be, in a great Measure, loft, and many of the Petitioners, who depend upon the Rents thereof, or upon the Money received for houseing and keeping Goods therein, for the Support of themselves jmd their Families, will be brought to Poverty and Distress; and that the Petitioners conceive that, in Consideration of their Cafe, as above stated, they are entitled to an adequate Compensation or Indemnification for the Loss and Injury they will sustain by the said Plan being carried into Execution 1 And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Provision may be made in the said Bill for Compensation or Indemnification as aforesaid, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and the first-mentioned Petitioners are to be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

1 Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Parish Church of Saint Margaret, is a very ancient one, and for a great Length of Time, at the lead One Hundred and Fifty Years, has been, and now is, considered by' the Petitioners as the Church peculiarly applicable to the Religious Purposes of this House, and certain Parts of it have always been set apart as appertaining to the Speaker, and other Members thereof; and that the House has usually exercised its Munificence by Grants, from Time to Time, for the Repairs of the said Church, more particularly in the Year 1734, the Sum of £.3,500 being found necessary, on a Survey taken, and Estimate made for repairing the Church, on Application to the House, that Amount was granted, and applied accordingly; and that, in the Progress of those Repairs, other Defects were discovered, and, it being absolutely necessary to remedy them, a further Application was made to the House in the Year 1737, Rating, that the Parish had necessarily exceeded the former Grant of £-3 500 by the Sum of £.1,590. 18 s.5 d. but which had not accomplished all necessary Repairs, and, being unable to raise the AmoUht of that Excels, the House, in the Year 1739, granteditsfurther Aid, to the Extentof£.2,000; and that in the Year 1758, a further Grant of £.4,000 was made by the House, for the Purpose of new pewing and decorating the said Church, and doing other interior Works thereto, but the Roof, and other external Parts thereof, have had no Repairs since the Year 1734, except occasional Repairs thereto, af the Expence of the said Parish; and that the said Church is now in a very , defective State indeed, particularly in its external Parts,

lo much so, that the Petitioners are apprehensive of the most serious Mischiefs; and that the Petitioners have lately had the same thoroughly surveyed and examined by Samuel Pepys Cockerell, an eminent Architect and Surveyor, and in his Judgment the Sum of £.6,721. 18 j. j\d. is necessary to effect the Repairs thereof, allowing therein only the Sum of £.366. ior. for partial Decorations,.as fer as he conceives them fairly and moderately suited to the necessary Repairs of the

Church; and that the said Parish, in consequence of its very heavy Poor's Rate, of late Years greatly increased by additional Poor, particularly the Wives and Children of Soldiers belonging to His Majesty's Regiments of Guards, and other public yet necessary Burthens, is absolutely unable to accomplish the above-mentioned Repairs, and to make a Rate for the Purpose of such Repairs, would manifestly lessen the present decreased Occupation of Houses in the said Parish: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that its usual and munificent Aid on the present urgent Occasion may be granted to the Petitioners, to enable them to effect the Repairs and Purposes before-mentioned.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that t-hCy do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Alan Gardner, Mr.

&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to Committee on resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to King' Mef-consider further of His Majesty's most Gracious Mef- t^IrckndT sage of the 2 2d Day of January last;

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, to consider how far it would be consistent with Justice and Policy, and conducive to the general Interests, and especially to the Consolidation of the Strength of the British Empire, were Civil Incapacities, on Account of Religious Distinctions, to be done away throughout His Majesty's Dominions;

Art Amendment was proposed to be made to the'
