A Petition of the Fish Curers and others, concerned in the Fisheries of Hajlings, Rye, BrightJielmftone, and New Romney, in the Counties of SuJJ'ex and Kent, was presented to the House; and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, it is enacted, that all and every Fiili Curer or Fish Curers shall produce to the Officers of Excise, well and perfectiy cured, all such Fish as he, she, or they, shall have cured, which Fish, being Red Herrings, shall be packed in Barrels of Thirty-two Gallons, for which 65 lbs. of Salt shall be allowed, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity, and that the Petitioners being obliged to pack their Herrings in Barrels, causes them an Expence of £.3. per Last: That, the Herrings cured in the Towns of Hastings, Rye, Brighthelmstone, and New Romney, not being exported or lent Coastwise, as from the great Fisheries of Tarmovth and but for the most

Part retailed to Rippiers and Fruiterers, and by them vended in the different downs and Villages of the Counties of Kent and Sussex, the Expence and Trouble of barrelling them is therefore useless, and prohibitory to the Petitioners carrying on the Trade, and, the Fish for such Consumption not being sufficiently dried to be packed in Barrels, it is injurious to them; and that the Petitioners and others are, by the aforesaid Act, allowed 65 lbs. of Sait to every Barrel containing 800 of full Herrings, but they beg to observe, that 56 lbs. of Salt is sufficient to cure 1000 of full Herrings, and so allow for Walle; and that, by Acts 29 Geo. II. and 26 Geo. III. Scotch Herrings are allowed to be brought into any Port in Great Britain Duty-free, and to be dried and re-fold

without being required to be barrelled, to the great Prejudice of the Fishery and of the Fish Curers of the several afore-mentioned Towns: And therefore praying, That that Part of the Act of the last Session of Parliament, requiring Red Herrings cured to be actually barrelled, may be repealed; at the same Time the Petitioners are willing to submit to any Regulation that may appear necessary to the House for securing the Duty on Salt, either by making Returns on Oath, or otherwise.

Ordered, That tire said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are appointed to enquire into the State of the Herring Fisheries,

and into the most effectual Means fur their Improvement and Extension.

A Petition of sundry Noblemen, Gentlemen, and others, Subscribers to an Institution called The Veterinary College, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, in pursuance of the Plan Hated to the House, in a Petition presented on the 6th of Februr ary 1795, their Exertions have been continued to carry into Elfedl the several beneficial Purposes proposed to be derived from the Establishment of a College for the Study and Practice of Veterinary Science; that for the general Benefit of the Proprietors of Horses, and other valuable Cattle, they have Pleasure in Hating, that Fifty-nine Pupils have passed Examination at the said College, many of whom are now lettled in different Towns of the Kingdom, and are practising the Knowledge they have acquired, to the great Advantage of the Public; and it is with peculiar Satisfaction the Petitioners are enabled to state, that, the Importance of the Institution having been taken into Consideration by I iis Royal Highness; the Commander in Chief, the Propriety of appointing Persons, educated at the College to be Veterinary Surgeons' in the several Regiments of Cavalry, has been determined on, in pursuance of a Report from a Board of General Officers, to whom the Subject had been

referred; and, in consequence of such Decision, Twenty-six Pupils, whose Education has been completed, are engaged in the Service of the Army, and Twenty-eight other Piipi!s are now«pursuing their Studies at the College, several of them intending to fill similar Situations as loon as they shall be deemed duly qualified each of them being subject to the same rigorous Examination of the Medical Committee, and to be certified in the same Manner as has hitherto been practised in respect of the other Pupils of the College: And the Petitioners further state, that, desirous of rendering, to the utmost of their Power, their Institution advantageous to the Public Service, the Colonels' of the different Cavalry Regiments have been invited to fend each a Farrier to the College,- in order to his being taught the Structure; Economy, and different Diseases, of the Horse's Foot, and instructed.in a Mode of Shoeing, tending very materially to its Preservation, and that many Army Farriers have been consequently admitted into the College for Instruction in that particular Part of Veterinary Knowledge; that the College continues under the Direction of the Profelfor, Mr. Coleman, a Gentleman of Talents and Skill, and wdto, by many ulcfui and important Discoveries in the Science, has, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, fully jullified the Expectations formed of its Improvement, from his Exertions; and that the Peti-' tioners have already Hated to the House the Difficulties which have occurred in the Execution of their Plan; and particularly from the embarrassed Slate of their Finances; and, though the Aid so liberally granted by Parliament has, in a great Degree, alleviated their Difficulties, it has yet proved inadequate to remove them entirely, notwithstanding the Petitioners have, with the utmost Frugality, reduced their Annual Expenditure much within the Estimate of the Committee of the House, to whom the former Petition was referred, and within those Limits to which, they are still of Opinion, it would be proper to extend it, in order that the Public may derive the full Benefit of such an Establishment; and the Petitioners have again, with Regret, to state, that (under the heavy. Pressure of Debt, of which an Account is before the House) without further Aid from Parliament, it will be impossible to bring to Perfection an Establishment, which, from the Advantages accruing from the more skilful Care of so important a Branch of Public Property as the Horses of the Army, is become more than ever ah Object of National Importance: And therefore praying. That such Relief may be granted as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the Petitioners are Dealers, to a considerable Extent, in Home-made Spirits, a Line of Business which affords Employment to a great Number of Persons in Scotland, and which, by Means of the annual Licences taken out by them, in their Characters of Dealers, contributes, in no small Degree, to the Sup port of the State; and that it was not until the passing of the Distillery Licence Act in 1786, which went effectually to the Exclusion of Fraud on the Part of the Distillers, that the Proses-fion of a Spirit Dealer in Scotland became in any Shape reputable; prior to that Period, the great Quantities of Spirits manufactured and brought to Market, in an illegal Manner, rendered it the next Thing to an Impossibility for any Dealer in Spirits tp carry on his Business in a fair and lawful Way; it behoved him either to purchase, at inferior Prices, the Spirits which had been illegally made, and to vend the fame, in the Course of his Trade, or to suffer himself to be thrown out of Employment by the numerous Hawkers and Smugglers who travelled the Country, and who, as it was, kept Possession of a great Proportion of the Market; by the frequent Seizures, and other Embarrassments, the confront Attendants on illicit Commerce, no Spirit Dealer in Scotland, (with a very few Exceptions) was at this Period successful in Business, their Gains were precarious, and their Credits suspicious and doubtfulj but since the Introduction of the System of Licence upon the Distillery, Hawking and Smuggling have been annihilated. Spirit Dealers have been left in the natural Pursuit of an honest Profession, and thus has their Business become equally respectable, and their Credit, in the Scale of Merchants, equally high with any other Class of Commercial Men; it is with sincere Regret, therefore, the Petitioners take the Liberty to Rate, that, since the passing of the Distillery Act of last Session of Parliament, imposing a Duty of One Shilling per Gallon on all Spirits manufactured by Distillers, in Addition to the Licence Duty, the Evils, formerly felt by the Spirit Dealers, have been, in a great Measure, revived; the Quantities of Spirits, to which this Duty is to attach, are ascertained in so loose and uncertain a Manner, that the Distillers find no Difficulty in fending to Market large Quantities of Spirits, without Payment of the Duty, which, indeed, must be ever the Cafe, more or less, where there is no other Check than the Survey of an Officer of Excisej hence Hawkers and Smugglers have returned to their former Occupations, and thus are the natural Customers of the Petitioners supplied with Spirits from the old Sources: As the Consequences of this must be ruinous to the Petitioners, and as the Subject of the Distillery Laws is soon again to be resumed by the House, the Petitioners therefore pray the House to consider the Premises, and to cnaft such Regulations as will effectually prevent the Smuggling and Hawking of Home-made Spirits, or otherwise to make such Provision, for the Protection and Security of the Petitioners, as the House shall think meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

and that the Petitioners have derived very considerable Emoluments asTradefmen, as well as by Dock Charges, from the Reception of Ships and Vessels into their laid Docks at Rotkerhithe and Blackwall, Ship Owners having found it advantageous to resort to the Petitioners, because equal Accommodation in the Port of London was not to be met with elsewhere) and that the Expectation of a long Continuance of such Advantages, was the great Inducement with the Petitioner, John Perry, for engaging in such an hazardous Undertaking; and that the said Wet Docks are not only of the utmost Consequence, and of very great Value to the Petitioners, but, as they conceive, of great Public Utility, in as much as they have tended to lessen, in no small Degree, such Evils as are proposed to be remedied by the said Bill; and that, if the said Bill shall pass into a Law, in its present State, it will be ruinous in its Consequences to the Interests of the Petitioners, by materially reducing the Number of Ships frequenting their said Docks, as it will be wholly impossible for them to withstand the Influence of a Body so powerful and opulent, as the Persons engaged in the Undertaking intended to be carried into Effect by the said Bill, whereby the Petitioners will be deprived of that Part of their general Trade as Shipbuilders, which arises from, and is dependant thereon; and that, although the Petitioners apprehend the most serious Injuries to their Property and Interest, from the Adoption of the Plan proposed in the said Bill, yet, at the same Time that they leek Redress of their Grievances, they do not wish to impede a Public Benefit by any undue Expectations, being willing to dif pose of their said Docks, or either of them; A Petition of the President and Members of the Board of Agriculture, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty rs Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to- the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That, His Majesty having been graciously pleased, in consequence of an Address from the House, to constitute, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal, a Board of Agriculture, for promoting the internal Improvement of the Country, the Petition-, ers have much Satisfaction in acquainting the House, that the important Purposes intended by that Institution are carrying on, and are likely to be attended, with very beneficial Effects to the.Public: And there-, fore praying, That they may be- supported by a further Grant for the present Year.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Proprietors of Estates within the Parish of Cin the County of Herts, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the said Parish, several Open and Common Fields, and Common Lammas Meadows, containing together 1,555 Acres, or thereabouts, and also a certain Common called Cheshunt Common, containing 1,186 Acres, or thereabouts, all which may be greatly improved in Value, if divided into specific Al- . lotments, according to each Person's Right and Interest therein, and if the same were inclosed; and that there are, within the said Parish, several Messuages, Tenements, and old inclosed Lands, containing 5,375 Acres, or thereabouts, belonging to various Persons having Right of Common in and over the said Lands and Grounds: And therefore praying. Ordered, That Mr. William Adams do make the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lords and Ladies of the Manor of Brixham, in the County of Devon, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred.

Mr. William Adams accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place) and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Samuel Tozer, being examined, said. That there is an

ancient Harbour, Pier, or Quay, at Brixham Quay, with in and Part of the said Manor, and that a very considerable Fishery hath long been established there, and hath, of late Years, been increased in a great Degree; that the said Harbour, Pier, or Quay, is much injured by Time and Tempests, and is not sufficiently large to serve the necessary Purposes of the Fishermen there; and the Tolls and Duties received from Vessels belonging to, or frequenting the said Harbour, are so small, that the said Harbour, Pier, or Quay, cannot be kept in Repair out of the Produce thereof. And being further examined, he said. That there is, and hath been, an ancient Market at Brixham Quay aforesaid, but that there is no convenient Place for holding the fame; and that the -Population of Brixham hath of late increased so considerably, that a regular Market will be of great Utility to the Inhabitants of the said Place, and to the Public in general.

Mr. Arthur Farwell confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Lords of the Manor of Brixham, in the County of Devon, to repair and enlarge, or rebuild, the Pier or Quay at Brixham Quay, within the said Manor, to improve the Harbour there, to regulate the Moorings of Vessels therein, and to establish a Market there: And that. Mr. William Adams and the Lord Arden do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

John Davidson, Esquire, being examined, said, That

in pursuance of the said Act, the Commissioners thereby- appointed divided and allotted the said Tract of Waste Land, and have let out several Roads through or over the fame; but the Commissioners were not, by the said Act, authorized to ascertain what Parts of the said Roads were to be amended and kept in Repair by the respective Townships wherein the said Aloor or Waste Land was situate, or to which Allotments of the said Waste Lands were set out, and therefore Doubts and Disputes have arisen touching the fame, and that the said Act is in other Respects defective.

And the Witness added. That the said Doubts and Disputes cannot bo obviated or settled, or the said Act rendered effectual, without the Authority of Parliament.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, being desirous of tnaking competerit Provisions for the honourable Support and Maintenance of His dearly beloved Sons, Prince Edward, and Prince ErneJl Augustus, which the Monies applicable to the Purposes of His Majesty's Civil Government would be insufficient to defray; and being also desirous of being enabled to extend to His beloved Daughter, the Princess Amelia, the Provision which He has been enabjed to make out of the Hereditary Revenue for the other Branches of His Royal Family; desires the Alii fiance of -Parliament for this Purpose; and His Majesty relies on the Affection of His faithful Commons, that they will make such Provision as the Circumstances of the same may appear to require.

G. R.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Petition of thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors, Lessees, and ^oTware- Occupiers, of Warehouses, situated in the Vicinity of boufts, neaimt the Legal QuayS of the Port of London, and in various London Peck other Parts of the City of London, was presented to the 1 6 House,

'by

39 Geo. III. 1i° Martii. 299

House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London; and Setting forth, That the aforesaid Legal Quays have been -established for a long Period of Years, by virtue of certain Royal Commissions, proceeding under the Sanction, and by the Authority, of divers Acts of Parliament; and that the Warehouses of the Petitioners have been erected at a very great Expence in the Vicinity of the said Quays, and in various other Parts of the said City, convenient to the Merchants thereof, in Confidence that Parliament would, at all Times, protect the said Quays', which had been established under its own Sanction, and are occupied principally by Goods apd Merchandize landed upon, or shipped from, the said Quays, and have been and are not only productive q£ considerable Profit to the Petitioners, but also of great Convenience and Accommodation to the said Merchants, and all Persons concerned in the Importation and.Exportation of Goods at the said Quays; and that the Petitioners have been, for several Years last, continually erecting new and additional Warehouses for the Accommodation of the Merchants, in order to keep Pace with the Increase of the Commerce of the Port of London; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, and the Business now transacted at the said Quays be removed to Wapping, the Warehouses of the Petitioners will cease to be wanted by Merchants and others for the Reception of their Goods, and consequently will become useless, the Money expended in the Erection of . them will be in a great Measure loft, and many of the Petitioners, who depend upon the Rents thereof, or upon the Money received for Housing and keeping Goods therein, for the Support of themselves and their Families, will be brought to Poverty and Distress; and that some of the Petitioners have already presented a Petition to the House, dating the Mischiefs which they apprehend will arise to them from the Operation of the said Bill, and soliciting that Provision may be made therein for their Security and Indemnification, but that the Petitioners now find it to be expedient that they should be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect their Rights, Interests, and Property, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now (lands: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against such Parts of the said Bill' as may affect them, and‘that Provision may be made therein for the Security and Indemnification of the Petitioners, and all other Persons being Proprietors, Lessees, and Occupiers, of Warehouses situated as aforesaid, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Your Committee have proceeded to an Examination of the Matters referred to them, and they beg Leave to present to the House the following Statements; containing — -I. First, An Enumeration of all the Public General Laws which have expired withinTwelve Months preceding the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament, which by Retrospect includes all which have expired since 20th November 1797: — II. Secondly,

An Enumeration of all those which are about to expire within Twelve Months subsequent to the Commencement of the present Session, or in the Course of the pext Session, or at the End thereof, in which it is thought proper to include, prospectively, all which may expire before the 24th of June 1S00; distinguishing such of the said Expired or Expiring Laws as have been revived, continued, cr made perpetual by any Act or Acts of the present Session of Parliament: — III. And,

Thirdly, They have thought proper to subjoin a further Enumeration of some Statutes whereof the Duration is temporary, but uncertain, depending upon contingent Circumstances, such as the Continuance of lives, Char-, ters, the Laws of other Countries, Treaties with Foreign Powers, Hostilities, &c.; conceiving it to be also necessary that these Laws should be brought within the View of the House, in order that it may be enabled more distinctly to foresee and provide for any of the Exigencies which may arise upon their Termination,

Mr. William Tates, being examined, said. That the beneficial Purposes of the said Act has hitherto been frustrated, and cannot be carried into Execution, unless the said Act be amended, altered, and rendered more effectual; or new, and more extensive Powers be granted for that Purpose; that the Inhabitants of the said Town, as well as the Seamen in the Port of Liverpool, are at present subject to great Inconvenience and Expence, by the Want of a sufficient Supply of wholesome fresh Water; that the Springs of Bootle would afford a very desirable Supply of pure and wholesome Water, for the said Town and Port.

And the Witness further said, That the Petitioners are the Proprietors of, or interested in, the said Water Springs, and they are desirous, at their own Expence, of conveying the same into, and through, the several Streets of the said Town, for the Use of the Inhabitants thereof, and the Ships and other Vessels frequenting the said Port, which will be of great Convenience to the Public.

That an Act was passed in the Thirty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for dividing, allotting, inclosing, draining, embanking, and improving, the Open and Common Fields, Ings, Meadows, Pastures, and other Commonable Lands an4 Waste Grounds, Vo 1. 54.

within the several Townships of Morton, Walkeritk, East Stockwith, Bliton, Wharton,.Pilham, and Gilby, in the several Parishes of Gainsburgh, Bliton, and Pilham, in the County of Lincoln; and that, by the said Act, it is provided and enacted, that, immediately after a certain Plot or Parcel of Land therein mentioned shall have been, in the Judgment of the Commissioners appointed for executing the said Act, sufficiently improved by Flooding and Warping, they the said Commissioners shall set out and allot a Part of the said Common called Morton Carr, not exceeding 400 Acres in the Whole, in order by Sale to raise a Sum of Money for or towards paying the Charges and Expences of obtaining and passing the Act, anti <?f executing the fame, so far only as all such Charges and Expences Ihguld relate to or concern the said Common called Morton Cart", and it was also provided, that, in case the Money arising by the Sale of such Allotment, should not be tuliicient to defray the Expences aforesaid, then that such Deficiency should be made up by the several Persons interested in the said Common called Morton Carr, in the Manner directed by the said Act; and that, according to the Provssions of the said Act, as above stated, it is necessary that the Sale of the said Portion of Land, or so much thereof as should be necessary, must be had and made before any Rate can be made on the Owners or Proprietors of the said Carr, but it has been found impracticable to fell the said Portion of Land, whereby the further Execution of the said Act is flopped, and all the Improvements expected to arise therefrom are suspended, and must so remain, unless Power is given to the Commissioners to lay and collect, by Way of Rate, on the Owners and Proprietors of the said Carr, such Sums of Money as may be necessary for fully executing the Powers of the said Act, without waiting until the said Allotment shall be actually fold; and that it is also by the said Act expressly directed, that tVhen and so loon as the Works of Drainage and Warping, thereby directed to be done, should be executed, and the said Carr should, in the Judgment of the said Commissioners, be sufficiently improved, the said Carr should be divided and allotted, but that, in all Events, such Division and Allotments should be made before the Expiration of Five Years from the Time of passing the said Act; and that, from the various Impediments and Delays that have arilen in carrying the said Act into Execution, it appears manifestly that the said Carr cannot be put into such a State of Improvement, as that a Division and Allotment thereof can, with Propriety, be made amongst the several Owners and Proprietors thereof, and Persons interested therein, within the Time so limited as aforesaid, and it is therefore necessary that the Term for making such Division and Allotment should be extended; and that the Necessity of applying to Parliament for an Amendment of the said Act, in the particular Instancesabove-mentioned, was not ascertained, until a Meeting of the Proprietors of, and Persons interested in, the said Carr, which was held on Thursday the 28th Day of February last, being after the Time limited by the House for receiving Petitions for Private Bills; and that, for the Reasons above mentioned, the Improvement of a Tract of 4,000 Acres of valuable Land must be delayed, without the further Aid of Parliament, and, unless it shall please the House to receive a Petition for that Purpose, notwithstanding the Time limited for receiving Petitions for Private Bills is elapsed, great Loss must accrue to the Proprietors of the said Carr: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to exhibit a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill to explain, amend, and enlarge, and render more effectual, the Powers of the said Act, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Owners and Proprietors of Land in the said Open Common Pasture called Morton.

Mr. Tyrwhittreported from the Committee, to whom

the Petition of William Taylor, of the Haymarket, Esquire, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Paving Bills, had not been complied with, because the Whole of the Premises, intended to be taken for making the Openings and Improvements mentioned in the Petition, being the Property of His Majesty, it was expedient that the Permission of the Crown Oilicers to proceed should be obtained, before any Steps preparatory to an Application to Parliament could be taken, and that such Permission was not obtained till the Time appointed for giving the said Notices was elapsed; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations-of the said Petition, Mr. Vincent Frederick, being examined, said, That the Street called Pall Mall, is one of the principal Approaches to Saint James's Palace, from the Eastern Parts of the Metropolis, and is a very great Thoroughfare, but that the East End thereof is not so wide as the other Parts of the Street, by which Means Obstructions and Inconveniencies frequently occur in that Part, and more particularly on the Nights of Performance at the Opera House, to which it nearly adjoins. And being further examined, he said, That, if the said East End of Pall Mall, from the Haymarket aforesaid to Market Lane, were widened, and a new Street were made and opened from the said Haymarket into Charles Street, leading to Saint James's Square, it would be a very great Convenience to the Public in general, and would also be a great Convenience and Accommodation to the Nobility and Gentry, and all others resorting to the said Theatre, by rendering the Access thereto more easy and commodious, and would also tend to their Safety, by making the said Theatre more secure from Fire, and would, as he conceives, tend very materially to increase the Value of the circumjacent Houses, and other Property.

Mr. Frederick Waljh, confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

have long suffered from the exorbitant Charges made by . HAVE proceeded, in obedience to the Orders of the House, to the Consideration of the Matters referred to them.

The System thus established, gradually acquired the Means of disturbing the Tranquillity of the Country in all its Parts; of impeding the Execution of Justice, by forcible Resistance to the Authority of the Laws; by the Protection of accused Persons; by the Rescue of Prisoners; the Seizure of Arms; and, at length, by the Assassination of Informers, of Witrtcfifes, of Magistrates, and of Jurymen; till, by the general Terror which was diddled, the loyal Inhabitants in different Counties were successively driven into the Towns, or compelled v'holly to quit the Kingdom. At the Head of this extensive Conspiracy was placed a Committee; terming itself ‘ An Executive Diredfory,' extending its Influence and Power, over the Disaffected, through every Part of the Kingdom, by Provincial and Baronial Committees;' through whom, and by the Million of itinerant Delegates over the Country, an universal Correspondence was established, between this Executive Directory and all the subordinate Powers and Members of this System. An Intercourse was maintained, in the Name of the Whole, with Individuals and Societies in this Country, as well as with the Governments of His Majesty's Enemies; and the Conspirators were thus enabled to conceal, or dilplay, their Numbers at will; and, conle-questly, to magnify their Power, or to hide their Weak-ness; to circulate, with Rapidity and Effect, the most atrocious Calumnies against His Majesty's Person and Government, and against all Descriptions and Bodies of Men, whom they thought it their Interest to vilify; to raise Contributions, extorted frequently even from those who had not become Members of their Union; to procure, dnperfe, and conceal Arms, Ammunition, and Artillery; tocolledt Military Information; and, finally, to raile an Army, formed of all, those among them capable of bearing Arms, and placed under the Command of Officers, in Military Divisions corresponding with those established for the general Purposes of the Conspiracy.

It is material to state, in Detail, the Formation of the different Branches of this System, in order to compare it with the Institutions of a similar Nature, which have been since formed in Great Britain, and which will be hereafter mentioned. Each of the inferior Societies consisted, according to their original Institution, of Thirty-six Members; which Number was afterwards reduced to Twelve. These Twelve chose a Secretary and Treasurer; and the Secretaries of Five of these Societies formed what was called A Lower Baronial Committee;' which had the immediate Direction and Superintendance of those Five Societies. From each Lower Baronial Committee, thus constituted, One Member was delegated to an ‘ Upper Baronial Committee ;' which, in like Manner, assumed and exercised the Superintendance and Direction of the Lower Baronial Committees in the respective Counties. The next Superior Committees were, in populous Towns, distinguished by the Name of District Committees,' and in Counties, by the Name of County Committees;' and were composed of Members delegated by the Upper Baronial Committees, each Upper Baronial Committee delegating one of its Members to the District or County Committee; and the District or County Committees had the Superrntendance and Dire ft ion of the Upper Baronial Committees. Having thus ‘ organized ' (as it is termed) the several Counties and populous Towns, a Committee, called A Subordinate Directory,' was

erected in each of the Four Provinces of Jler, Munster, and' Connaught, composed of Two Mem-

bers or Three, according to the Extent and Population of the Districts which they represented; who were delegated to a Provincial Committee, which held the immediate Direction and Superintendance of the several County and District Committees in each of the Four Provinces; and a General Executive Directory,' composed of Five Persons, was elected by the Provincial Directories; but the Election of this Directory was so managed, that none but the Secretaries of the Provincial Directories knew on whom the Election fell. It was made by Ballot, but not reported to the Electors; the Appointment was notified only to those on whom the Election devolved; and the Executive Directory, thus composed, assumed and exercised the supreme and un-controuled Command of the whole Body of the Union, which, by these secret Modes of Election, was kept utterly ignorant who were the Persons to whom this implicit Obedience was paid.

§ 2.

Infiitutimi of United Irishmenin 1791; and Rife of different Societies in Great Britain.

For the Purpose of obtaining a comprehensive View of the Attempts which have been repeatedly made, in the Course of the last Eight Years, for establishing a similar System in this Country, and of the Means by which they have been hitherto defeated, as well as in order to enable the House to judge fully of the Perfe-verance with which the System is purlued, and of the Nature and Tendency of the Measures which are carrying on at the present Moment, Your Committee deem it necessary, before they advert to more recent Transactions, to go back to that Period, when Societies of this Tendency first appeared in both Kingdoms, and to trace, as shortly as they can, their Progress and Intercourse to the present Time.

The Society of United , was established in

the Year 1791; and other Societies in Great Britain, particularly The Constitutional Society (which had long existed, but about this Time assumed a new Character) The Corresponding Society (which was instituted in the Spring of 1792) and the Societies of Persons in Scotland terming themselves ‘the Friends of the People,' (which originated at nearly the farhe Period) appear to have adopted, in their fullest Extent, all the extravagant and violent Principles of the French Resolution. The Events which followed, in the Course of that Year and the Year 1792, encouraged among the leading Members of these Societies, and other Persons of similar Principles, a sanguine Hope of introducing, into both Countries (under Pretence of the Reform of Abuses) what they termed, a new Order of Things,' founded on the Principles of that Resolution. The Degree of Bigotry and Enthusiasm with which they attached themselves to these Principles, was manifested, as well by the Speeches and Writings of the Members of the Societies, as by the Zeal with which they laboured to propagate, among the Lower Clafies of the Community, a Spirit of Hatred and Contempt, for the existing Laws and Government of the Country.

It can hardly be necessary to recall to the Rccolleftion of the House, the Industry with which they endeavoured to disseminate these Sentiments, by the Circulation of their own Proceedings and Resolutions; uniformly directed to vilify the Forms and Principles of the British Constitution; to represent the People of this Country as groaning under intolerable Oppression; to eradicate

all religious Principle; and to recommend a Recurrence to Experiments of desperate Innovation, similar to those which were at that Time adopted in France. For the same Purposefthe Works cf Paine, and other seditious and impious Publications, were distributed, throughout almost every Part of the Kingdom, with an Activity and Prefufun beyond all former Example.

So confident were the Societies of the Efficacy of these Measures, that they appear almost universaliy to have looked forward from the Beginning, to the entire Overthrow of every existing Establishment in these Kingdoms, and to the Creation of some democratical Form of Government; either by uniting the Whole of the British Empire into One Republic, or by dividing it into Two or more Republics. The Conspirators in Ireland, unquestionably, always meditated the complete Separation of that C juntry from Great Britain: All, however, considered themselves as engaged in one common Cause, as far as related to the Destruction of the existing Constitution; all looked to the Success of the Disaffected in each Country as forwarding their common Views; and each was ready to support the other in any Resistance to the lawful Government; a frequent Intercourse among them was therefore considered as important to their Ends; and they all invited, or expected, the-Countenance and Aid of France.

The Attempts made in the Beginning of this Conspiracy, to dil'guise the real Objects under false Pretences, which ought at no Time to have imposed even onfuper-ficial Observers, have long since been abandoned. Sub-lequent Transactions have not merely shewn the Extremes to which the Nature and Principles of these Societies naturally led, but have completely unveiled the original and settled Designs of the Persons chiefly concerned in them. Your Committee beg Leave, in this Place, to refer the House to His Majesty's Proclamation of the Year 1792, and the several Addresses of both Houses of Parliament thereupon; to the Reports of the Committees of Parliament in this Kingdom and in Ireland; and to the different Trials for Treason and Sedition in both Kingdoms. And they are confident, that an attentive Examination of those Documents can leave no Doubt in the Opinion of the House (even on the Circumstances known at that early Period) respecting the real Nature and Extent of the original Conspiracy.

Attempts to assemble a Convention of the People in *

The leading English Societies, which have been already stated to have lent Delegates to the Scotch Convention, had, during its Sittings, and for a considerable Time previous thereto, been actively employed in Measures directed to similar Objects. For the Purpose of . promoting their Seditious Projects, they had carried on a constant Correspondence with all the numerous Country Societies, which had been formed in many populous Towns in different Parts of the Kingdom. They had, Correspond-as early as in May 1792, presented an Address, suffi- HiiiVocicuf ciently expressive of their Principles, to those whom with France, they styled, " The Friends of the Constitution at 'Paris,

" known by the Name of Jacobins." In the End of the same Year, after receiving a Letter of Approbation from Persons calling themselves " Friends of Liberty and " Equality in France," they instituted a regular Committee of Foreign Correspondence; and they had even proceeded to present Adresses to the National Convention in France, which had then assumed the whole legislative and executive Power, and was assembled for the Purpose of framing a new Constitution, and proceeding to the Trial of the King. In one of these Addresses, particularly noticed in the Report of 1 794, but ' which Your Committee think it material again to advert to, they styled the Convention, " Servants of a " Sovereign People, and Benefactors of Mankind."

They rejoice that the Resolution had arrived at that Point of Perfection, which enabled them to address them by such a Title. They extol the Proceedings of the 10th of August as a glorious Victory; and add,

" The Benefits will in Part be ours, but the Glory will " be all your own; and it is the Reward of your Perseverance, the Prize of Virtue." In January following, at the Eve of the Murder of the French King, and of the Commencement of Hostilities against this Country, Barrere, Roland, and St. Andre, active Members of the French Convention, had been defied Honorary Members of the Constitutional Society: And Two Speeches made by Barrere and St. , delivered for the express Purpose of accelerating the Condemnation and Execution of the King, alierting the Doctrines of the Sovereignty of the People, and deducing, as its Consequence, the unlimited Rights of a National Convention, and the personal Responsibility of the Monarch, were entered on the Books of the Constitutional Society; and the Resolution for this Purpose was publillied in the Newspapers. Afluated by these Principles, the English Societies persevered in their Design; and notwithstanding the Dispersion of the Meeting at Edinburgh, which had assumed the Appellation of " The " British Convention," proceeded on a Plan, which they ‘ had long had in Contemplation, for assembling, in England, a similar but more extensive Meeting, under the Appellation of " A Convention of the People."

At a General Meeting of the Corresponding Society, Address from held at the Globe Tavern, on the 20th January 1794, a Resolution and Address to the People of England were „uary 1794. agreed to, and ordered to be published; expressly directed to the Object of assembling a General Convention of the People.

At another General Meeting of the same Society, held Meeting at at Chalk Farm, on the 14th of April 1794, among a Variety of inflammatory Resolutions, they declared, 1794. that the whole Proceedings of the late British Convention at Edinburgh, claimed their Approbation and Applause. The Invasion of Ireland, which was attempted in December 1796, was arranged at an Interview which took place on the Frontier of France between Lord Edward Fitzgerald, Arthur O'and General Hoche, in the Summer of that Year. After the Failure of this Attempt, the Solicitations of the Irish Directory were renewed; a Proposal, which arrived from France early in 1797, was accepted, and an Answer transmitted, through England, by the Means of Arthur nor; Lewins was dispatched to Paris in April, and

McNevin in June. Both were employed in urging the Invasion of Ireland; and in counteracting the Nego-ciation for Peace with the French Republic; which His Majesty's MiniHer was then carrying on at Lijle. A Conference was held in the same Summer, in London, between Lord Edward Fitzgerald and a French Agent who came from Hamburgh, in which further Arrangements were made for the intended Invasion.

The ArreH of several Persons in Ireland, and the Flight of others; and the memorable Defeat, by Lord Duncan, of the Fleet intended to protect the Expedition fitted out from Holland, again disconcerted the Projects of the Conspirators. After this Event, the French Government appears to have repeatedly urged the Leaders of the Irijli Union to immediate Insurrection; but the more cautious amongH them were unwilling to act, until the French should actually have landed; and their Opinion for a Time prevailed.

The Correspondence was in the mean Time continued: The Projects of Rebellion and Invasion were ripening; and at this Period the Hopes of the Irish Conspirators derived fresh Encouragement from Reports of the Progress of new Societies in Great Britain, formed on the same Plan with themselves. A regular Communication was kept up between the Irish and English Committees, through Arthur O'Connor, who

had come from Ireland to England early in January 1798; and in the Reports transmitted by the English Societies to Ireland, the Force of the United Englishmen (a Society which had been recently formed on the Model of the United Irish, and of which a more particular Account will be given hereafter) was represented to be considerable, though Your Committee have Reason to believe that there was much Exaggeration in these Reports. Arthur O'Connor , in a Letter to his Bro-

ther, dated London, 13th February 1798, and seized'in Lord Edward Fitzgerald's Apartments at Hates, " that Scotland is Irish all over; that the People " here give no Opinion, though it is easy to learn " they look for a Change."

Three Delegates had " been sent from the United Britons to the Irish National Committee, and from that Moment the Irish " were to consider England, Scotland, and Ireland, all " as One People, acting for one common Cause." An Address was at the same Time produced, which it was Hated the Delegates of Britain had brought with them to the Irish National Committee. It was also Hated, that the PricH O'Coigly was one of the Delegates mentioned to have been then lately returned from France; and it was added, that he, and another PrieH who had fled from Ireland, were the principal Persons who had opened the Communication with the United Britons.

At another Provincial Meeting, held on the 27th February 1798, it appears to have been Hated, " that a " Delegate had arrived from France; that the French u were using every Endeavour to have the Expedition " for Ireland completed; and that the Delegate came Home to cause the United Irish to put themselves into a State of Organization to join them, as " the Directory positively assured the Irish Delegates, " that the Expedition would set out for Ireland the " End of April, or the Beginning of May." It was also Hated, that there had been a Meeting of all the Delegates in England and Scotland held in London; but that their Resolutions could not be obtained till the next Provincial Meeting, to be held on the 25th of March.

Further Intercourse between the United Jrijhmen, the French Government, and the British Societies; Formation of new Societies, and their Proceedings.

At the Meetings of the London Corresponding Society, for above Two Years before this Time, it had been avowed, that the Object of the Society was to form a Republic, by the Assistance of France. Reform in Parliament, or even Annual Elections, or Universal Suffrage, were therefore no longer mentioned. Your Committee have abundant Reason to believe, from the Information laid before them, that a Person of the Name of Ashley(one of the Persons arrested in 1794)

and who had, for a long Time, been Secretary to this Society, was now ailing as their Agent at Paris, ^nd had recently given them hopes of the Succour of a French Army. Meetings were held, to contrive the Means of procuring Arms, to enable them to cooperate with a French Force, in case of an fnvafion. The leading Members of the disaffected Societies were also in the Habit of frequenting an Occasional Meeting, which was held at a Cellar in FurnivaPs , and was first formed for the Purpose of reading the libellous and treasonable Publication, called " The Press." This Place gradually became the Resort of all those who were engaged the most deeply in the Conspiracy. It was particularly attended by Arthur O'Connor and

O' Coigly, previous to their Attempt to go over to France; and' by the Persons chiefly instrumental in . carrying oil Correspondence with the Irish Conspirators; and Secret Consultations were repeatedly held there, with a View to Projects, which were thought too dangerous and desperate to be brought forward in any of the larger Societies. Among these Plans, was that of effecting a general Insurrection, at the same Moment, in the Metropolis and throughout the Country, and of directing it to the Object of seizing or affaffmating the King, the Royal Family, and many of the Members of both Houses of Parliament. Ah Officer, of some Experience in His Majesty's Service, was selected as their Military Leader; and fangiiine hopes were entertained, that they could command a fuflkient Force to effect their desperate Purpose, in the first Instance, by Surprize. But although the Apprehension that they could not as yet collect sufficient Numbers to maintain and secure their Advantage, appears, for the Time, to have deterred them from the Attempt; yet the general Language held Vot. 54.

among these Persons, at this Period, proved, that they Report from had brought themselves to the Opinion that Matters were nearly ripe for Measures of open Violence.

Attempts were at the same Time made to form in London, upon the Plan of the United the

Society of United Englishmen, or United Britons-, before referred to: And O'Coigly and John Binns, appear to have been leading Persons in that Design. It was proposed to divide this Society into Four Districts, including a large Part of the Coasts of this Kingdom the most exposed to Invasion: And it was also in Contem- plation to combine the Operations of this Society with those of a Society of United Irishme; of which Your Committee will find it necessary separately to take Notice.

Most of the Societies through England, which had used to correspond with the London Corresponding Society, had also about this Time adopted the same Plan of forming Societies of United Englishmen; and finding their Communications by Writing to be hazardous, they avoided, as far as possible, the keeping any Papers; used Cyphers, or mysterious Words, in the few Writings that passed between them, and principally carried on their Intercourse by Agents, who went from Place to Place, and were recognized by Signs, which were frequently changed. Many ignorant or incon-fiderate Persons, throughout the Country, were gradually involved in these Criminal Tran factions: And the Influence of the destrudive Principles from which they proceeded, was still further extended by the Establishment of Clubs, among the lowed Classes of the Community, which were open to all Persons paying One Penny, and in which Songs were sung, Toads given, and Language held, of the most seditious Nature.

And this System was so construded, as to aamit of still further Subdivision, if the Increase of Numbers had been such as the Leaders hoped.

The Accounts which have been obtained of his Conversation and Conduct at Manchester, leave no Room to doubt the Objects of his different Journies between Great Britain, Ireland, and France, and particularly of his intended Journey to France, which was prevented by his Arred, and there appears also little Reason to doubt, that.many, both of the United Englishmen and United at

and in its Neighbourhood, were aware, of the general Purport at lead, of his Million, and anxiously expected that Affidance from France, of which they received, from him, very drong Assurances.

The Society at Manchester seems to have been the central Society of an extensive District; and to have been managed by a very zealous and active Committee.

It frequently sent Delegates to Places in the Neighbourhood, and to various Parts of

Nottinghamshire, and Cheshire. Their Correspondence appears to have extended to the most distant Parts of England, as well as to Edinburgh and Glajgozv.

Liverpool also became the Seat cf another central Society, presiding over ajurremnding District, and corresponding with other Parts of England, and with Scotland and Ireland; and different Emissaries, some of whom were Foreigners, about this Time were sent through various Parts of the Kingdom, for the Purpose of ascertaining the Numbers and Dispositions of the Societies of United English and United Irish.

Whild the Societies in England were thus endeavour- Society of ing to form a Society of United Englishmen, or of United Scotf‘ Britons, on the Model of the Irish Society, Attempts were made in Scotland to form adidindt Society of United Scotsmen' on the same Plan. And Your Committee cannot forbear to remark the Industry with which it has been attempted in this Indance, as well as in others, to separate Scotland as well as Ireland from England, and to found, on the Ruins of the established Government,

Three didindt Republics of England, Scotland, and Ireland.

The Attempts to form a Society of United Scotsmen had made little Progress till the Spring of 1797; but from the Month of April 1797 until November following (when a Discovery was made in the County of on which George Mealm'aker was brought to Trial, and convicted of Sedition) these Attempts appeal- to have been attended with more Success, and particularly in the Neighbourhood of Glasgow, and in the Counties of Ayr, Renfrew,

Lancrk, Dumbarton, Fife, and Perth. and the County of Ayr, were the Places in which this Spirit fird manifeded itself, and from which Emissaries were sent, into different Parts of the Country, for the Purpose of increasing the Numbers of the Society, and diffeminating what they termed, ‘ Political Knowledge.'

The Societies thus formed in Scotland, appear to have been reduced to a Sydem almod as regular and complete as that which was established in Ireland; the Outlines of the Plan were the fame, and the dudied Secrecy of the Proceedings, and the' Gradations of internal Arrangement, formed its great idic.

By a general Rule of their Association, no Society was to confid of more than Sixteen Members, and when any Society had obtained a Number of Members exceeding Sixteen, it was to divide itself into Two Societies. In some small Towns there were Three or more such Societies, all of wffiich were sometimes assembled, by their individual Members, or by a Committee from each Society j and such Assemb'ies were termed Parochial Meetings.' Each of these Parochial Meetings had a Secretary, who was also Trcal'urer; and One or

Two

19

Two Delegates were chosen to represent the Parochial at the County Meeting, which was composed of Delegates from all the Parochial Meetings within the County or District, and was held every Six Weeks. The Delegates were elected by Ballot; but the Ballot was so conducted, that no Person knew on whom the Choice fell, except the Secretary and the Person cholen. This Election was sometimes made, by each Member whispering in the Ear of the Secretary the Name of the Person for whom he gave his Vote; and as there could be no material Check on the Declaration of the Secretary, it is evident that the Election of Delegates might be managed in any Manner most agreeable to the Leaders of the Society. The Meetings called County Meetings' were not restricted to the known Divisions of the Counties, but were composed of Delegates from Parochial Meetings, within either larger or smaller Districts, according to the Number of United Scotfmcn in each Neighbourhood. At the County Meetings, Delegates were elected, to represent the Societies at a National Meeting,' in the same secret Manner as w'as used for the Election of the Delegates to the County Meetings; and the Place of that Meeting w'as not generally disclosed. The Secretary of the County Meeting gave the Delegate, when chosen, a small Slip of Paper, containing the Name of a Person to whom he was to apply, and who was to take him to the Place of the National Meeting. This Person was called The Intermediate.' The Counties also were distinguished by Numbers, and not by their Names; and the Delegate received, on another Slip of Paper, the Number of his County, and the Time appointed for the National Meeting.

The Meeting affirming this Name was a Committee formed of Delegates from the County Meetings, and assembled every Seven Weeks; and there the moll important Business of the Society was transacted. This Meeting received Reports from a Secret Committee, and nominally directed its Conduct, but the Secret Committee really had the chief Management. This Committee was elected from amongst the Delegates at the National Meeting, in the same secret Manner as those Delegates "had been chosen at the County Meeting, the Persons elected being only known to the Secretary; and the Committee, thus secretly formed, did not disclose itself in the Transaction of Business; all of which was con-dudted through the Intervention of a Person (already noticed) called ‘The Intermediate ;' who delivered their Orders, and who was the same Person to whom the Delegates had been directed to apply for Information respecting the Place of Assembly of the National Meeting. Except therefore to the Intermediate, to the Secretary, and to each other, the Persons composing the Secret Committee remained wholly unknown.

Every Proceeding was involved in the same myfte-rious Secrecy; and though this System of blind Obedience had the Effect of disgusting and alarming some of the Delegates, who perceived themselves to be Instruments in the Hands of an unknown Authority, for Purposes, of which the Extent was never fully disclosed to them; yet the Committee, thus fonned, continued to preserve its general Influence; disbursing at its Pleasure the Money coiledled; giving all Orders for the Places of the National Meetings; fending Missionaries, diflemi-nating Papers, receiving Information, and conducting every Part of the Business without Controul.

The National Meeting was generally, if not always, held in or near Glasgow; and from Reports of what passed at those Meetings, it appears that they corre-lponded with the Society of United Britons, and sent Delegates to England, and received Delegates from thence. When the Meeting broke up, each Delegate received a Note of the Time appointed for the next Meeting; which he was to deliver to the Secretary of

Their Communications with different Parts, and particularly with England, were feklom carried on in Writing: Some Papers, however, have been dil'covered, which clearly shew that the Society had the most dangerous Objects in View; and that some of its Members were sanguine enough to profess an Opinion, " that if the " flattering Accounts which they received from " were real, the Emancipation of the Country was at " no great Distance, when they should rally round the " Standard of Liberty."

This System of Union, as well as that of the United Englishmen, was evidently borrowed from Ireland; and there is Reason to believe that it was introduced by Delegates from that Country. Signs were adopted for the Purpose of distinguishing the Members, as was practised in Ireland; but the Knowledge of the Signs seems to have been only imperfedtly diffuted; they never have been generally understood; or having been altered at different Times in different Places, without Concert, were never uniform in all Parts of the Country.

In their sanguine Expectation of Success, these Conspirators formed wild and extravagant Plans of seizing, in the same Night, all the leading People over the whole Island. If these Persons should relict, they were to be put to Death; if they submitted quietly, their Lives and Property were to be spared, but they were to be kept in Custody till a new Constitution should be formed; which was clearly meant to be conformable to French Principles.

An Oath or Test was formally administered, and printed Papers were circulated under the Title of " Resolutions and Constitution of the Society of United " Scoifnen; " a Copy of which is let forth in the Ap- (N° 15.) pendix.

The Measures of this Conspiracy were difccncerted by the Arrest of Mealmaker, of Dyer, and of Archibald Gray, the latter of whom, after his Indictment, escaped to the Continent, and has become a Member of a Society at Hamburgh, which will hereafter be noticed, by the Name of The Philanthropic Society.'

In Addition to this View of the Proceedings of the Societies both in England and Scot, at this Period, it is material to remark, that whilst the Rebellion was at its Height in Ireland, there were found Individuals, in this Country, who so strongly manifested their Desire to support the Cause of the Rebels, that they became the Objects of Criminal Prosecution. Among these, a Man, of the Name of Martin Dwas indicted for distributing, at Gosport, the Address stated in the Appendix, intituled, " An Irishnas Address to his (N° 16.) " Countrymen in England; " the Contents of which perhaps might have warranted a Prosecution for a higher Crime, and are so striking a Specimen of the Intentions of the Disaffected, that although the particular instance relates only to the Conduct of One Individual, Your Committee have thought it highly deserving of Notice.

This Man was convicted at the last Summer Assizes at Winchester, and sentenced to Two Years Imprisonment.

Societiwof While these Proceedings of the United Irishmen in Irion'in Lon Fleet exhibit so dreadful a Picture of their fangui-don, See. nary Deligns, and of the Similarity of their Views and Principles to those which have produced so much Cala- mity and Bloodshed in Ireland, their Conduct on Shore

Your Committee have no Helitation in, stating, on the cleared Proof, strongly confirmed by recent Circumstances, that among the various Bodies enlisted, in ‘any Part of Great Britain, for the Purposes of Sedition and Treason, the Societies which have been formed by the United Irishmen in this Country, are in all Respects the most formidable, particularly at the present Moment; whether considered with a View to their Combination, their actual Numbers, or the atrocious Nature of the Designs of which they are preparing, in a very short Time, to attempt the Execution in direct Cooperation with France.

The Danger to be apprehended from these Societies is much increased, from the constant Communication which they maintain with the Societies in Ireland; their mutual Confidence in each other; and the alanning Circumstance of their being, at this Moment, subject to the same secret Direction, and the same Chiefs.

These Societies have been instituted, not only in London, but in different Parts of the Country, and have (N° 23 & formed themselves into Subdivisions. The Reference in these Certificates to the Constitution and the Test, confirm the unquestionable Information whichYbur Committee have received, that these Societies form a Part of the dreadful System which was unhappily established in Ireland. The Constitution of the United Irishmen, such as it was acted upon in Ireland, appears to regulate their Proceedings; and Copies of this Constitution have been found in she Possession of Persons principally concerned in promoting these Meetings. The Views which they entertain at this Moment, and the sanguine Hopes with which they look to their Accomplishment, are apparent in an inflammatory and treasonable Paper recently found at one of these Meetings, of which Government had received Intelligence, and the Persons present at which were consequently apprehended.

This Paper is inserted in the Appendix. Other Papers, 2C,) seized at the same Meeting, strongly confirm the Account which Your Committee have received, that a Mode has lately been adopted by these Societies (similar to that practised both in Ireland and Scotland) of keeping the Accounts of the Society, by substituting different Numbers for the Names of the Members. Your Committee think it also not immaterial to insert in the Appendix, Copy of a printed Card, which has been (N°26.) found in the Possession of different Persons, and particularly among other seditious Papers, in that of a Person recently apprehended, who, there is Reason to believe, has been very lately cholen to act as General Secretary to the different Societies of United Irishmen now in London. The Person named in this Card, and the Transaction to which it relates, are such as to require no Comment.

Your Committee have received different Accounts of the Numbers of this Society; but though their Force is probably exaggerated by themselves, for evident Rea-fons, there is sufficient Ground for believing that their Numbers have been long considerable. Many Irish, ordinarily resident here, chiefly among the lowest Classes of the Community, have been gradually induced to become Members of this Society. But the most active Part consists of those Irish Rebels who have fled to this Country; rendered desperate by their Crimes, not daring to return to Ireland, and either unable to make their Way to the Countries subject to France, or not receiving sufficient Encouragement to attempt it, they remain here, waiting for the Opportunity of executing those violent and desperate Projects, to which they have become familiar. And they appear to be under the Direction of some Persons of a higher Qlafs, who lbrne-times furnish pecuniary Aid, and form the Committee, by Means of which, a constant Correspondence is carried on, through Hamburgh, with France.

Among these Plans, there is good Reason to believe, plans of that early in 1798, it was ferioutly in Agitation among United irilhr the Conspirators in Ireland, to convey, in small Vessels, men‘ from Ireland to England, a great Number of United Irishmen; and to land them on different Parts of the Coast, with Instructions to divide themselves into small Bodies, and to endeavour to make their Way to the Capital in the Manner least liable to Suspicion, under the Dilguife of those Trades and Occupations in which the Irish, commonly resorting hither, are principally engaged. Their Object is represented to have been that of co-operating with the Corresponding Society, in effecting an Insurrection in Lonaon, at the Time of the Rebellion breaking out in Ireland, for the Purpose of distrading the Military Force and preventing Reinforcements being sent to that Country; and the Plan is laid to have failed from the Corresponding Society Ihrinking from the Execution of it. About the same Period, another Project was secretly formed (of " which Your Committee have received more distinct Information) for collecting at one Point, a chosen Body of the most Determined from among the United Irish employed

But, notwithstanding the Continuance of every Precaution, and although these Conspirators cannot be ignorant of the prepared and formidable Force, and the determined Spirit and general Loyalty with which such an Enterprize would be immediately refilled, Your Committee have received undoubted Proof that Plans of this Nature are now, more than ever, in Agitation. Attempts are actually making, by Agents from Ireland, to concert with the French Government the Time for a fresh and general Insurrection in Ireland. Intelligence has been received, that in the Ports of France the utmost Diligence is used in preparing another Expedition to cooperate with the Rebels in that Kingdom. The Time for making this Attempt, seems to be, in a great Mca-sure, fixed. The Expectation which appears to be generally entertained among the Traitors in Ireland tallies, in this Relped, with the Intelligence which has been laid before Your Committee; and this Expectation has been particularly communicated from thence to their Confederates in this Country. It seems to be intended, at the same Time to attempt a Diversion by another French Force on different Parts of the Coasts of this Kingdom. The Manner in which such Expeditions are likely to be calculated to advance the Ends of the Conspirators, both in Great Britain and Ireland, and the Species of Warfare which the French have had in Contemplation, will be sufficiently evident from a Reference to the Instructions of Fate, who was made Prisoner in Wales (which are printed in the Appendix to the Report made last Session, on the Treatment of Prisoners of War) and to those of Humbert, who commanded the Force which landed lall Year in Ireland, and who had also been destined to command an Expedition against Cornwall, fN° 27 & are indrted in the Appendix to this Report. Societies at Hamburgh.

lit Addition to this Mass of Treason, in Great Britain and in Ireland, Your Committee find, that, for the Purpose of more convenient Communication between France and Ireland, a Committee of United Irishmen has been formed at Hamburgh. That Place has long been the Receptacle of those disaffected Persons who have fled from Great Britain or Ireland, either from Apprehension of the Consequences of the treasonable Practices in which they have been engaged, or for the Purpose of assisting the Conspiracies carried on against their respective Countries; and with the latter V lew it has been the Center of a Correspondence, which has long subsisted among the Britishand Irish Societies established at that Place, as well as in London and; and this Correspondence with Great Britain and Ireland, has frequently been covered by the Pretence of Commercial Transactions, or of communicating Intelligence for the public Newspapers.

Hamburgh has also been the Resort of the Disaffected of every other Country, whose Intrigues are constantly directed to the Object of spreading the Principles of Jacobinism in Holjlein and the North of Germany, and generally in all the Northern Parts of Europe. Many Emissaries, English, Scotch, and Irish, have been dispatched

from Time to Time from Hamburgh to Great Britain and Ireland, and to various Parts of the Continent, as Circumstances required. There has recently been established at Hamburgh, Altona, and the Neighbourhood, a Society called The Philanthropic Society' for the Purpose of Correspondence with the Republicans of all Countries, upon the Plan of the Corresponding Societies established in Great Britain and Ireland-, and whose avowed Object is the Reform of all Kingdoms and States.

The leading Members of this Society, who direct all the rest, compose a Committee of about Twenty Persons,

British, French, Dutch, and Germans. The Members of thelubordinate Societies at Hamburgh and Altona are all under the Controul of the Committee or principal Society before-mentioned. This Committee constantly corresponds with Great Britain and Ireland, and all Parts of Germany. It has Secretaries {killed in different Languages, and corresponding Agents in different Towns, particularly in London. It may become a formidable Engine in the Hands of the French Directory,

and it appears to be making considerable Progress; but there is Keafon to hope that it has at length attracted the Notice of the Governments of those Places.

UPON a Review of all the Circumstances which Condufon. have come under the Consideration of Your Committee, they are deeply impressed with the Conviction — That the Safety and Tranquillity of these Kingdoms have, at different Periods from the Year 1791 to the present Time, been brought into imminent Hazard, by the traitorous Plans and Practices of Societies, acting upon the Principles, and devoted to the Views, of our inveterate Foreign Enemy:

That, although the Society of United in

Ireland, has alone been enabled to attain its full Strength and Maturity; yet the Societies instituted on similar Principles in this Country, had all an undoubted Tendency to produce similar Effects, if they had not been checked by the general Demonstrations of the Zeal and Spirit of His Majesty's faithful Subjects, and by the timely and judicious Use of those extraordinary Powers, which Parliament has, in its Wisdom, from Time to Time confided to His Majesty's Government:

That, either directly or indirectly, a continual Intercourse and Connection has been maintained between all

"<wiW.Cy real Objects of the Instigators of these Proceedings, in — — »> both Kingdoms, were no other than the entire Overthrow of the British Constitution, the general Confifca-tion of Property, and the Erection of a Democratic Republic, founded on the Ruins of all Religion, and of 411 Political and Civil Society, and framed after the Model of France.

The vigorous Resistance opposed to the Rebellion in Ireland, the Succels of the Measures which have been employed for detecting and defeating the Deligns of the Conspirators here, and the general and ardent Spirit of Loyalty and Attachment to the Laws and Constitution, have hitherto counteracted the Progress of the Mischief, and averted impending Danger; but even these Circum-ft^nces by no Means appear to Your Committee to justify the Hope that the Mischief is eradicated, or the Danger passed.

The Principles and Views of the Conspirators remain unchanged. Their Reliance on the Assistance and Cooperation of France, by which they expect ultimately to effect their Purposes, continues undiminished. And the System of those secret Societies, which are at once the Instruments of seditious Conspiracy at Home, and the Channel of treasonable Correspondence with though in many Parts broken and interrupted, is by no Means destroyed.

Your Committee have already referred to the positive Information laid before them, stating that hostile Preparations are now making, with extraordinary Vigour and Exertion, in some of the Ports of France, for the Invasion of this Country, or of Ireland. The Activity of Seditious and Treasonable Societies, in their Corre-Ipondence with France, and in their Endeavours to gain Proselytes here, keeps Pace with the Preparation? of the Enemy; and the Principle of Secrecy, generally enforced by unlawful Oaths, which is the great Cha-racteriftic of these Societies, peculiarly fits them for the most desperate Enterprizes, and by holding out a Prospect of Security, increales the Means of Seduction. It has, at the same Time, an obvious Tendency to elude Detection, in the first Instaace, and to defeat legal Enquiry in the next. To this Principle, therefore, in the Opinion of Your Committee, such further Measures as Parliament in its Wisdom may think fit to adopt for the Public Safety, should be more imme--diately and decisively pointed.

Your Committee have seen, with Satisfaction, the Towers which, in Conformity to the ancient Practice and true Principles of the Constitution, have from Time to Time, as the Urgency required, been confided to His Majesty's Government; and they feel it their Duty particularly to remark, that, the Power of arresting and detaining suspected Persons (a Remedy so constantly resorted to by our Ancestors in all Cases of temporary and extraordinary Danger) has, under the present new and unprecedented Circumstances, been found particularly efficient. It has greatly interrupted and impeded the Correspondence with the Enemy, and has checked, from Time to Time, the Progress and Communication of Sedition and Treason at Home. But from particular Circumstances which have come under the Observation of Your Committee in the Course of their Enquiry, they feel it their Duty to

remark, that the good Effects of this Measure would be rendered more complete, and the public Tranquillity better secured, if the leading Persons who have been, of may be, hereafter detained on Suspicion of Treasonable Practices, shall hereafter be kept in Custody in Places sufficiently distant from the Metropolis.

The Whole of the Secret Information which has been laid before Your Committee, has strongly confirmed them in theif Opinion of the Necessity of confiding these extraordinary Powers to His Majesty's Government; and the very Circumstances which created this Necessity, and which continue at this Time to operate more powerfully than ever, have rendered it their peculiar Duty to abstain from disclosing, in its full Extent, the particular Information, of which they have dated to the House the general Refuit, and on which their Judgment is founded; but they trust that they have laid before the House sufficient Grounds to justify their Persuasion, that the multiplied and various Attempts by which the Enemies to their Country carry on their dangerous Conspiracies, can only be defeated by a corresponding Vigilance on the Part of Government, and by the Exercise of such additional Powers, as may, from Time to Time, be entrusted to it by Parliament, and may be best adapted to the peculiar Exigency of the Moment. And although Your Committee do not think it any Part of their Province to suggest particular Measures, the Consideration of which must be left to the Wisdom of Parliament; they cannot forbear particularly and earnestly pressing their unanimous Opinion, that the System of Secret Societies, the Establishment of which has, in other Countries, uniformly preceded the Aggression of F, and, by facilitating the Progress ot her Principles, has prepared the Way for her Arms, cannot be suffered to exist in these Kingdoms, compatibly with the Safety of their Government and Constitution, and with their Security against foreign Force and Domestic Treason.

Your Committee have great Satisfaction in adding that if this growing and formidable Evil can be effectually repressed, and if the same System of Vigilance and Precaution which has been successfiilly adopted fot some Years past, is adhered to, there is every Reason to look forward with Confidence to the ultimate Disappointment and Defeat of the Projects which have been, so long pursued by our Foreign and Domestic Enemies, Impressed with a just Sense of the Blelfings enjoyed under our happy Constitution, which distinguish this Country from every Nation in Europe, all Ranks and Conditions of Society have shewn their Determination to preserve those Blessings entire, and have flood forward with a becoming Ardour and Alacrity in their Defence. While this laudable Spirit continues to pervade every Part of the Kingdom, and while the Wisdom of the Legislature encourages and directs its Exertions for the Public Safety, Your Committee entertain a full Conviction that the Religion, the Laws, and the Constitution of Great Britain, and with them the InterefU and Happiness of all Classes of His Majesty's Subjects, will, in the Midst of surrounding Danger and Calamity, and in Spite of every Machination at Home or Abroad, rest under the Protection of Divine Providence, on the surest Balls, (ecured by the Energy and Firmnels of the Government, and by the Courage, the Patriotism, and the Virtue, of the Nation.
