Mr. Long, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Duties payable on the Import and Export of Goods imported into this Kingdom, and sold at the Public Sales of the India Company, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House j which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon all Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, imported into this Kingdom by the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the Eojl Indies (except Tea, Nutmegs, Macc, Cloves, and Cinnamon), according to the Gross Prices at which such Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, shall be sold at the Public Sales of the said Company, and also the Duties now payable on every Piece of Plain White Callicoe, and on every Yard of Plain White Dimity, and on every Hundred Weight of Sugar, imported into this Kingdom by the said Company, do ccafe and determine, except the Duties of Customs imposed by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, for the better Protection of the Trade of this Kingdom, and for other Purposes therein mentioned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon all Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, having been imported into this Kingdom by the East India Company, and exported directly from the Warehouses in which the same shall have been lodged and secured (except on Tea, Nutmegs, Mace, Cloves, and Cinnamon, and except the Duties of Customs imposed by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, for the better Protection of the Trade of this Kindom, and for other Purposes therein mentioned) do cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Vol. 54.

That there be charged for every One Hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of all Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, imported into this Kingdom by the India Company (except Bullion, Diamonds, and other precious Stones, Tea, Nutmegs, Mace, Cloves, and Cinnamon), according to the Grol's Price at which tuch Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, shall "be sold at the Public Sales of the said Company, a Duty of Two Pounds and Ten Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Fifty-three Pounds Nine Shillings and One Penny be charged for every One Hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of all Arrangoes imported into this Kingdom, according to the Gross Price at which the same shall be sold at the Public Sales of the East India Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Forty-five Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Seven Pence be allowed for every One Hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of all Arrangoes exported from this Kingdom, according to the Gross Price at which the same shall have been sold at the Public Srles of the East India Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Six Shillings and Eight Pence be charged upon every Piece of Plain White Callicoe imported into this Kingdom by the India Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Six Shillings be allowed upon the Exportation of every Piece of Plain White Callicoe having been imported into this Kingdom by the East India Company. '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Twenty Pounds Nineteen Shillings and One Penny be charged upon every One Hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of all Plain White Callicoes imported into this Kingdom, according to the Gross Price at which the same shall be sold at the Public Sales of the East India Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Nineteen Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Two Pence be allowed for every One Hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of all Plain White Callicoes exported from this Kingdom to , according to the Gross Price at which the same shall have been sold at the Public Sales of the East India Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Fourteen Pounds Four Shillings and Three Pence be allowed for every One Hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of all Plain White Callicoes exported from this Kingdom to any Colony or Plantation in America, or to any of the United States of America, according to the Gross Price at which the same shall have been sold at the Public Sales of the East India Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of Nineteen Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Two Pence be allowed for ever}' One Hundred Pounds of the true and real Value of ail Callicoes, according to the Gross Price at which the same shall have been Ibid.at the Public Sales of the India Company, exported from this Kingdom to any Parts or Places beyond the Seas (except to any Colony or

That the said Bridge has been found of great Utility to the Public at large: But the Petitioner not being authorized to demand any reasonable Toll for the Passage of Carriages, Cattle, and Foot Passengers, and the Gratuity or Salary to be allowed him by Government, being by no Means adequate to the Intern ft of the Capital invested in building the said Bridge, or to enable him to keep it in the proper and necessary State of Repair, the same cannot be done without the Petitioner is enabled to demand and receive certain Payments by Way of Toll for the Passage of Cattie, Carriages, and Foot Passengers, over the said Bridge.

cerned in the African Slave Trade, was presented to the House, and.read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That, if the same should pass into a Law, it will entirely ruin the Trade; and that the Petitioners feel this the more severely, as it neither has been stated, nor can be proved, that any Evil or Inconvenience whatsoever is experienced by the Negroes from their present Mode of Transportation, but, on the contrary, the latest Returns of Arrivals in the West Indies fully demonstrate that no beneficial Alteration can be made in the present Mode of carrying the m; and that, by an Act, passed in the Thirty seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Height between Decks was fixed at Four Feet One Inch, conformably to which many Merchants have caused their Vessels to be altered at a very great Expence; and that, as several Ships so altered, and all that Class of Vessels in which the Slaves are carried in the most perfect Health, and which it has been the uniform Rule of the Legislature to encourage, will be utterly excluded from the British carrying Trade, as the Reduction of the Number of Slaves to be carried in the large Ships will render it impossible to continue them in the Trade with any probable Prospect of Advantage; and moreover, as the Vessels which will be so excluded from this Trade are so constructed as not to bq fit for any Other, and an enormous Loss will consequently be incurred by the Owners: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agent, against the said Bill, at the Bar of the House, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now Hands.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agent, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, Searchers, and Alnstants, of the Company of Cutlers in and of the Merchants, Dealers in, and Conlumers of, Copper and Brass in the Town and Neighbourhood of Sheffield, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have, for several Years last past, laboured under great Inconveniences and Disadvantages from the increasing Price of Copper and Brass, and they observe with Satisfaction that the House have taken into Consideration the State of the Copper Trade, and that a Bill is introduced for the Purpose of giving Relief to the Conlumers of Copper; and that the Petitioners, being unacquainted with the Provisions and Remedies intended by such Bill, beg Leave to represent that His Majesty's Kingdom of Ireland contains Copper Mines, some of which are now working, and, by reason of their Vicinity to the Ports of this Kingdom, a certain Supply of Copper Ore might be obtained therefrom; and that, if the Duties now imposed oh the Importation of Copper and Copper Ore into this Kingdom‘were abolished or modified, great Benefit would be derived to the Petitioners am' all other Consumers of Copper and Brass in this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take the same info their Consideration, and to adopt such Measures for encouraging the Importation of Copper and Copper Ore, and regulating the Exportation thereof, as to the House shall l'eem expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the Petitioners, and divers other Persons, have, at a very great Expence, made and constructed many large and extensive Ship Yards and Dry Docks, adjoining to the River Thames, and have employed large Capitals in the necessary Establishments for carrying on the Trade or Business of building and repairing Ships, to an Extent fully adequate to the Demands of the Port of London, and to the great Convenience of the Public at large; and that the Operation and Effect of the said Bill, if the same should pass into a Law in its present Form, will be highly injurious to the Properties of the Petitioners, and other Ship Builders, and Owners and Proprietors of Ship Yards and Dry Docks, adjoining to the River Thames, in the Port of London, in as much as the said Company will be empowered, if they shall so think fit, to make Slips into their Docks or Basons, or upon their Quays or Wharfs, for building Ships or Vessels, and also to make contiguous to their Wet Docks, Dry Docks for repairing Ships or Vessels, and will also be empowered to make B.ifons or Canals into other Dry Docks, to be dug or made for the Purposes aforesaid, upon adjoining Pre-miles of or belonging to other Persons, and likewise to do large Repairs to Ships or Vessels whilst the same are lying in their Wet Docks; and that the Petitioners, and such other Persons as aforesaid, will thereby be injured in their Properties and Trade to a very great Extent, for which no adequate Compensation can be made to them by the said Company; and that the Petitioners, having applied to the Promoters of the said Undertaking for such Provision being made therein as might guard them against the Injury they apprehend V<)L.

they shall fyftain, if the several Powers before-mentioned should be carried into Effect, and not having succeedod in such their Applications, now find theml'elves under the Necessity of applying to the House for such Relief as they conceive they are entitled to: And therefore praying. That Provision may be made in the said Bill for their Protection and Relief in the several Matters before-mentioned, and that they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now stands, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Sir John William Anderson reported from the Commit- Petition of tee, to whom the Petition of the several Master Mill- Matter M u-wrights, whose Names are thereunder subscribed, was ^^ <1!' " referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

John Rennie, being examined, said, That a dangerous Combination has for some Time existed amongst the Journeymen Millwrights, within the Metropolis, and the Limits of Twenty-five Miles round the fame, for enforcing a general Increase of their Wages, preventing the Employment of such Journeymen as refuse to join in their Confederacy, and for other illegal Purposes; and that frequent Conspiracies of this Sort have been set on Foot by the Journeymen, and the Masters have been as often obliged to submit, and that a Demand of a further Advance of Wages has recently been made, which not being complied with, the Men, within the Limits aforesaid, have refused to work; that a Compliance with such Demands of an Advance of Wages, hath generally been followed by further Claims, with which

which it is impossible for the Masters to comply, without occasioning so considerable an Advance in the Price of Mill Work, as most materially to affect the said Business, and the different Manufactories connected therewith; that in Support of the said Combination (notwithstanding the y complain of the Insufficiency of their Wages) the Journeymen have established a general Fund, and raised Subscriptions, and so regular and connected is their System, that their Demands are made sometimes by all the Journeymen, within the above Limits, at the same Time, and at other Times within-some one particular Shop, and, in case of Non-compliance, the different Workshops (where their Demands are refilled) are wholly deserted by the Men, and other Journeymen are prohibited from applying for Work until the Master Millwrights are brought to Compliance, and the Journeymen, who have thus thrown themselves out of Employ, receive Support in the mean Time from their general Fund; that the only Method of punishing . such Delinquents, under the existing Laws, is by preferring an Indictment, at the Sessions or Assizes, after the Commission of the Offence, but before that Time arrives the Offenders frequently remove into different Parts of the Country, so that, even if their Places of Residence should be discovered, it would be a long Time before they could be brought to Trial, and the Expence of apprehending and bringing them back to the Place where the Offence was committed, is so heavy to the Masters, whole Buiinesses have been Hopped by the Defer-tion of the Journeymen, that (aware of these Difficulties) the Journeymen carry on their Combinations with Bold-ness and Impunity.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent unlawful Combinations of Workmen employed in the Millwright Business, and to enable the Magistrates to regulate their Wages within the Limits therein mentioned: And that Sir John Anderson and Mr. Alderman Lufuington, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the Petitioner, forfome Years past, hath been in the Practice of trading largely on the Coast, in the Vicinity of Sierra Leone, and hath now Property there to the Amount of £.30,000, and upwards; and that Obligations from different Traders having been taken by the Agents of the Petitioner for Slaves, for which the Petitioner has paid Value, such Property will be wholly irrecoverable should the said Bill pass into a Law: And therefore praying to be heard, by himself, his Agents, or Counsel, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law, without adequate Compensation being made to the Petitioner.

the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted, a great Part of which still remains due, and cannot be paid oft', unless the Term of the said Act be continued, and some further and other Powers are given to the said Trustees, and it is expedient that some additional Tolls should be granted. A Petition of the Mayor, Aldertnen, Bailiffs, and Common Council of the Town of Liverpool, in the of Liverpool, County of Lancaster, in Common Council assembled, against Liver was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice w t«r of the Bill for better supplying the Town and Port of Liverpool with Water, from certain Springs in the Township of Bootle, in the County Palatine of Lancaster; and Setting forth, That an Act was passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for opening, making, widening, and altering. Certain Streets,

Passages, and Places, within the Town of Liverpool, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, for supplying the said Town with fresh and wholesome Water, for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein, for appointing additional Market Places, and for extending so much of the Powers of an Act, of the Second Year of His present Majesty, as relates to Hackney Coachmen, Chairmen, Carters, and Porters, to a certain Dise tance beyond the Liberties of the said Town, whereby the Common Council, for the Time being, of the said Town, are invested with Powers to make several Improvements therein particularly mentioned, for the Accommodation and Benefit of the Inhabitants, and also to dig for Springs or Fountains, and make Reservoirs, and all other requisite Works for raising, conducting, , and conveying Water into the Town, for the Use and Benefit of the Inhabitants thereof; and that, by the Powers and Provisions contained in the said Act, the Petitioners are fully enabled to supply the Inhabitants of the said Town with Water, and have actually, feme Time past, purchased a Spring in the said v Town, and have made other Preparations for that Purpose, and also have in Contemplation the perfecting of Contrafts for other Springs within the said Town, which have been offered for this intended Public Supply of the Town; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, that the Springs at Bootle are inadequate to the Supply of the Town with a sufficient Quantity of Water, and the said Bill would also, if passed into a Law, be in other respects prejudicial to the Rights and Interests of the Petitioners, and inconvenient to the Inhabitants of the said Town t And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that they may be heard, by themselves, and their Counsel, against the said Bill, or that they may have such other Relief in the Pre mises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

" for regulating, until the First £)ay of August One " thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-nine, the shipping and carrying Slaves in British Vessels from the " Coast of Africa," be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee. That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill for continuing the said Act.

A Petition of the there-undersigned Merchants and others, residing at Liverpool, concerned in the African Slave Trade, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That, if the same should pass into a Law, it will entirely ruin the Trade; and that the Petitioners feel this the more severely, as it neither has been stated, nor can be proved, either by the Official Returns now before the House, or otherwise, that any Evil or Inconvenience whatever is experienced by the Negroes from their present Mode of Transportation, but, on the contrary, the latest Returns of Arrivals in the West Indies fully demonstrate that no beneficial Alteration can be mado in the present Mode of carrying the m; and that, by an Act, passed in the Thirty-seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Height between Decks was fixed at Four Feet One Inch, conformable to which many Merchants have caul'ed their Vessels to be altered at a very great Expence; and that, as several Ships so altered, and all that Class of Vessels in which Slaves are carried in the most perfect Health, and which it has been the uniform Rule of the Legislature to encourage, will be utterly excluded from the British carrying Trade, as the Reduction of the Number of Slaves to be carried in the large Ships, will render it impossible to continue them in the Trade with any probable Prospect of Advantage, and moreover, as the Vessels, which will be so excluded from this Trade, are so construded as not to be fit for any other, an enormoiis Loss will consequently be incurred by the Owners: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agent, against the said Bill, at the Bar of the House, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table,

Resolved, That this House will-, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of the Number of Vessels that have cleared from the Ports of Liverpool, Bristol, and London, for the Coast of Africa, with the Number of Slaves taken on board, as far as the same can be made up from the Returns made by the respective Custom House Officers in the West Indies, and, where such Returns are not received, from such Journals as may have been delivered into the Custom House, Lond'm, since the 5th of January 1797.

The House was moved. That the Order, made upon Friday last, for taking into further Consideration, Tomorrow, the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to prohibit the Trading for Slaves on the Coast of Africa, within certain Limits, was committed, might be read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Order be discharged.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Thursday Morning next.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Report of Mr. William Dundas reported from the Committee

Cold^B-uh °n appointed to enquire into the State of His Majesty's Fields rriibn. Prison in Cold Bath Fields, and to report the

lame, as it should appear to them, together with their Opinion thereupon, to the House, and who were empowered to report their Proceedings from Time to Time; that the Committee had enquired accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read, and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine into the several Matters referred to their Consideration; and in the Investigation of this Subject, have directed their Enquiry to the general State of the said Prison, and the Plan which has been adopted for its Regulation and Management.

It appears to Your Committee, not only from the Evidence adduced to them, but also from their personal Observation, that the Prison, is erected on a high and dry Situation; that it is kept perfectly clean; that the Cells for solitary Confinement are dry and airy.

It also appears, from the Evidence laid before Your Committee, that the Health of the Prisoners has been generally good, and that when, from Two hundred and Fifty to Three hundred Prisoners were in the Prison, there were not more than Four or Five Sick in the Hospital at any one Time; that the Provisions are sufficient, good, and wholesome, and that no Complaints at any Time have been made to the Magistrates respecting the m.

Your Committee have, however, to remark, that the printed Regulations for the Management of the Prison, have not been hung up in a conspicuous Part of the Prison, as is required by the Statutes relating thereto; and that the Journals of the Prison, as directed by the Regulations, have not been fully and regularly kept.

Vol. 54.

Your Committee have, besides, directed their Atten- Report on tion to the Petition of Edward Marcus which p,j^'u

states, That he had been confined a dole Prisoner, under a Warrant from the Duke of Portland, since the 22d of J

April till the 25th of November last; that he was confined in a damp Cell about Seven Feet Square, with no Article of Furniture, except a Bed laid on some Oaken Planks fastened to the Wall, and that, during the First Six Weeks of his Confinement, he had no Allowance but Bread and Water.

It appears in Evidence to Your Committee, That the Circumstances of the Time, and the Public Safety, rendered it indispensably necessary that Edward Marcus Defpard should be kept, at the Time of his Commitment, inclose and separate Confinement; that the Cell in which he was (b confirted was not damp as stated in his Petition; that he was removed, on the 25th of November, into a Room with a Fire in it, and glazed Windows; that although, for the First Six Weeks of his Confinement, he had only the Prison Allowance for Persons committed for Re-examination, yet that during the Whole of that Period he was supplied with Provisions sent in by his Friends, or procured for him at a reasonable Rate in the Prison. It is also alledged in the Petition, that his Health was materially injured; but that certainly does not appear from the Evidence before Your Committee, for he has never applied for medical Assistance; and his only Disorders seem to have been, after the fullest Examination on this Head, a Return of Rheumatism contracted Abroad, and occasionally Chilblains on his Feet. It is Rated in the Petition, that he was not allowed to walk in the Garden; but it appears that he had Permission to walk in a Court; and that, after the First Two Months of his Confinement, he was permitted to walk a Part of the Day uninterruptedly with his Wife in an open Part of the Prison, adjoining to and communicating with the Garden, and distinct from the Court of his Cell.

Your Committee do not think themselves called upoA to state a Variety of other Circumstances which have come under their Consideration; but they are anxious to refer the House to the Evidence in the Appendix, td prove how much it has been their With and Endeavour to fulfil the Objects of their Appointment; that they have examined the Persons mentioned by Edward Marcus Defpard in his Petition, as to the Facts alledged in it; and that they have themselves visited the Prison, and have found every Part of it in the highest Degree of '

Order, clean and dry, the Prisoners healthy, and their Food good and wholesome.

Your Committee have also to remark, that from the very laudable Vigilance and Attention of the Visiting Magistrates, it is extremely improbable that any Impropriety of Conduct, or unnecessary Severity in the Gaoler, could long have escaped their Notice.

Your Committee have peculiar Satisfaction in being able to state to the House the Result of their Enquiries, as a full and direct Refutation of the unfounded Statements, and absurd and wicked Reports, which have been industriously circulated, with respect to the Prison and its internal Management: And upon the Whole,

Your Committee have come to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Prison in Cold Bath Fields is erected in a dry and airy Situation, and is well adapted for the Purposes of its Institution as a House of Correction, as w^ll as for those of close and separate Confinement and fafo Custody.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Parts of the Prison are kept perfectly clean, and that the Health of the Prisoners has been remarkably good.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Attention of the Magistrates, to the general Management of the Prison, has been exemplaiy and meritorious.

Were the Regulations between 1795 and 1794 the same as those delivered in? — No.

What were. the Regulations previous to the Year 1794? — Not any; I had no Rules or Orders to go by.

In what Manner was the Prison conducted? — There was no Rules or Orders for conducting it; every Thing was improperly conducted j fuel) as Men and Women being allowed to be together. I mean in the old Prison. The Friends of the Prisoners were allowed to go into the different Yards, and were frequently fighting, drunk, and rioting. The Second Day after I was appointed I flopped it, which was the 7th of November

1793-

Were those printed Regulations adopted immediately on your entering the new Prison ? — Yes.

Have they been acted upon ever since ? — They have.

' At what Date or Period did you enter into your Office in the new Prison? — I suppol'e about June 1794.

You have said, that those Orders and Regulations, -which you have produced, were not hung up in the Prison; were any Orders or Regulations'hung up in the Prison ? — There has not.

Were the Orders and Regulations which you have delivered in, at any Time, generally or individually, published to the Prisoners? — Never.

Are all Prisoners kept separate in the House of Correction? — Every one, except the seditious People, Thirteen of them, committed under Warrant from the Duke of Portland.

Are those Thirteen Prisoners kept to the same Rules and Orders as the other Prisoners ? — They are not.

State the Distinction? — There is Seven of them in one Room, and Six in another. Those Rooms are floored. They lay in those Rooms as well as eat there.

State the Size of those Two Rooms? — Each Room is about Twenty-seven Feet square.

What is the Height ? — About Fourteen Feet.

' What Number of Windows are there in each Room? — There are Six, glazed, in each.

Are there Fire Places in each Room ? — Yes.

Mr. Arts Called in, and Examined. '

Mr. Ans. Are you Governor of the House of Correction in Cold Bath Fields? — Yes.

How long have you been Governor there? — Six Years.

Were you the First Governor? — I have been Governor ever since the Prison was finished.

Apprmlix, [Mr. Arts delivers in a Paper, intituled, " Rules,

z' Orders, and Regulations for the Management

of the new House of Correction for the County of Middlesex, approved and confirmed by the Justices at the Middlesex Quarter Sessions 1794-"]

Have there been any other Rules or Orders made for the Regulation of the House of Correction, since the Year 1794? — No.

Are those Orders, or a Copy of them, hung up in the Prison? — They are not; nor has it been customary to hang them up, I never having received Orders to that Effect.

What Number of Beds is there in each Room? — I think the London People have each a separate Bed; as to the other Seven I am not positive, but think Five Beds are allotted to them.

Of what Materials are those Beds composed? — A Linen same fluffed with Straw, a Blanket, and a Rug each. There is a Fire in both Rooms all Day; they have Chairs and Tables, Knives and Forks.

What are the Size of the Windows? — About Two Feet Square.

Do the Windows open? — Yes.

Are there any Window Shutters? — No.

State what Food those Thirteen Prisoners receive? — I cannot exaClly say; a Man of the Name of Ballard provides for them.

Have they the same Allowance as the other Prisoners? — They have nothing to do with the other Prisoners; they have each Day a Loaf which weighs a Pound, and 13 j. 4 d.per Week each allowed by Government.

Who has the Direction of laying out the 13 s. 4 ? —

Joseph Ballard, one of my Servants.

By whole Appointment doth he lay out the 13J. 4 ' — I order him to provide for them; every Month a Bill goes to the Under Secretary of State, and the Order for the Money, I receive from Mr. IVkite.

Have the Prisoners the Power of ordering their Provisions themselves? — No; Joseph Ballard provides for them.

Have you as Governor, received any Complaints from those Thirteen Prisoners, respecting their Food ? — Never from any of them; the Manchester Men have frequently said to me, the Meat was good, and they had no Cause of Complaint; they had about One Pound per Day,

Are the Prisoners informed what is allowed them by Government? — Yes, they are.

Did you ever hear any Complaints as to the Quantity of Provisions ? — Never.

Do you keep the Prisoners generally to Hard Labour? — Yes, I do; some of them to the different Trades they happen to be bred to, such a? Bricklayers, Carpenters, and Taylors, &c. and they who have no Trades pick Oakum.

Are the Prisoners who are committed under the Duke of Portland's Warrant, employed by you in Labour? — Not one of them.

Do they employ themselves in any Labour ?-^No, they do not.

Are the Prisoners in general informed of Means of Employment being provided for them, and of their being entitled, by the Prison Rules, to a certain Proportion of the Profits from such Employment? — They are.

Have those Thirteen, whom you state to be unemployed, been so informed? — Never; it is understood by the Rules, that People under Conviction are to be so employed; but I in general employ every Person who comes in after being fully committed to take their Trial.

Has it not, in Fact, been usual to offer the Means of Employment to Prisoners fully committed for Trial, and to state to them the Proportion of the Profits from their Labour; namely, One Half thereof, to which they would be entitled by the Thirty-fifth Rule? — It has not been usual to state that; it has not been usual to set all of them to work; some of them, if sent for an Assault or trifling Offence, are set to work.

Is the Committee to understand that you exercise your Discretion as to the Propriety of setting the Prisoners to work; and is it stated from Time to Time, to the Visiting Justices, which of the Prisoners are and which are not employed? — Yes; I do exercise my.Discretion with regard to setting the Prisoners to work; I deliver in a List to the Justices of the Number of Prisoners in the Prison, and how they are employed, and those who are not employed.

Do you keep a Journal of the Events of the Prison, according to the Third Rule? — I do.

Has that Journal been called for and submitted to the Visiting Justices, from Time to Time? — At every Committee, which meets sometimes Twice in Five Weeks, or Twice in a Month, it is laid upon the Table.

Do you fee most of your Prisoners Daily, as by Rule the Fourth? — In general so; some of them Ten Times each Day.

Have any of them, at any Time, stated themselves to be dissatisfied with their Treatment, Food, Lodging, or other Particular ? — The Mutineers are very often complaining that they are starving, and should be starved to Death.

Have you mentioned those Complaints to the Visiting Justices? — Always; some of them have been examined by the Committee in consequence of my Report.

Vol. 54.

Are the Cells in which the Prisoners are confined Report cm separately, liable to damp? — They are not damp; I examined the Cells after the Frost, and they were comnutd. as dry as this Room; and a Number of Magistrates examined themalfoat that Time; Mr. , Mr. Soane, r' '. and others did so.

What is the Nature and Degree of solitary Confinement in ordinary Cafes ? — They are generally locked up, according to their Behaviour; a Number of them, that are orderly and qiliet, have their Cells unlocked in the Morning, and left open all Day, and they may go in and out at Pleasure; others, who are refractory and idle, are confined in their Cells till they have done their Work.

Are they locked in their separate Cells at Night ? —

They are.

The Rules prescribe that a certain Proportion of the Profits shall belong to the Prisoners; when do they receive these Profits for their Labour? — At their going out of the Prison, when they are discharged.

Is any Attention paid, on the Discharge of Prisoners, to their future Situation? — Not at all Times; sometimes they are discharged with a Pass, and sometimes not.

Is Care taken to provide the Prisoners with clean Bedding from Time to Time ? — Always.

Are the Prisoners allowed to receive Articles of Food, or other Comforts, which may be sent them by their Friends ? — Never, except ordered by the Doctor or Apothecary, excepting Prisoners before Trial; they are at Liberty to receive any Food their Friends lend them in, but no Liquor of any Kind.

How often do the Visiting Justices visit the Prison? —

The Magistrates come frequently, but I do not know there are any regular Visiting Justices; Dr. Glajje generally comes Twice a Week, and other Magistrates.

State the Names of such Magistrates as you recollect to be frequent Visitors of the Prison? — Dr. Mr.

Hole, Mr. Cross, Mr. Matthew, Mr. Bond, and many others.

Are Persons committed for Want of Sureties, or for safe Custody, allowed to have Food sent them by their Friends ? — Always. I should have mentioned before, in addition to the 13 . 4 dper Week and the Loaf each Day, they are at Liberty to receive any Food their Friends chuse to bring the m; I mean the seditious People, the Thirteen before-mentioned.

May the Mutineers likewise receive Food from their Friends, if they chuse to fend it ? — No.

Are the Mutineers committed for Trial or under Sentence ? — 'They are under Sentence of Death.

Have you known the Prison, particularly the foparate Cells, or any of them, to be dirty, or infefted with Vermin ? — There has been sometimes Vermin brought into them; but they are cleaned every Day; the Convicts we receive from Newgate arc in a shocking State, from Filth, &c.

Have you in general observed the Health of the Prisoners to grow worse or better, during their Confinement ? — In general much better; I have known them come in in a weak State, and have gone out as well as ever they were in their Lives.

Have all the other Prisoners Bedding of the same Quantity and Quality as before described ? — All alike throughout the Prison.

Is the County Loaf allowed to the other Prisoners of a better Sort, than that allowed to the Seditious? —

No; all alike.

Have the Mutineers, during any Part of the Day, Acceis to a Fire ? — -Not one, no Part of the Day, except One Man, who is in the Infirmary; they had, the Whole of them formerly; and the Reason why they were afterwards denied Accel's to a Fire was from the Information of one of them, that they were contriving Means to make their Efcaj>e; that was communicated to the Magistrates, and an Order was made that they should be locked up in separate Cells.

Were they denied the Use of Fire as a Punishment, or because they availed themselves of JFire for the Purpose of Mischief or Escape ? — When they had Access -to a Fire, they were Eight or Ten together in a Room; when I received Information from one of them, that they were contriving Means to make their Escape, and threatening some of the Servants, even to murder them, I received an Order from the Magistrates to lock them up in the Cells, and to discontinue the Fire.

Have the Mutineers, at present, any Opportunities of getting further Provision than their accustomed Allowance, either from what their Friends fend them, or they can buy ? — They have no Inch Opportunity, unless supplied by my own Servants.

If supplied by your own Servants, would it meet with your Approbation ? — It would not.

Was that the same before the Mutineers attempted to make their Escape ? — Yes, it was; the Orders were, they should live on the Gaol Allowance; but in Fa<ft, in some Instances, when the Wife, Mother, or Father have come to fee them, and have brought something for them, in general I have taken it in, and sent it up to the Prisoners, and very often have delivered it with my own Hands.

Do you allow Conviifts in general to receive from their Friends, or to buy, any further Provision than the accustomed Allowance ? — We do not allow them to buy any Thing; where the Prisoners are orderly and industrious, we allow a Sunday's Dinner to be brought in by their Friends; and that is under the Direction of the Doctor.

Have the Cells any Fire-place ? — No.

The Reverend Dr. Glajfe, Millington Buckley, Esquire, and Thomas Collins, Esquire.

Called in, and Examined.

Dr. cleife. Are you the Visiting Justices appointed by the ;--- --' General Court of Quarter Sessions for visiting the Prison

in Cold Bath Fields ? — We are.

Were yoja all appointed at the same Time ? — Myself and Mr. Collins were appointed in Epiphany Sessions 1796; Mr. Buckley was appointed somewhat later.

How often, in the Discharge of that Duty, have you been accustomed to visit the Prison ? — It has been our Custom to hold a Committee Twice between every

Sessions, to take Minutes of pur Proceedings, and Dr- Glcjje, make our Rc{>ort thereon on the Thursday in every Sessions, which is the County Day.

Do you visit and inspect the different Parts of the Prison on the Days you hold your Committees ? — It has been an invariable Rule with us to summon before us the Governor, the Surgeon, and the Chaplain, at every Visit, to enquire respectively of them into the general Order of the Prison, into the Health of the Prisoners, and particularly to the last of-these Officers into his moral Conduit; and as our Meetings were stated, and generally known by the Prisoners, if any of them had any Grievance to complain of, he was at full Liberty to bring it forward, and such Complaint never passed unnoticed or unenquired info, the Party complaining always being brought before the Committee; but with respect to visiting the different Parts of the Prison, it has not been the constant Custom though frequently done.

Whether Dr. Glajfe has himself occasionally visited and inspected different Parts of the Prison ? — Frequently, as a Member of the Committee, and much more frequently as an Individual Visiting Magistrate.

In the Course of such Inspection, did the different Wards or Cells of the Prison appear to you dry and healthy, and kept perfectly clean ? — I never recoiled t<? have seen them otherwise; the only Place we apply the Word Ward to is the Infirmary, and that is remarkably clean indeed. I am a Governor of many public Hospitals, and I never saw an Infirmary kept so perfectly clean and inoffensive as those Wards are.

In the different Cells, did the Bedding appear to be wholesome, sufficient, and clean? — Different perhaps as to the Degree of Cleanness, according to the Time such Bedding may have been in use; but none of it in any respect, to the best of my Observation, insufficient, unwholesome, or improper.

Did the Bedding ever appear to you to be defiled by Vermin, or did any Prisoner complain, in your Presence, to such Effed ? — Never; I have made frequent Enquiries on that Subjed, and strictly charged the Governor to be particularly careful in that relped.

Did you perceive that Urinals, or like Conveniencies, were provided for the Cells ? — I have never been inattentive to that Particular, knowing how much it contributed to their Health and Comfort, and I never law a Cell without them.

Did the Cells appear to you, either from the Windows, or other Aperture, exposed to Rain, or the Entrance of wet in any other Manner ? — One of the Windows opens to the Passage, and cannot admit any damp or moist Air; the other, which is exposed to the outer Air, may possibly receive some Degree of Moisture from the Wind setting immediately against it; but I never once heard it complained of by any Prisoner, the Prisoner having it in his Power to prevent it by drawing up the Shutter, of which he has the entire Command.

Are the Committee to understand that each Cell has Two Windows, in the Manner described ? — Certainly j one over the Door, and the other in opposition to it: it is univerlal throughout the Prison, with a very few Exceptions only, that Two Windows are in every CelL

On the Ground Floor did you perceive any Marks of Rain or Wet beating under the Doors of the Cells ? — I do not recollect ever having perceived it, and I think from the Situation of the Cells it could not be, from the Situation of the Cells, and the Inclination of the Step outwards, it could not well be; there are Two. or Three Steps to ascend to them.

Are the Cells white-washed ? — They are; and are fresh white-waCbed every Year at least.

Is there any Allowance of Cloathing, or any Regulation relating thereto, adopted in this Prison ? — Cloathing is allowed to all Prisoners under Sentence of Execution for a Length of Time; and when either Vagrants or Prisoners from other Prisons enter the House of Correction in a filthy State, tl)eir own Cloaths arc taken away and clean Prison Cloathing is put on; this has no Application to the same of the State Prisoners.

Dr. Gl

The Prison was built on Ground, which was loose Rubbish, brought there after the great Fire in London in the Year 1666, which rendered it necessary to go a considerable Depth for a good Foundation The Rubbish consists of Brick, Lime, &c. and the River Fleet runs on one Side below the lowed Level, and drains it very completely.

Did you ever examine yourself the Quantity and Quality of the Allowance of Provisions given out, and did they seem sufficient and good of their Kind ? — I have been frequently present at the Distribution of the Food, and have not only inspected but taken a Part of it, and have always been satisfied both as to the Quantity and Quality of the Food prepared. The Quantity has been a Quart of well-made Broth of Soup, with Plenty of Vegetables, and Seven or Eight Ounces of Meat clear of Bone in the Soup or Broth.

Were any Complaints ever made to you on that Head by the Prisoners ? — Complaint was once made (about a Year ago) to the Committee, that the Weight of the Bread (which should be One Pound each Loaf) was defective; the Committee examined the Officer who receives and weighs the Bread, and found his Accounts perfectly correct; they then ordered the Complainers to be present, and to fee several of the Loaves weighed before them, out of which several were above Weight, and not one deficient; no Complaints have been made since (the Officer's Name was Wood ward.)

Is the Provision Allowance general, and given the same to all Descriptions of Prisoners, and if any Excep-ceptions, what are they ? — Alike to all, except in the same of those Persons committed for Treason or treasonable Practices, who have an Allowance from Government.

Have you any Controul over, or did you ever inspect the furnishing Provisions under that Allowance by Government ? — Although I never considered myself as having any Controul over it, yet having known that bne of the Officers of the Prison, by the Name of Ballard, had engaged to furnifti the Prisoners of this Description with Food, I have been induced, on my Visit at the Prison, to examine the Food so prepared for them, and I have always found it not only good, but of a superior Quality. I have examined the Butcher's Bills, and have feenthat he paid thefirft Price for every Kind of Meat; I was induced to this, having heard an Out-door Complaint that they were not wellferved.

You have said that the Infirmary was remarkably clean} in the Men's Infirmary, what Number of Sick might there be on your visiting it ? — When the Number of Prisoners Iras been between 250 and 300,1 never recoiled to have seen more than Four or Five at the most, and some of these rather confined by Accidents than by bodily Disease.

Are all sick Prisoners generally removed to the Infirmary ? — Always when the Surgeon (Mr. Webb) who appears to be very (kilful in his Profession, discovers that the Complaint is real, and not fictitious *

Are not Prisoners in every same removed to the Infirmary, when the Surgeon suggests the Propriety of de-Vol. 54.

Is Attention duly paid to the religious Duties and moral instructions of the Prisoners ? — All the Prisoners are required to attend Divine Service on,

Wednesdays, and Fridays, agreeably to the 40th Regulation, except that lately, in the same of the Mutineers, on a serious Design of endeavouring to make an Escape by a Ru(h from the Chapel, it was thought adviseable to dispense with their Attendance in future.

Have the Regulations, as adopted in Sessions, toge ther with those ordered by Act of Parliament, been hUng up in the Prison ? — Three Editions of the Regulations have been printed, and a Number of them have been always left in the Office, for the Use of any Body in the Prison; but they have been printed in such a Form, as to render it impoffibie to place them against the Wall of the Prison.

Might they not have been printed in a convenient Manner to be affixed to the Prison Wall ? — Certainly they might.

Have they at any Time been read to, or otherwifo communicated to the Prisoners in general ? — Not to my Knowledge.

Have you known the Prison froth its first Establishment ? — I have.

Do you uilderstand it to be a House of Correction, a Common Gaol for lafe Custody, or both ? — Its original Purpose was for the Correction of convicted Delin- quests; but it has of late been made use of as a Place of safe Custody for Offenders of various Descriptions, convicted or not.

At what Period was the Prison first applied for the the Two latter Purposes ? — Chiefly since the Con-1 viction of the Mutineers at the Nore and elsewhere, and since the Commitment of Prisoners for Treason and treasonable Practices j but the Magistrates have always conceived themselves at Liberty to fend Persons to this Prison for further Examination, and previous to their Trial.

Were any State Prisoners ever committed merely for safe Custody, and before Trial, to Cold Bath Fieldst before the Thirteen sent by the Warrant of the Duke of Portland ? — I do not recollect any.

Are you acquainted with the printed Rules of the Prison ? — -Yes, 1 am perfectly.

In point of Fa<ft, doth the Treatment of the State Pril'oners differ from that of other Prisoners ? — It differs very materially in many Respects; in the first place with respect to their Food, which is much more liberally administered; and in the second place with respect to their living in Society with each other, which is not the same with other Prisoners; and also with respect to their Exemption from Labour.

Might not a Prisoner be locked up by the Governor, so as not to be able to prefer his Complaint ? — I believe not, because, under every Circumstance, every Prisoner is Daily accessible by the several Officers of the Prison, namely, the Surgeon and Chaplain, to whom, such Complaint might be made.

Do the Two Justices, appointed at the Sessions to visit the Prison Twice a Week, visit it so often ? — Since the Appointment of a Prison Committee, the Office of Visiting Magistrates has been superseded, the Prison having been more frequently visited by individual Magistrates, since the Appointment of the Prison Committee, than when there were Visiting Magistrates.

When Complaint was once made, about a Year ago, as to the Bread, and you had it weighed, was this Time of your visiting the Prison known beforehand ? — It was on one of the stated Days of the Committee, and must have been known beforehand.

In the Adoption and Formation of those Regulations, load you any Idea of their Application to State Prisoners confined merely for safe Custody? — At the Time of the Formation of those Rules, the Magistrates had it not in their Contemplation that State Prisoners would ever be committed for safe Custody to that Prison.

Have you ever stated to Government, that the State of the Cold Bath Fields Prison was such as to render it unfit for the Reception of State Prisoners for safe Custody only ? — Certainly not, as from the Body of Magistrates, although in private Conversation with some of the Officers of State, the Inconvenience arising from the Unfitness of the Prison for the Reception of such Prisoners has been individually stated.

What is the Size of the separate Cells ? — I think Eight Feet by Six Feet Two Inches.

What is the Height ? — From Nine to Ten Feet.

Have those Cells any Fire Places ? — None.

Are the Windows glazed ? — They are not.

Are those Cells on the Ground Floor reserved for any particular Offenders ? — No.

Have you ever heard, on your Visitation of the Prison, any Complaint made by the Prisoners respecting the Dampness of the lower Cells ? — I never recollect to have heard such Complaints.

Has there been any recent Alteration made in any of the Cells? — I believe in Two or more Instances Two Cells have of late been thrown into One.

For what Purpose were those Two thrown into One ? — I believe for the Accommodation of Convalescents.

Is there any Fire Place in those Two Cells thrown into One ? — I believe there is.

Are the Rugs used to cover the Beds of the Prisoners thin or thick ? — The Rugs and Blankets have been both produced, and examined before the Magistrates; the former are as good, and the latter better than I have generally seen in other Places of public Reception.

Did yob ever discover that Mr. Arts the Governor, or any of the Persons employed about the Prison, fold Malt or other Liquor to the Prisoners ? — Certainly not. When I have seen Liquor, on my Visit at the Prison, brought within the Gates, I have never failed to enquire for what Purpose it was brought, and have always received for Answer, that it was for the Use of the Servants belonging to the Prison, and for other Persons employed in extraordinary Labour, for whom a certain Quantity of Beer, never exceeding One Pint in a Day, is allowed, at the Discretion of the Surgeon.

Have you ever had Reason to believe that Mr. Arts had any Interest in any Contract for feeding and cloathing the Prisoners ? — I never had.

Have you ever had Reason to believe that he took more than One Shilling per Night for lodging a Prisoner in a better Manner than usual ? — There are a few Rooms near the Entrance of the Prison, for which, by a Custom established long before the erecting of this Prison, the Sum of One Guinea per Week has been demanded and received, but not for the Governor's Benefit, but carried to the Account of the County.

Did you ever know, or have you any Reason to believe, that he has at any Time maltreated the Prisoners in any way whatsoever? — I have occasionally, but it has been very rarely, heard of the Governor striking a Prisoner with his Stick, and have made Enquiry concerning the Provocation; it has always been answered, that it was for refractory Behaviour, and sometimes in Self-defence.

Is the Time of your holding Committees generally known at the Prison ? — I believe always, the stated Days being the Monday subsequent to the preceding Session, and the Monday previous to the ensuing.

How can you know whether a Prisoner has any jeasonable Grounds of Complaint if One of the Visiting Magistrates do not, at every Time they attend, examine and inspect every Part of the Prison, and fee every Prisoner ? — The Magistrates assembled in Committee have invariably required the Governor, the Surgeon, and the Chaplain, to state the real Circumstances of the Prisoners, an<d to bring forward any Complaint which they

You have said it has always been answered, but by whom ? — By the Governor.

Is the Governor justified by the Rules in beating the Prisoners ? — I think not, except in Cafes of Self-defence.

Has he not a Power of putting a Prisoner into Irons ? — By the Eighteenth Rule he has that Power.

Have you ever had Reason to believe that Mr. Arts, since his Appointment as Governor, has been guilty of any Kind of Dictionefty in the Discharge of his Office? -r-Far from it.

In what Manner could the Prisoners get their Complaints to the Magistrates in any other Manner than through that of the Officers of the Prison? — I know none, except by Letters, by which Means Complaints have found their Way to the Committee; and by personal Application to some or other of ^ie Magistrates belonging to the Committee, Two or more of whom have very frequently gone round the Prison on the Committee Days, and conversed with the Prisoners.

Can the Prisoners write Letters to the Magistrates, or any one else, without the Inspection of the Officers of the Prison ? — They have conveyed such Letters to their Friends at the Gate, by whom they have been transmitted to the Magistrates fitting in Committee in the Prison, through the Governor.

By what Means can their Friends fend their Letters to the Magistrates without the Intervention of the Governor? — It is a general Rule of the Prison, that all Letters put into the Hands of the Officer at the Gate be in the first Instance delivered to the Governor.

Are the Prisoners allowed to convey their Letters to their Friends without the Intervention of the Governor ? — I believe not; the Governor's General Orders are, that no Paper go forth from the Prison, or be brought into it, without being submitted to his In-lpedtion.

Is it possible for them to do it by Stealth, Turnkeys, and other Servants, always being present at the Interview with their Friends? — I believe it is possiblej it has been often done.

Is the Governor not paid a Salary by the County, and to what Amount ? — The Governor receives a settled Salary of, I believe, £.300 a Year; and in Consideration thereof he is required, by the Thirteenth Rule, to take or receive to his own Use, nd Fee, Gratuity, or Emolument, except those allowed by the Table of Eees, from any Person whomsoever in his Custody.

You have specified personal Application to some or other of the Magistrates belonging to the Committee, who go round the Prison on the Committee Days, and converse with the Prisoners, as one of the Modes by which the Prisoners might state their Grievances; have any Complaints been at any Time made on these Occasions ? — I believe there has in several Instances.

Have the Magistrates, on these Occasions, satisfied themselves as to the Justice or Injustice of these Complaints ? — I believe the Magistrates have never failed, on such Occasions, to make proper and diligent Enquiry into the Ground of the Complaint.

Have the Friends of the Prisoners the Opportunity of conversing with them, upon Application being made to the Magistrates ? — Any Person applying to a Magistrate is admitted to fee and converse with the Prisoner by an Order from such Magistrate.

Is there any Thing to prevent the Prisoner, at that Interview, from dating to his Friend any Ground of Complaint he may have respecting his Treatment ? — Nothing; but this must be done in the Presence and within the hearing of One of the Servants of the Prison.

Are you, and have you long been, conversant with the Management of Prisons and Houses of Correction ? — I have for many Years past made personal Enquiries into the Care and Management of various Prisons in this Kingdom.

Do the Regulations and Management observed in the Cold Bath Fields Prison appear to you inferior or not to those of other Places of Confinement, since the general Reform of those Institutions has, in some Degree, taken place ? — The Rules, for the Manage-

Is the habitual Inspection of the Prison by Magistrates restricted to those who compose the Committee, or is Encouragement given to other Magistrates, whose . Convenience it may suit, to superintend and assist in the due ObferVance of the Regulations ? — Although,

a Prison Committee is established, and only the Members of that Committee are summoned, it is an open Committee, and has been frequently attended by Magistrates not named as Part of the Committee; I believe that every Magistrate feels himself at full Liberty to visit, and many of them do frequently visit,

the Prison independently of the Committee.

Have any Inconveniencies been found to result from the Opportunities of Intercourse between the Prisoners and their Friends at large coming to fee them in their Confinement ? — I believe that many Inconveniencies have arisen from surreptitious Communications between the Prisoners and their Friends without, and that an Escape of Seven Prisoners, on the ift of April last, was the Result of such clandestine Communication; it was impossible it could be effected otherwise; besides which, it is well known that Knives, Files, and other Instruments for effecting Escape, have been conveyed in consequence of this secret Intercourse.

Has the Prison Allowance of Food, the Prison Lodging, Labour, and other Particulars in the Situation and Treatment of the Prisoners, been often found, in fact, to prove injurious to the Health of Persons during their Confinement ? — So for from it, that in several Instances a gradual Amendment has taken place in the Prisoners Health; that several that have been long confined, even for the Term of Two Years, have been brought before the Committee previous to their Discharge, and have been observed to have every Appearance of most perfect Health.

Have any Instances occurred, tending to prove, in a moral Point of View, the salutary Effects of the general System observed in the Fields Prison,

with regard to Labour, Abstinence from strong Liquors (except in particular Cafes) and occasional Solitude ? — The Magistrates have, with Pleasure, observed that many good Effects, in a moral Point of View, have followed from a Perfevetance in their System of Discipline, and that Habits of Industry have been established, that a Proficiency in useful Arts has been acquired, and the Prisoner furnished with better Means of Subsistence on his Discharge, than he possessed previous to his Commitment.

What is the Conduct commonly observed with respect to Persons discharged from the Prison after any long Period of Confinement; and does it vary according to their good or bad Behaviour in the Prison ? — The Twenty-ninth Rule, respecting the Governor's Conduct previous to the Discharge of the Prisoner, is absolute; and he is required to see that every such Prisoner be taken before a Magistrate, to be examined respecting his legal Settlement, and his future Dispo-lal; and, in point of Fad, the Relation of the Prisoner, or some other Person in a creditable Situation, has frequently appeared, and become responsible for placing the Prisoner in a State of immediate Employment.

Has there been any Occasion on which the System of Discipline established in the Cold Bath Fields Prison, and the practical Effects of it, have received an honourable Testimony of Approbation from any of the Judges ? — The Magistrates refled, with great Satisfaction, on a Message conveyed to them by the Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench, near the latter End of November 1798, in the following Terms: " That his strongest Approbation U a cold Manner of expressing the Sentiments he entertains of the Conduct of " those, whose Angular and laudable Attention in fu« 44 perintending the Arrangement of the Prison, has so importantly contributed to the very useful Purposes for which it is intended; that the Public, and in- deed every Individual who forms a Part of it, mull feel the Obligation of such essential Services."

When these Rules for the Regulation of the Prison were made, was it in Contemplation that Prisoners would be committed there for safe Custody only ? — I am very sensible, that when the Rules were formed, it was in Contemplation to receive within the House of Correction Prisoners for Trial, to be kept in safe Custody, and also for further Examination but I find, on a Reference to the Minutes of the Prison Committee, taken soon after its Establishment, that such Inconveniencies were found to arise from receiving Prisoners of that Description, as to induce the Committee to recommend it to the Magistrates not to fend Prisoners to the House of Correction, who were only committed for Re-examination, or for Trial, except on special Occasions; because Prisoners in that Situation require Intercourse with their Attornies, which disturbs the Order and Tranquillity of the Prison.

When they were committed on thele special Occasions, were they confined to separate Cells ? — Generally so, except in Cafes which have been already mentioned, when Prisoners, capable of paying for that Indulgence, have been permitted to have the Use of a more commodious Apartment.

What Allowance of Food have Prisoners committed for further Examination ? — They who have Friends ca-1

pable of supplying them, have been permitted to re- Dr. ceive Food over and above the Prison Allowance, which is the same with that of the other Prisoners.

Have they any greater Indulgence than the other Prisoners, in respect of seeing their Friends ? — Persons committed for Trial, or for Re-examination, are allowed such Intercourse with their Friends as may be needful to prepare them for their Defence j nor is there any other Difference.

What was the Occasion of your Conversation with the Officers of State respecting the Unfitness of the Prison for the Reception of State Prisoners ? — The Indulgence which such Prisoners expect has been found to militate against the quiet and peaceful Nature of that Confinement, for which the House of Correction seems more immediately calculatedi

Is the Committee then to under ft and, that the Nature of the Objections stated against these Persons being committed to the Prison was, rather that they were unfit for the Prison than that the Prison was unfit for them ? — I think that Prisoners of that Description are less fit to be committed to the House of Correction than to any other Prison; and that the House of Correction is less fit to receive such Prisoners, than any other Place of Confinement.

Did you state the Prison as ill suited to State Prisoners, independent of the Effect of their distinct Treatment, Situation, and Conduct, in relation to good Order and Management of the other Prisoners? — I stated, that the House of Correction appeared to be unfit for the Reception of such Prisoners, on the grounded Experience, that more Disorder has prevailed within the Prison in the Course of the last Twelve Months, since which Time such Prisoners have been committed, than in any preceding Period of Time; and which I conceive to have arisen from such Prisoners not being subject to the ordinary Discipline of the Prison; independent of these Effects, this Prison is as fit as any other.

Whether any Instance is known of a Prisoner applying to a Magistrate for Permission to fee his Friends, have ever been refused ? — I know of none.

Have the Friends of any Prisoner ever been refused Access to him ? — This Question I can only answer with respect to myself: During Burkes' Confinement, a Person from Norwich, who called himself a Graduate of the University of Cambridge, obtained an Order from some Magistrate to visit the said Burkes; but his Conversation, in the Presence of the Governor, was of so dangerous a Nature, and of which the Governor had informed me, that upon his Application to me for a second Order, I felt it to be my Duty to refuse him.

I never should have refused a first Interview.

Withdrew.

William Wickham, Esquire, Called in,-and Examined:

Do you recollect about what Time the first Repre-fentation was made to you relative to Colonel s

Situation in the Cold Bath Fields Prifop ? — I cannot exactly recollect; but I can produce all the Letters received at the Office from Mrs. Defpard — The First is a Letter without a Date, but think it was sent soon after the Commitment of Colonel Defpard — The Second Letter is without a Date — The Third is a Letter f om me addressed to the Keeper of the Cold Bath Fields Prison, dated 4th May 1798; I also gave a verbal In-struclion to the Keeper of the Prison to allow Colonel Defpard to have any Books, except those of a political Nature. — I have another Letter from Mrs. Defpard to Mr., Ford, without a Date, but which I think was writ-

ten subsequent to the 4th of May, and previous to the 5th of June — I understood from Mr. Ford that he had t-old Mrs. Defpard that the proper Person to address was the Duke of Portland or me, in consequence of which I received a Letter, which I now produce. [Produces a Letter from Mrs. Defpard to Mr. Wickham, dated 6th June.] I never received any other Letters, except perhaps a Card, wishing to fee me. — I immediately carried the last Letter to the Duke of Portland, who considered the Whole of it, and directed me to fend for the Gaoler-, and give these general Instructions, without entering into a Detail, that Colonel Defpard should receive every Indulgence that the Nature of the Commitment, keeping in View the Nature of the Warrant in which the Word " dole" is used, and by which I understand " separate Confinement, and the Safety of " his Person," for which he was strictly answerable, would possibly admit, but paying Attention to Colonel Defpard's Situation in Life, provided his Conduct should merit it.

What were the Reasons which induced Government, confident with your Knowledge, to commit Colonel Defpard to separate Confinement in a House of Correction, in place of fending him to Newgate or any other Prison? — 1 humbly conceive that there are some of the Reasons which I cannot, confidently with my official Duty, or with the public Safety, at present disclose; there are others which 1 conceive may be revealed: At the Moment when Colonel Defpard was arrested, the Arrest of a very considerable Number of Persons was immediately in contemplation; it was not known, from Day to Day, to what Extent those Arrests might go; the Rebellion was expedited to break put every Day in

Ireland, and an Invasion in one or other of the Countries Mr Wickham.

was hourly expected. Government having Knowledge v — v '

of the Charge against each Person arrested, and against

each of those it was in Contemplation to arrest, did take

into Consideration the Manner in which all those Persons

could be confined with the least Danger to the State,

arising from their possible Means of communicating

with each other; no Question about the Nature of the

Gaol as a House of Correction was under the Considera-

tion of Government; its Object was, having Relation

to the Circumstances previously stated> the providing

safe Custody and Room for so large a Number of

Prisoners, and classing them in such a Manner as that

those, whose Communications with each other might be

dangerous, should be kept apart.

Was there any Period, between the 25th of April and '

the 25th of November, during which the Confinement of Colonel Defpard might have been less rigorous without Danger to the State? — It being a Matter of Opinion, I do not think myself competent to answer; but I know that during the whole Time that the Irish Rebellion was raging, and that Armaments were failing or about to fail from France to the Coast of Ireland, and particularly after the first Check the Rebels received.

Numbers of them were coming over here, and carrying on a Communication with their own Country on one Side, and with France, through the Medium of Hamburgh, on the other; Government had the strongest Reason to consider the Country to be in a State of Danger, and did so consider it. I have, however, no Hesitation in saying, that a more early Application of the Nature of that made by Mr. Reeves, coming from good Authority, would have been attended to, as far as ref'pects the Mode of Confinement in that House.

State to the Committee what passed, consistently with your Knowledge, relative to Colonel Defpard, subsequent to the 6th of June, and the Duke of Portland's Instructions of that Date? — The same Day, or the next,

I wrote to Mrs. Defpard, requesting her to call upon me; the came in consequence, and I examined her as to all the Points contained in her Letter; I, after having heard her Statement, sent for the Gaoler, and gave him the Instructions that I was directed to do by the Duke of Portland-, I particularly mentioned the Circumstance of his Wife being permitted to fee him with more Liberty, and I mentioned particularly, that he should make some Distinction between Colonel Defpard and the other Prisoners; I rather think I added a Reserve of this Kind, provided he behaved in a Manner conformable to his former Situation in Life; and with respect to that Part of the Instructions that I gave him for his Wife's seeing him with more Freedom, the Gaoler answered me, that the Indulgence which had been given, in consequence of my Letter of the 4th of May, had been ftiamefully abused; that I.otters and Papers had been carried in and out, and I think he said, one of the Wives of the Prisoners had behaved very violently, and collected a Mob about the Prison: I think I gave Directions at the same Time, that Colonel Defpard should have the same Allowance as those confined in Newgate.

I then questioned the Gaoler as to the Complaints stated in Mrs. Defpard'sLetter, as to the rigorous Man-

ner in which her Husband was confined; he allured me, that this Account was grossly exaggerated, but that he certainly should have the belt Accommodation that the Prison could afford. — I with to add, to what I have before stated, that I was ableat about a Week, in the Month of September, during \yhich Time it is possible that a Letter may have been lent by Mrs. Defpard, which I never received.

Did the Gaoler ever complain to you of Colonel Defpard's Conduct at that Time? — Never, previously to the 25th of November.

Do you think this is more the same now they are constantly together ? — They always had an Opportunity of communicating together.

As the Prisoners cannot communicate with their Friends, except in the Presence of the Governor or some other Officer about the Prison, what improper Consequences can arile from the Communication ? —

The receiving improper and seditious Papers.

I wish to Hate, in addition to my former Evidence, that a Baker, by my Desire, sent Veal and Pease once a Week to the Colonel, and a Fruit Pye once a Fortnight; Biscuits and Cheese most commonly every Two or Three Weeks, and sometimes a Fowl. In respect of what I have said-of the Colonel's Health, I beg to add, that when he was in the Cell, he said he had Chilblains, which were disagreeable and painful, and desired I would fend him some Stuff, which I got from a Doctor's, and he used it.

Mr. Matthew, who is a Magistrate, desired that Colonel Vol. 54.

Defpard might be called before us. I told Colonel Defpard that I had come there in consequence of seeing the before-mentioned Letter, and that 1 wished to know whether he had any Complaint to make relative to the Treatment he had received in the Prison, and what might be the Nature of it. His Answer was, that he had no Complaint to make against the Governor, or the Treatment he had experienced in the Prison; that his Complaint was against the Duke of Portland, as Secretary of State, having sent and detained him there, without bringing him to his Trial, under the Susperilion of the Habeas Corpus Act; that until the 25th of November, he had been confined apart, but that since that Time, in consequence of Representations that had been made to Mr. Wickham, he had been treated with more Indulgence, and had had a Room, with a Fire and other Accommodations; that in the Beginning of November the Cold had affected him, being subject to the Rheumatism; and that he had had Chilblains on one of his Heels, but that he had made no Complaint, and was determined to make none, whatever Treatment he might have experienced, as he considered his Grievance to proceed entirely from the Treatment of the Secretary of State. I observed to him, that, if he made no Complaint to the Surgeon, or to any one, of those Chilblains, which were Hated to be Ulcers in Mrs. s

Letter, he could not tax the Surgeon, or' any other Person, with Neglect; but that it struck me that, with his Determination not to make any Complaint, it was extraordinary that a Complaint to the Public, through the Medium of Mrs. Defpard, had made its Way into the Newspaper. His Answer was, that he had not been consulted by his Wife, or any one, on the Subject of the Publication of that Letter, for if he had it would never have been published. He also said, that Mrs. Defpard had frequent Access to him, and without Restraint, for several Hours at a Time. After thi§ Conversation, I went to visit the Cell in which Colonel Defpard had been confined until the 25th of November, it having been Rated in that Letter that the Cell was damp, and I found it then, as w'ell as upon a preceding Visit, which I made about a Fortnight or Three Weeks before, to be perfectly dry and airy, though no Person, as they told me, had been confined in it since Colonel Defpard's Removal. Withdrew.

This Man the Gaoler spoke very favourably of The Man said he had -no particular Complaint against the general Conduct of the Gaol, but that he was nearly starved in consequence of the very short Allowance of Provisions; that the Quantity of Meat, though Rated to be Half a Pound put into the Mess, he was lure did not exceed a Quarter, and appealed to us whether or not a Man could be supposed to exist upon that Allowance every other Day, with Fourteen Ounces of Bread, and the intermediate Days only the Fourteen Ounces of Bread. We then went into One or Two other Cells, which we found much in the same State with Doughtys, which contained a Bed upon Two Oak Planks fixed in the Wall; they spoke much in the same Language as Doughty had done, until we came to a Cell in which a Man by the Name of Was; he was lying on his Bed in a very deplorable State indeed, scarcely able to answer the Questions we put to him with respect to his Complaint. The Gaoler, upon my asking him why this Man was permitted to remain in such a wretched State of Health, and in such Weather, said, he did not know he had been so ill, but that fie would fend the Surgeon to him, whispering me at the same Time that this IVolfe was a damned Rascal. IVolfe gave us to understand, and was not contradicted by the Turnkey, that he had been for a considerable Length of 'fime confined to his Bed, and contiqually lpitting Blood; he looked shockingly ill. The next Cell we went to, was one in which a Man by the Name of Davis was confined. T his Man was also well reported of by the Gaoler, but he loudly complained indeed of the Shortnels of his Provisions, and all'o of several Articles which had been brought to him in the Prison not being permitted to reach him.
