This I objected to, considering it as extremely impertinent, that the Gaoler should make any such Proposition to Sir Francis Burdett. We then went into another Part of the Prison, upon Sir Francis Burden's defiling to fee a Mutineer by the Name of Jones (where a Man of that Name was confined) who very loudly complained of the barbarous Usage he had received, not only from the Turnkeys, but the Gaoler himself. The Statement of his Treatment was very feebly refilled by the Gaoler, and in a certain Degree supported by the Silence of the Turnkeys. I allude to that Part of the ill Usage he received from the Gaoler. He stated, that one Day looking into thff Court, which the greater Part of his Prison looked into, he was observed by the Turnkey walking in the Court, who damned him, and aiked him how he durst presume to look into the Court, or speak to any of the People walking the re. The. Man replied, and laid, he did not think there was any Mann in speaking to his Fellow Prisoners through his Grate. The Turnkey said he would shew him the Difference, and if he did not immediately go down he would make him repent it. Upon his making some Reply to this, the Turnkey in violent Passion. opened his Cell Door; with the Key which he had in his Hand he made a Stroke at the Prisoner, which.fortunately was lightened by the Key striking the Wall near the Bed on which the Prisoner fat, but at the same Time it came so heavily on his Side, that he spit Blood for, several Weeks after. His {pitting Blood was confirmed by one of the Turnkeys present. As a Proof of what he then said, he wished us to go into the Cell, where at that Time lie had been confined, where we should fee upon the Wall the Mark the Key had made. This not being controverted either by Arts or the Turnkeys we considered as admitted. The Gaoler made loud Complaints of this Man's ill Conduct during the whole of his Confinement, and declared that he had attempted to strike him, and he was therefore obliged to ule him with more than usual Severity. Jones implored us to hear what he had to say upon that Part of his Conduit now alluded to by the Gaoler: That in consequence of some Dispute or other in the Prison, Aris had ltruck l m; that upon his complaining, Arisordered Two Men to take hold of him; that when he was thus pinioned Aris beat him with his Stick until he broke it over his Back; this Stick he declared to be of the Thickness and Substance of the Stick I had then in my Hand. Aris did not deny his having beaten him, but on the contrary said he would do so to him or any other Person who should insult him in the Prison. So far from his being a Person of the Dil'position described by Mr. Aris, he begged of us to enquire of the different Officers with whom he had failed, and he would venture to stake the Truth of what he had said upon the Report of the different Officers, of his peaceful, quiet, and good Conduct during the Time he was under their Command. This Enquiry Sir Francis Burdett said he would make. I think it right here to llate, that neither I or Sir Francis Burdett, as he told me, ever belonged to the Corresponding Society. Joseph Ballard Called in, and Examined.

How long have you been employed as Cook in the Mr. Salieri. Cold Bath Fields Prison ? — Better than Three Years. —

Do you remember the Time when Colonel was committed, and came to the Prison ? — He was in about Five or Six Weeks before the 9th of June, which I remember by the Government Allowance being made to the State Prisoners on that Day.

For the Five or Six Weeks which you express, in what Manner, and by whom, was. Colonel Defpard provided? — He had oftentimes Things sent in by Mrs.

Defpard, and in regard to Breakfast, I furnished him the greatest Part of the Time; his Dinner was not regular; sometimes Mrs. Defpard brought him Things, and sometimes he had them from me.

When he had Provisions from you, what did you charge Colonel Defpard for his Breakfast, and what for his Dinner ? — One Shilling for Breakfast, and One Shilling for Dinner.

Did you make any extra Charges whatever on account of either Meal ? — None.

Did you serve him. with Supper at any Time ? — e No.

In the Meal at Dinner, did you fumish him with Bread ? — I did not.

Do you know how he was furnished with Bread at Dinner ? — He had the County Bread.

Of what Quality was the Meat you furnished at Dinner, and what was the Price Pound you paid for it?

— Mutton and Beef from Six Pence to Seven Pence;

Veal about Eight Pence per Pound.

How much did Colonel Defpard, during those Five or Six Weeks, pay you altogether for Provisions About Thirty Shillings.

Is that the Whole of your Charge to Colonel Defpard? — No; there is Twenty-three Shillings not yet paid.

Did Mrs. Defpard furnish Colonel Defpard with Provisions the Days you did not ? — Yes; sometimes (he brought a Meat Pye, which lasted a Day or Two.

Have you any Salary ? — I have 15J. a Week.

Do your Profits arise solely from your Salary ? — Yes, for the greatest Part; it is my whole Dependance, with the Help of a House and Firing.

Have you no other Profits than arise from your Salary, and House and Firing, which are allowed you ? —

There may be some little; sometimes I find myself, at the Week's End, something in Pocket, and sometimes not.

Explain how you could be out of Pocket at the Week's End, as you have a fixed Salary ? — I have so much a Head for each of these Gentlemen; sometimes I have bought more Meat than has served them, Vegetables, Butter, Sugar, and the belt Wheaten Bread. I mean to say, in providing those that have 13 4 per

Week, I have sometimes been out of Pocket.

When you are out of Pocket, is the Deficiency made up to you, and by whom ? — rl have said sometimes I was out of Pocket, and sometimes a little over at the End of the Week.

Doth the Exceeding of the one Week make you Amends for the Deficiency of the other ? — Certainly it doth.

The Reverend John Owen

Called in, and Examined.

Mr. Owm. Have you possessed Opportunities of becoming ac-; -y — ' quainted with the State and Management; of the Prison in Cold Bath Fields ? — I have gone there merely in the Capacity of a Clergyman at Times; from the Institu-tion of the Place, for the first Six or Seven Months, I acted as Chaplain; all that I have seen in the Prison is honourable to those who have the Conduct of it; as a Clergyman, I could not make the Enquiry the Magistrates could, but all I saw was creditable to those who had the Management of it;'I particularly observed I never heard an Oath from the Turnkey, the Governor, or any of the Prisoners.

Were your Visits frequent during the Time of your officiating as Chaplain ? — They were; constantly Three Time a Week to officiate in the Chapel, and at other Times to visit the Sick.

Did you take Occasion, in visiting the Prison during the Time of your officiating the re, to observe its State, and the general Treatment of the Prisoners? — I have frequently gone round the Prison and talked to the Prisoners; nothing objectionable occurred tome, but, on the other Hand, the Appearance of civil and kind Treatment; the Governor in particular appeared to be a Man of great Humanity, of which I could give many Instances, such as making little Presents to poor Women that were discharged, and speaking to all the Prisoners always in a kind Tone of Voice; his Demeanor, in every respect, appeared to me exemplary.

Have you occasionally, from Time to Time, visited the Prison since the Period of your regularly officiating the re to the present Time ? — Yes.

Are your Observations meant to apply to the Whole of that Period ? — Yes.

Did the Prison, or the Management or Treatment of it, appear to you to be injurious to the Health of the Prisoners ? — Directly the opposite; it appeared to me that their Health mended in many Instances; an Exception or Two in the same of some Mutineers arose from closer Confinement, in consequence of their boisterous Behaviour.

When there was any Sickness, did there appear to you sufficient Medical Care, and sufficient Attention paid to the Sick ? — There did, and all in the Hospital eemed to me extremely comfortable.

- Vol. 54,

Did the Building, and in particular the Cells, ap- Report on pear to you to be dry or damp ? — To ascertain this Fast, p£,^sd . £„, particularly after officiating on the ioth of February last in the Chapel, I went into the Cells on the Ground Tier; it was the Day on which the great Frost broke ^r‘ up; and I had the Satisfaction of finding the Walls, and the Floor under the Beds, perfectly free from Moisture. The Snow, brought in on their Feet, had made a little Moisture before the Bed.

Do you recollect the Time when you ceased to officiate as Chaplain to the Prison ? — I began about November 1794, to some Time in the Summer 1795.

Since you ceased to officiate as Chaplain, what Distance of Time has usually elapsed between your Visits?

— During the Summer I have commonly been absent;

I have been out of Town — The whole of the Time which I have been in Town, I have visited the Prison, with Intervals rarely of more than Three Weeks, and considerably oftener in the Course of the last Twelve Months.

When you visited the Prison, was it previously known at the Prison that you would be there on that Day ? —

It was never known but to the Chaplain, and very often not to him, because I have commonly called on a Sunday.

Was it your Custom, when you visited the Prison, to inspect the Whole, or the greater Part of the Cells ? — -When I inspected, it was generally confined to the Hospital; occasionally I have converted with Persons that were in their Cells.

Have you ever had Opportunities of seeing the different Prisoners, without the Presence of the Governor or Turnkeys, during the Time you officiated as Chaplain, or afterwards ? — I have occasionally spoke to some of them when no Person was within hearing.

Did the Prisoners, on these Occasions, make any Complaint to you against the Governor or his Assistants ? — No.

Did any express Satisfaction at the Conduct of the Governor ? — I have repeatedly heard them express Satisfaction at his Conduct.

Withdrew.

Appendix (N° 2.)

RULES, Orders, and Regulations, for the Management of the New House of Correction for the County of Middlesex; approved and confirmed by the Justices at the Michaelmas Quarter Sessions, 1794. London, printed by G. Stafford, Crane Court, Fleet Street, 1795.

GENERAL DIVISION OT THE PRISONERS IN THE HOUSE OF CORRECTION.

Class I. Prisoners convicted of Felonies: and other atrocious Offenders.

Class II. Prisoners convicted of lesser Offences.

Class III. Prisoners committed for Trial.

VISITING JUSTICES.

The Appointment of Two Justices at the Sessions to visit the Prison twice a Week, or oftener, seems absolutely necessary; whose Report of the State and Management of the Prison shall be delivered in Writing on their Resignation of their Charge on the County Day of the Session, when a Re-appointment shall take place, in such Manner as shall be judged to be most convenient.

II. Are the Prisoners properly maintained, respecting the Articles of Prison Allowance, Beds, Clothing, Cleanliness?

III. Are the Sick duly attended by the'Surgeon and

Apothecary ?‘and are Minutes entered by him in a Book provided for that Purpose, naming the Number of sick Prisoners upon every Visit, and the Nature of their Diseases ? ,

IV. Is there any, and what Care, taken of the Prisoners' Instruction in religious Duties ? and is their Attendance on Divine Service duly enforced i

IX. To fee, or order the Turnkeys to fee, that the Prisoners Daily wash their Faces and Hands; for which proper Citterns and Towels will be provided in each Yard near the Pump: that their Hair be kept iliort and constantly combed, and that this be done before any Food is delivered.

X. To provide Paillafles, or Linen Bags, for the Re ception of Straw; and acquaint the Visiting Justices when any fresh Bedding is wanted, that the same may be renewed; and to see that the foul Straw, Rags, and Filth of every Kind, be instantly burnt.

RULES, &c,

THE GOVERNOR.

I. To order every Prisoner, upon his or her Commitment, to be stripped and cleaned, and to be thorn or shaved, if necessary, and the Clotlies fumigated, baked, or destroyed.

II. To be exact in classing and separating the Prisoners, according to the Nature of their Offences; never exercising a discretionary Power when his Orders are positive; and taking particular Care, that the Male and Female Prisoners have no Intercourse with each other.

III. To provide a proper Book, to be kept as a Journal of the Daily Events of the Prison; such Journal to be produced when called for by the Visiting Justices.

IV. To execute his Office in Person, and to fee every Prisoner in his Custody once, at least, in every Day; to attend the Prisoners at the Chapel, and notice their Behaviour in his Journal: Not to absent himself for a Night, except on urgent Occasions; entering in the Journal, upon his Return, the Cause of his Absence; and to take Care that his Turnkeys, and other Servants, constantly lodge within the Prison.

V. To examine every Day the State of each Cell, in order to discover whether any Means have been made use of towards effecting an Escape, or whether any Mif-chicf has been done to any Part of the Building.

VI. To examine Daily the Locks, Bolts, and Bars of the Prison, and the State of the Irons by which those Prisoners are confined, for whom Coercion is found necessary; and note his Observations, on both these Articles, every Day in his Journal.

VII. To fee that the Talk Master, Turnkeys, Servants, and Assistants, conduct themselves with Prudence, Firmness, Attention, and Sobriety; and that they be in all Respects obedient to his Direction and Command; noting in his Journal such Matters respecting their Conduct as he may judge proper, for the Information of the Visiting Justices.

VIII. The Prison Allowance to be One Pound of Bread per Day, with an Addition of other wholesome Food, in Proportion to the Prisoner's Labour, at the Discretion of the Visiting Justices; but no Malt Liquor, nor any Liquor, except Water, shall in any same be allowed; except . when Wine is prescribed by th? Surgeon and Apothecary to the Sick.

XII. To have no Interest in any Contract or Agreement for feeding or clothing the Prisoners; but to take Care that neither the Prisoners nor the County be defrauded, and to keep Weights and Scales for that Purpose.

XIII. To take or receive to his own Use no Fee, Gratuity, or Emolument, except those allowed by the Table of Fees, from any Person whomsoever in his Custody.

XIV. To attend diligently and carefully to the Observations most humanely and judiciously made by Sir George O. Paul, in his Book of Regulations of the Gloucester Prisons, respecting the Nature, Degree, and Extent of solitary Confinement; to mark attentively its Effects on the Prisoners, and make his Report thereon to the Visiting Justices.

XV. To regulate the Confinement of the Prisoners according to the different Behaviour of Offenders, and ItriClly to observe the Rules and Provisions for keeping them, as directed by the Warrant of Commitment, or the Sentence of the Court.

XVI. To take Care that every Prisoner convicted by a Jury, and ordered by the Sentence of any Court to be kept to Hard Labour, be kept, as far as possible, in solitary Confinement; and allowed no Intercourse with any Person from without the Prison, except by an Order, in Writing, from the Committing or Visiting Justices.

XVII. To fee that the same Regulations be also observed, respecting all Prisoners convicted of any Offence before any Justice or Justices out of Sessions; excepting such Intercourse with their Friends, as may be needful to prepare them for their Defence, in Cafes where there is an Appeal or Reference to the General or Quarter Sessions, or other superior Courts.

XVIII. To put (if he rtiall fee Cause) Handcuffs or Fetters on any Prisoner who shall behave in a refractory Manner, or shew a Disposition to break out of Prison; such fettering, &c. to be entered in the Journal, with the Reason thereof; and to give Notice to One of the Visiting Justices within Forty-eight Hours; but not to be continued more than Six Days, without an Order, in Writing, from One of the Visiting Justices.

XIX. To hold no unnecessary Conyerfation, nor suffer his Servants to do it, with any Prisoner.

XX. To take Care that the necessary Correction be jjiven with Temper and Humanity, yet not in such a Manner as to render it either trilling or ridiculous; but with every Circumstance of Scrioulnels and Solemnity, and to be always given in the Presence of the Governor.

XXI. To abstain himself, and strictly to require his Servants to abstain, from all violent and angry Expressions; and by no Means to use Oaths or Curies under any Prorogation whatfgever,

XXII. It being unqucftionably true, that the proper Employment of Pril'oners is one leading Step towards their Amendment, especially when united with due Degrees of lblitary Confinement; the Governor is to provide Means for letting to work all Persons not sentenced to Hard Labour, and to let those to work who are lb i'eritenced, according to their Ability.

N. B. It is very difficult to enumerate the several Kinds of Works, to which the Talents and Abilities of the several Prisoners may be 1110ft properly applied: Of this the Task-master will be the fitteih Judge; and, if he understands his Buftncfs, he will so direct the Employment of every Person, as to render the Work moil beneficial to the Pril'oners, as well as moll; serviceable to the Public.

XXIII. To keep the Prisoners separate during the Hours of Labour, as far as the Nature of the Employment will admit.

XXIV. To examine the Contents of every Parcel, whether of Food or Cloaths, or other Matter, which is brought within the Walls of the Prison, before it is delivered to the Prisoner.

XXV. To demand of every Person committed for safe Custody only, and not inExecution, requiring to be lodged in a better Manner than the rest of the Prisoners, and able to pay for a Bed, the Sum of One Shilling Night; and to keep Qnc or more Beds always lit for Use, in Cale such Beds should be wanted. With respect to Liquor for such Persons, to adhere strictly to Rule VIII.

XXVI. To take Care that every Prisoner, when W'ashed in the Evening, having received his Allowance, be immediately locked in his Cell; and also to admonish every Prisoner, that, on his quiet Resignation to the Prison Rules, and his decent Submission to the Officers, will depend the Governor's Report to the Visiting Justices, and the greater or less Degree of Indulgence which he may expect to receive.

XXVII. That the Governor give every Prisoner to understand, that refractory arid obstinate Behaviour will be opposed by more than ordinary Punishment and Restraint, till the Mind of the Prisoner isfubdued.

XXVIII. That the Business of Washing for the Prisoners be executed by the Female Prisoners; and that they be allowed some Proportion of Recompence as 'other Prisoners working by Talk; that this Work be clone under the Direction of some prudent Female, to be appointed by the Governor, for the Purpose of not only serving him as a Maid Servant, but of being employed in inspecting the Female Prisoners when tick; and assisting, if qualified and disposed so to do, in improving the Morals of the Prisoners of her own Sex: Such Servant to receive extra Wages for attending to the Duties of the Prison.

XXIX. That he give Notice to the Visiting Justices, or, in their Absence, to the justices at one of the Public Offices, when the Time of Discharge of any Convict is approaching; that such Prisoner may be examined as to his or her legal Settlement; and, if the Justices shall think proper, passed to the fame; unless some creditable iHousekeeper shall appear, and be responsible for placing such Prisoner in a State of immediate Employment, to the Satisfaction of the said Justices.

THE TASK MASTER.

XXX. The 'I'ask-master to be appointed by the Justices; but in all Respects to be subordinate to, and under the Controul of tiic Governor.

XXXI. The First Bell to be rung at Six o'Clock in the Morning, from Lady-da to Michae!mas-day, and at Seven o'Clock during the Winter Half \ear; in Half an Hour the Second Bell to be rung, and the Prisoners to walh themselves, as directed by N° IX.

XXXII. After washing, the Daily Allowance of Bread shall be delivered to every Prisoner, in a separate Loaf, of the exact Weight allowed and directed by N° VIII.

XXXIII. That at Seven o'Clock in the Morning in

the Summer, and at Eight o'Clock in the Morning in the Winter, on every Day, except Sunday,?

Day, and Good Friday, the Prisoners be let to work, after Enquiry into the several Occupations to which they may have been bred; and, where admissible, that the Prisoner be set about the Work to which he or she has been accustomed.

XXXIV. That the Prisoners of the First and Second Class be allowed One Sixth of the Profits of their Labour; and that the Profits of their Labour be applied. One Sixth to the Prisoner's Benefit, and the Remainder to go to the County Fund.

XXXV. That One Half of the Profits of the other Prisoners Labour be applied to their Benefit, and the other Half to the County Stock.

XXXVI. That an Account be kept of the Profits arising from the Labour of the Prisoners; and that the same be paid to them on their Discharge, or applied to their Benefit, in such Way as the Visiting Justices shall direct: or approve.

XXXVII. That at Twelve o'Clock at Noon , except on Wednesdays and Fridays, the Bell be rung, and the Prisoners cease from their Work, and have their Allowance of Food; and that at One o'Clock the next Bell be rung, and their Labour be resumed.

' XXXVIII. That at Six o'Clock in the Summer Half Year, and at Sun Set in the Winter Half Year, the Bell be rung as a Signal for leaving Work; that every Pri-fonet be again required to be washed; that an Account be taken of the Work done, and the Tools, iBc. be delivered to the Officers of the Prison, to be safely laid up by them; after which, the Allowance of Provision is to be delivered to the Prisoners.

XXXIX. That a Clerk be appointed by the Governor, and approved by the Justices in Sessions, for the Purpose of keeping the Books, and performing such other Duties as the Governor shall require.

THE CHAPLAIN.

XL. Much of our Hopes of the Prisoners Reformation will depend on the Chaplain's zealous and conlcientious, as well as prudent, Discharge of his Duty: He will be required to read Prayers, and preach, at least once on every Sunday, and on Christmas Day, and Good Friday,

and also to read the Morning Service on Wednesdays and Fridays; on which Days the Bell, which on other Days would be rung at Twelve o'Clock, will be rung at Half an Hour after Eleven o'Clock, and every Prisoner, in Health, will be required to attend. On these Occasions the Chaplain, it is hoped, will occasionally deliver a {hurt, but affectionate. Exhortation to tire Prisoners, to confides their Situation, and to form Resolutions of Amendment. He is also to attend such of the Prisoners as are lick, and give them suitable Instrujftions.

XLI. Books of moral and religious Inftroction shall be provided, and distributed by tire Chaplain at his Discretion, amongst fudi Prisoners as can read them, when they shall either express a Desire, or even seem capable of being benefited by them.

All indecent Behaviour in the Chapel, or dif-respectful Treatment of the Chaplain, or wilful Spoiling of the Books delivered to the Prisoners, or any wicked or profane Language, shall be punished by close Con-'inement, either iri their own, or in dark Cells, according to the Nature and Heinousness of the Offence.

XLIII. In the case of young Offenders committed, as Apprentices, &c. some one of the more orderly Prisoners of the same Class shall be employed to instruct them on Sundays, and at other proper Times, in reading, and both shall have an extra Recompence, the one for learning, and the other for teaching, at the Discretiort, of the Visiting Justices; this to be under the Direction of the Chaplain, and the Degree of llecompence to be regulated by his Report.

attend; for the Time.fixed is from Twelve to Two on Saturdays and Mondays; that I may be allowed to take him Books; that the usual Allowance of State Prisoners may be given to him. This is all that I request; I do not mention the State of his Health; his Thirty-two Years Service to the Country, in Situations of Danger and in unwholesome Climates, the continued Embarrassments to which he has been involved since his Return from the Bay of Honduras. All I entreat is, that he may not be treated worse than the State Prisoners in the Slower or Newgate.

I am your Grace's

Most obedient humble Servant, Catherine

His Grace the Duke of 'Portland.

XLIV. The Chaplain shall Once in every Week enter a short Minute in the Journal, of the State and Behaviour of the Prisoners.

THE SURGEON.

X'LV. To visit. the Prisoners in the Sick Wards every Day, and to enter a Minute of his Attendance in his Journal; and also an Account of the Nature of the Diseases of the Prifofters, with his Reasonfc for ordering an extra Allowance of Wine, Provisions, &c.

XLVI. To suggest to the Visiting Justices and Governor such Circumstances as he shall think necessary for the Promotion of Cleanliness, and Preservation of the Health of the Prisoners, and enter the same in his Minute Book.

CONCLUSION.

It any Rule or Order shall be found, on Experience, impracticable or inexpedient, the same may be suspended, or relaxed, by the Visiting Justices, who are required to enter a Minute thereof in the Prison Book, and report the same to the next Sessions.

Appendix, No. 4.

Letter from Mrs. Defpard to his Grace the Duke of Portland.

\ly Lord,

I request your Grace's Attention, for One Moment, to my Situation, and that of miy Husband, Colonel Defpard, who is now confined in the Cold Bath Fields Prison, where he is debarred from Books, Pens, Ink, Paper, and Fire; not allowed to fee any of his Friends, not even me, except for a few Minutes, and among Felons, and :that at a Distance, with Two Doors between us, where he has no Allowance whatever; in short, he is treated more like a Vagabond or Felon, thari in the Manner in which it is usual for State Prisoners to be treated. Situated as -I am, and thinking of nothing at , this Moment but of alleviating his Distress, I cannot help intreating, that your Grace will be pleased to direct some Change to be made, in respect to his Treatment; that I may be permitted to fee him at reasonable Times, and not at the Time when all Descriptions of People

Appendix, No. 5.

Letter from Mr. Wickham to the Keepers of

gate, Cold Bath Fields, and Tothill Fields Bridewells'; dated Whitehall,4th May, 1798.

I am directed, by the Duke of Portland, to inform you that the Wives of the different Prisoners, now in your Custody under his Grace's Warrant of Commitment for Treasonable Practices, may be permitted to have Access to them at convenient Times, and in the Presence of some proper Person, to be appointed by you for that Purpose.

Appendix, No. 6.

Letter from Mrs. Defpard, to Richard Ford, Esquire.

Sir,

I take the Liberty, of requesting to know of you, if there is any Order from his Grace the Duke of Portland, for the usual Allowance of State Prisoners to be given to Colonel Defpardi who is confined in the House of

Correction in Cold Bath Fields Five Weeks next , without the common Necessaries of Life. When he was first taken to that Prison, he had one of the upper Apartments given him, which he found very airy; but since his Commitment he has been removed to the Ground Floor, with not so much as a Chair to fit on, or a Table to take his yiCluals off, where he finds the Mornings and Evenings very cold, and not so much as a Fire to warm himself; and where he is deprived of Books, Pen, Ink, and not even allowed to fee me but for a few Minutes, and that among Felons and People of the worst of Crimes. Iri consequence of I wrote to his Grace the Duke of Portland this Day is a Week, to request his G race will be pleased to direct some Change to be made in respect to his Treatment; but as I did not mention my Address, I presume is the Cause of my not receiving an Answer. I entreat. Sir, that you will be so obliging as to let me know whether any Thing is done, or will be done, to alleviate his Distresses, for, in short, he is treated more like a Vagabond than a Gentleman, or a State Prisoner.

I am,'Sir,

Your most obedient Servant,

Catherine Defpard.

Friday Morning.

Upper Berkeley Street,

Appendix, No. 8.

Letter from his Grace the Duke of Portland to Mr. Jr is, Governor of His Majesty's Prison, Cold Bath Fields, Clerkenwell.

Sir, Whitehall, 24th November 1798.

It having been represented to me by Mr. Ford, One of His Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, that Messrs. Bone, Evans, Defpard,

Webb, and Roberts, now in your Custody under my Warrant, are liable to many Inconveniences during the present inclement Season, in the Places in which they are now confined, I am to inform you, that it will be proper that they should be removed from the same to the Room fixed upon by Mr. Ford in your Presence, in order that they may be therein better accommodated.

I am, Uc.

Portland.

That the Petitioners have long since regarded with Concern the alarming and extravagant high Price of Copper, and every other Metal made therewith: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Importation of Irish Copper Ore and Copper Duty-free, in Aid of that Supply which seems wanting for the general Purposes of Manufacture, and for such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of Edward Hawkins, in Behalf of himself, William Roe, and others, his Partners, in the Trade of Smelting Copper Ores, and making and manufacturing Copper and Brass, carried on under the Firm of Roe and Company, was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to regulate the Importation and Exportation of Copper; and Setting forth, That, in the Year 1787, the Petitioner, and his Partners, finding it difficult to supply themselves with Copper Ore for the Employment of their Smelting Works, and for the consequent Parts of their Manufactory, did, in Conjunction with others, purchase, and set to work, the Copper Mines of , and other

Copper Mines, within the County of Wicklow, in Ireland, in which they have expended upwards of £.40,000, and from which they have derived some Supply of Copper Ore, charged however on 'Importation into Great Britain with a very heavy Duty, whereby they are precluded from importing Ores of low Quality, the Duty on such Ores operating as a total Prohibition and that, if the said Duty was taken off, a considerable Supply of Copper would be derived from the Importation of Irish Ore, whereby the Manufactures of Great Britain would be much benefited, and useful Employment would be given to great Numbers of Persons within the said County of Wick/oiv: And therefore praying the House to take the same into Consideration, and to adopt such Measures as shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, appointed to enquire into the State of the Copper Mines and Copper Trade of this Kingdom; and to report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And the said Address was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty's. most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, humbly beg Leave to assure Your Majesty, that we have proceeded with the utmost Attention to the Consideration of the important Objects recommended to us in Your Majesty's Message respecting the Connection between this Country and Ireland.

We entertain a firm Persuasion that a complete and entire Union between Great Britain and Ireland, founded on equal and liberal Principles, on the Similarity of Laws, Constitution, and Government, and on a Sente of mutual Interests and Affections, by promoting the Security, Wealth, and Commerce of the respective Kingdoms, and by allaying the Distractions which have; unhappily prevailed in Ireland, must afford fresh Means of opposing at all Times an effectual Resistance to the

destructive Projects of our Foreign and Domestic Enemies, and must tend to confirm and augment the Stability, Power, and ltefourcos of the Empire.

Impressed with thele Considerations, we feel it our Duty humbly to lay before Your Majesty such Propositions as appear to us bell calculated to form the Balls of such a Settlement, leaving it to Your Majesty's Wisdom, at such Time and in such Manner as Your Majesty, in Your Parental Solicitude for the Happiness of Your People, shall judge fit, to communicate these Propositions to Your Parliament of Ireland, with whom we shall be at all Times ready to concur in all such Measures as may be found moll conducive to the Accomplishment of this great and falatury Work. And we trust that, after full and mature Confederation, such a Settlement may be framed and established by the deliberative Consent of the Parliaments of both Kingdoms, as may be conformable to the Sentiments, Wishes, and real Interests of Your Majesty's faithful Subjects of Great Britain and and may

unite them inseparably in the full Enjoyment of the Blellings of our free and invaluable Constitution, in the Support of the Honour and Dignity of Your Majesty's Crown, and in the Prel'ervation and Advancement of the Welfare and Prosperity of the whole tijli Empire.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Swale, being examined, said. That there are, within the Township of Long Preston, in the Parish of Long Preston, in the West Riding of the County of York, several Open and Undivided Fields and Parcels of Ground, containing together, by Estimation, One Hunr dred and Fifty Acres, or thereabouts; also, several Undivided Stinted Pallures, containing, by Estimation, Four Hundred Acres, or thereabouts; and also, certain Parcels of Ground, called Long Preston Ings, within the said Township, containing upwards of One Hundred and Fifty Acres: That the Petitioners are the Owners and Proprietors of the Lands and Grounds within the said Open Fields and Ings, and also Owners of the Cattle Gates or Beast Gates on the said Stinted Pallures, and the said Lands and Grounds in the said Open Fields lie dispersed and intermixed with each other; and the said Parcels of Ground, called The Jugs, are frequently overflowed by Water from a

certain Rivulet, called Long Preston Beck, and from a certain River, called Ribble. And the Witness further laid. That the said Open Fields, Ings, and Stinted Pallures, are not, in their present Situation, capable of Improvement, nor can be occupied to such Advantage as they might be if the said Rivulet, called Long Preston Beck was banked, the said Lands, called The Ings, drained, and the said Open Fields and Stinted Pallures divided and inclosed, and specific Parts thereof allotted to the several Persons interested therein, according to their respective Rights in the fame.

A Petition of the Colliers, as well Coal Hewers as Coal Bearers, at lundry Coal Works in the Counties of Linlithgow and Stirling, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland: And also,

A Petition of the Colliers, as well as Coal Hewers as Coal Bearers, at the sundry Coal Works in the County of Ayr, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland: And also,

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to prevent Combinations among Colliers, and other Persons employed in the Collieries, and to regulate their Wages and Services, and the Conduit of Coal Owners and Lessees in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and to amend an Act, made in the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for altering several Acts of the Parliament of Scotland, respecting Colliers, Coal Bearers, and Salters; and Setting forth. That the said Bill is most arbitrary in its Principle, and is in direct Violation of the Personal Liberty of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law; and that they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the fame.

A Petition of sundry Coal Mailers, Coal Owners, and Lessees of Coal, in the Counties of Lanark, Renfrew, Stirling, and Dumbarton, was also presented to the House, and read; Likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the same contains Clauses which the Petitioners conceive are highly objectionable, and will, in their Effect, be most detrimental to the Intered of the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners also conceive there should be laid before the House, Evidence of the Mode of working at the different Coal Works in Scotland, and of a Variety of other Facts equally important and necessary, to enable Parliament to form a just Opinion of the Regulations proposed; but, as it will require Time to procure and to apply this immense Body of Evidence, as Time ha^ not been given for the due Consideration of the Bill, and all its Consequences, immediate and remote as it is, a Measur which is not confined to Coal Maders and Colliers, but extends to the Community, and more immediately concerns all Manufacturers, whole Exidence depends upon regular Supplies of Fuel, the Petitioners humbly conceive that a Bill, so momentous in its Consequences, and embracing so many Intereds, should not be precipitated through Parliament, bur should be seriously considered, after full Information had, and obtained, upon the Subject: And therefore praying. That the House will direct that Evidence of such Particulars, as shall appear to be necessary, shall be laid before them, before the Bill shall be passed into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the lame, and that they may have such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall Item meet.

A Petition of Laurence Craigie, Esquire, Lord Provod of the City of Glasgow, for himself, and in Name and Behalf of the Magistrates and Common Council of the said City, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Also taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the said Bill will not be confined in its Effects to Colliers or Coal Maders, or Persons concerned in the working of Coal, but it will extend to the Community at large; and that the Principle of the Bill appears to be impolitic and pernicious, in as much as it goes to impose Redraints which would destroy all Competition, and thereby diminilli the Number of Persons employed in working Coal, and that the Bill may therefore be attended with very serious Consequences, as well immediate as remote, to the Trade and Manufactures of the City of Glasgow, and its Neighbourhood, by obstructing or diminishing the Heady Supply of that Quantity of Fuel on which the Prosperity and Exidence of Trade depends: And therefore praying, in Behalf of the Magistrates and Council of the City of Glasgow, as Guardians of the Intereds of its Inhabitants, that the said Bill may not pad into a Law, and that they may be heard, by themselves, their Agents, and Counsel, against the fame.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a ' Second Time; and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves, their Agents, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

and a Half per Centum, on Exportation (fot which the

Merchant will be amply compenl'ated by the Facilities of bonding and warehousing) the consequent Reduction in the Prices of such Goods will operate as a serious Injury to the Sale of British Manufactures, and tnuft evidently subject every Individual, interested in this important Branch of Trade, to extensive Losses and Disadvantages; and that although the Petitioners entertain strong Doubts as to the Policy of holding out any Inducements which will have the Effect of increasing the Company's Importations of manufactured Goods, yet, if it shall appear expedient to bond and warehouse the Cotton Manufactures of India, the Petitioners trust that, when such Goods are re-exported, these Advantages will not exist to the Prejudice of British Manufactures in Foreign Markets, but ‘that the old Duties on Exportation may remain, otherwise the Confluences will be detrimental to the Manufacturing Interest of this Kingdom; and that the intended Duty of Two and a Half per Centum, on Goods and Merchandize

imported from India, apparently comprehends Cotton Wool, Indigo, and other Raw Materials, brought from thence for the Use of British Manufactures, a Burthen which the Petitioners conceive was scarcely intended by the Promoters of the Bill, but which, however, the Petitioners submit as necessary to be obviated by an express Clause for that Purpol'e: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, except with such Alterations and Amendments as are manifestly necessary to the Protection of British Manufactures in the several Instances before Hated; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against the said Bill, or that such other Measures may be adopted, for the Purposes aforesaid, as to the House may appear most eligible.

A Petition oif the thereunder-signed Merchants, Manufacturers, and others, resident at , who are

interested in the Cotton Manufactures of this Kingdom, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the same would become highly prejudicial to the Cotton Manufactures of this Country, if passed into a Law; and that India Cotton Goods imported are not only limilar in Fabric, but are applied to the same Purposes of Consumption as Goods manufactured in Great Britain; and as the Duties on India Goods are proposed to be lowered so considerably, and only a Duty of Two and a Half per Centum, charged on Exportation (for which there will be an ample Compensation in the Facilities of bonding and warehousing) the consequent Reduction in the Prices of such Goods will become a serious Injury to the Sale of British Manufactures; and that, although the House may think it expedient to sanction the bonding and warehousing of Cotton manufactured Goods imported by the Company, the Petitioners trull that these Privileges will not be allowed to militate against the Sale of British Manufactures Abroad, but tli^t, by a Continuance of the old Duties, or some other adequate Means, such Advantages will be fully countervailed; and that several Raw Materials uled in the Manufactures of this Country, and brought from India for that Purpose, appear to fall under the proposed Duty of Two and a Half per Centum, which the Petitioners conceive was not intended by the Promoters of the Bill, and they submit the Necessity of an Alteration in this Respect: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, except with such. Amendments as will, in the several Cafes before Hated, afford competent Protection to the British Manufactures, or that such other Measures may be adapted to those Purposes, as the House shall approve.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Merchants, Manufacturers, and others, resident at Freston and the Neighbourhood, and interested in the Cotton Manufactures of this Kingdom, was also presented to the

House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the same cannot fail to be highly detrimental to the Cotton Manufactures of this ' Country if passed into a Law; and that these Manufactures, yielding as they do an Annual Profit to the Nation from Foreign Countries of £.3,000 000 Sterling, and upwards, are peculiar Objects of Legislative Protection; and that Cotton Goods imported by the East India Company are similar in Fabric with those manufactured in Great Britain, and applied to the same Purposes of Consumption; and, as the Bill in question proposes to lower the Duties on Goods, and to leave them only chargeable with Two and a Half per Centum, on Exportation (for which the Merchant will be fully compenl'ated by the Advantages of bonding and warehousing) the proportionate Reduction in the Prices of such Goods will form an Impediment to the Sale of British Manufactures, and subject all Persons therein interested to incalculable Losses and Disadvantages; and that, however strongly impressed the Petitioners may be with the Impolicy of giving the least Encouragement to the Company's Importations of manufactured Goods, yet, if it shall appear expedient to bond and warehouse the Cotton Manufactures of India, the Petitioners trust that, when such Goods are exported, these Advantages will not continue to the Prejudice of British Manufactures in Foreign Markets, but that the existing Duties on Exportation may remain, or that some other Means sufficient to countervail such Advantages may be lanCtioned, otherwise the Consequences mu ft be seriously felt by the Manufacturing Interest of this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners cannot think it was intended by the Promoters of the Bill to include, in the proposed Duty of Two and a Centum, Cotton

Wool, Indigo, and other Raw Materials, brought from India for the Use of British Manufactures, although the Bill, as it now Hands, appears to have this Effect; and the Petitioners therefore submit the Propriety of an Amendment, for the Purpose of clearly exempting those Articles: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, but that such Alterations and Amendments may be made therein as are calculated to protect the British Manufactures in the several Cafes before-mentioned, or that the House will adopt such other Measures as will effectuate the Purposes fought for.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Merchants, Manufacturers, and others, resident at Bolton, and the Neighbourhood, who are interested in the Cotton Manufactures of this Kingdom, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Alfa taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the same would, as the Petitioners apprehend, be highly injurious to the Cotton Manufactures of this Country if passed into a Law; and that Cotton Goods imported by the East' India Company are similar in Fabric with those manufactured in Great Britain, and applied to the same Purposes of Consumption; and that the Duty which the Bill in question proposes to retain of Two and a Half per Centum, on Exportation^ scarcely an Equivalent for the Privilege of bonding and warehousing, whilst the lowering of the old Duties will materially reduce the Prices of Indian Goods, and become an incalculable Injury to the British Manufactures; and that if the bonding and warehousing of Cotton manufactured Goods brought from India, shall appear to be a Measure

of Expedience, the Petitioners trust that these Advantages will not be permitted to operate against the Sale of British Manufactures Abroad, but that a Continuance of the old Duties will be provided for, or some Means deviled sufficient to counterbalance the Advantages before mentioned; and that Raw Materials, viz. Cotton Wool, Indigo, and others, imported from

India, and uled in the Manufactures of this Country, appear to be comprized (although probably without Intention) in the proposed Duty of Two and a Half per

A Petition of the Dean of Guild and Merchants Petition from House of the City of Glasgow, was presented to the GuiW^ku of House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to prevent Glasgow, Combinations among Colliers, and other Persons employed in the Collieries, and to regulate their Wages and Services, and the Conduct of Coal Owners and Lessees in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and to amend an Act, made in the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for altering several Acts of the Parliament of Scotland, respecting Colliers, Coal Bearers, and,

Salters; and Setting forth. That the Prosperity of ajl the Manufactures established in the City of G/afgozv, and the District of Country connected with it, and the very Existence of many of the most valuable and important Branches of these Manufactures, depend on a regular and plentiful Supply of Coal; and that the Petitioners are seriously apprehensive that the Restrictions and Regulations proposed by the said Bill, being, in several Re-spefts, different from those established respecting other Labourers, may, if passed into a Law, induce many bred Colliers to betake themselves to other Employments, deter others from engaging in or about Coal Works, produce Discontents, and occasion Stagnations in the Business, with Consequences ruinous to those engaged in the Coal Trade, and many important Branches of Manufacture, and highly distressing to all other Manufacturers, and to the Country at large: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, or that the Consideration thereof may be delayed to another Session of Parliament, or that such other Relief may be afforded in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet,

Revenue; and that a Plan has been laid before the Petitioners by Mr. R. Dodd, Engineer, for the Improvement of the Port of London, by Means of a Variation in London Bridge, to admit the Shipping through, and by deepening the River, and building Quays and Warehouses on each Shore, between London and Black-friars Bridges, which Plan seems to embrace the Objcdts of Accommodation and Security to Shipping, and of affording perfect Protection, better than any Plan which has been yet proposed, with the additional Advantages of its being attended by a comparatively small Expence and Loss of Time necessary for its Execution, and without laying any additional Expence on Shipping, and, above all, that it will not occasion any Subversion of Property, or turning Trade from its present Course, and removing the Seat of Commerce; but that such Plan \Vas not laid before the Petitioners until the ill Day of April last, nor was it determined upon to make Application for a Bill until the ift Day of this Month: And therefore praying. That, under the particular Circumstances of the Cafe, they may have Leave to present a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for carrying the intended Plan into Execution, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, for appointing Commissioners to take an Account of Damages in consequence of this Act.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with a Blank, which being filled up, the said Clause was read the Third Time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, for restraining Ships employed in the Slave Trade, from touching at any Part of the prohibited Coast; and if it arises from any necessary Cause, the Ship shall not depart without making a Report to the proper Officer.

And the said Clause was brought up, and Twice read, with Blanks.

And it being proposed to fill the said Blanks with certain pecuniary Penalties;

Resolved, That the said Clause be committed.

Resolved, That the said Clause be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, immediately, resolve itself into'a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Clause.

Reports which, upon the 22d Day of December and the 19th Day of March last, were made from the Committee appointed to enquire into the State of the British Herring Fisheries, and into the moll eliedu.il Means for their Improvement and Extension;

Ordered, That Mr. Nicholas do make the said Report.

Mr. Nicholas Vanfttart accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read j and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Bobnties per Ton ought to be granted to Vessels employed in the British Herring Fishery, except for the Time, and within the Limits, to be specified.

Resolved, That it' is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Ten Shillings for every Ion be allowed for Two Years, from the 5th Day of 1799, to the 5th Day of April 1801, to the Owner of every Buss or Vessel, of not less than Fifteen Tons Burthen, which has received the Tonnage Bounty in any of the Three preceding Years, and the Crews of which shall, in the Space of Twelve Months, take or purchase from British Fishermen, oft' any Part of the Coast of Scotland to the North of Oban, and to the West of Dung-fay Head, or off the Coasts of any of the neighbouring Islands, such a Quantity of Herrings as shall amount, when completely cured, either as White Herrings or as Red, to the Proportion of Five Barrels of Herrings, of Thirty-two Gallons Wine Measure

each, for every Ton of her Burthen by Admeasure-ment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Five Shillings per Ton should be allowed from the 3th Day of April 1801 to the 5th Day of April 1804, upon the same Terms. *

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Bufles or Vessels ought to be subject to no Regulations with respect to the Quantity of Salt, Barrels, or Netting, the Number of Men to be carried out, the Period of clearing out, or the Time during which they shall be employed in the said Fishery.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all White Herrings intended for Exportation (except to Ireland or the North of Europe) shall be completely cured, and Twice packed in Barrels of Oak, Elm, Beech, Birch, Alh, Lime, Plane Tree, or Alder, containing Thirty-two Gallons each, and full bound.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,' That all White Herrings intended for Home Consumption, or for Exportation to Ireland or the North of Europe, shall be completely cured, and packed in Barrels of Thirty-two Gallons, of the same Materials, and quarter bound.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no ungutted Herrings shall be packed in the same Barrels with those which are gutted, and that these different Sorts shall be distinguished by some viable and apparent Mark upon the Barrels.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Barrels, in which Herrings shall be packed, shall be of the same Thickness as is now required by Law.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of Thirty-two Gallons of gutted Herrings, packed and cured in the Manner required for Exportation (except to Ireland or the North of Europe) be granted a Bounty of Two Shillings for . Five Years, commencing from the 3th Day of April

1199- .

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for every Barrel of Thirty-two Gallons of ungutted Herrings, packed and cured in the Manner required for Exportation (except to Ireland or the North

6 0 of

J

5io 3 M 1799 *

oiEurope)-be granted, during the fameTerm,a Bounty of One Shilling and Nine Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of Thirty-two Gallons of gutted Herrings, packed and cured in the Manner required for Home Consumption, or for Exportation to Ireland or the North of Europe, be granted, during the same Term, a Bounty of One Shilling and Nine Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of Thirty-two Gallons of ungutted Herrings, packed and cured in the Manner required for Home Consumption, or for. Exportation to Ireland or the North of Europe, be granted, during the same Term, a Bounty of One Shilling and Six Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of Thirty-two Gallons of Red Herrings, completely packed and cured, be granted, during the same Term, a Bounty of Two Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the above Bounties be granted in addition to the Bounties now granted by Law on the Exportation of Herrings, and paid by the Collectors of the Port at which and by whom they are ascertained, in all Cases in which it Hull be practicable without Detriment to the Revenue.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Ports and Places in situated to the

Northward of the Fiftieth Degree of North Latitude, shall, for the Purpose of the preceding Resolutions, be deemed to be the North of Europe.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Bounty be payable upon any Herrings until they shall have been inspected and approved by the proper Officer.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it shall be lawful to cure and fell Red Herrings, for immediate Home Consumption, commonly called Bloated Herrings, without packing them in Barrels.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Red Herrings, commonly called Bloated Herrings, as, are cured for immediate Home Consumption, without being packed into Barrels, shall be in-Ipected by the proper Officer, as to the Sufficiency of their Cure, and shall not be entitled to any Bounty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Quantity of Salt, for which Credit shall be allowed to the Curers of Herrings, ought to be fixed, with a Reference to the various Classes distinguished in the preceding Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of White Herrings,'packed and cured in the Manner required for Exportation (except to Ireland, or the North of Europe) shall be allowed a Quantity of Salt, not exceeding Three Bushels and an Half, or One hundred and Ninety-six Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every- Barrel of White Herrings, packed and cured in the Manner required for Home Consumption, or for Exportation to Ireland or the North of Europe, shall be allowed a Quantity of Salt, not exceeding Two Bushels, or One hundred and Twelve Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That for every Barrel of White Herrings cured in the Winter Season, that is to say, between the First Day of October in any Year, and the First Day of March in the Year next following, the Quantity of Salt allowed shall be in each respective same One Half Bushel, or Twenty-eight Pounds, lets than is allowed in such same by the preceding Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That for every Barrel of full Red Herrings shall be allowed a Quantity of Salt, not exceeding One Bushel and Nine Pounds, or Sixty-five Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That for every Barrel of clean Shotten Red Herrings 4

shall be allowed a Quantity of Salt, not exceeding One Bushel, or Fifty-six Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That for every One Thousand of full Red Herrings, commonly called Bloated Herrings, cured unbarrelled for Home Consumption, shall be allowed a Quantity of Salt, not exceeding One Bushel, or Fifty-six Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every One Thousand of Clean Shotten Red Herrings, commonly called Bloated Herrings, cured unbarrelled for Home Consumption, shall be allowed a Quantity of Salt, not exceeding Forty-eight Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Quantities of Salt now allowed by Law', Dutyfree, for the Cure of Fish, except in the Cafes in which they are varied by the preceding Resolutions, shall be allowed as well upon Fish cured for Home Consumption, as on those which are cured for Exportation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Power should be given to some proper Officer, to make a further Allowance of Salt in Cafes in which the Necessity of a Second re-packing of the Fish, after it has been completely cured, shall be proved in a latis-fadlory Manner.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Nets shall be used for the Purpose of catching Herrings, of which the Meshes shall measure lei's than One Inch from Knot to 'Knot.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Power ought to be given to some proper Officer to settle Disputes among the Persons employed in the Herring Fishery, and to punish Offenders against the Regulations which are or may be established, in a funv mary Manner.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Stamp Duty shall be payable on any Bond, Certificate, or other Instrument, required by Law to be executed for the Regulation of the Herring

Fishery, or for entitling the Adventurers therein to any Bounties thereon payable, and that no Fee shall be demanded by any Officer for the drawing up or executing of any such Instrument.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Herrings caught on the Coasts of the Isle of Man, either by British Filhers, or by the Inhabitants of the Island, shall be subject to the same Regulations, and receive the same Bounties, as Herrings caught by British Fishers on the Coasts of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon TuesdayMorning next.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors of Lands and Common Rights in the Open Fields and other Commonable Grounds within the Parish of Cheshunt, in the County of Herts, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, Common Lammas Meadows, and a certain Common called Cheshunt Common, within the Parish of Cheshunt, in the County of Hertjord; and Setting forth, That a very great Proportion of such Open Fields and Commonable Lands are of so bad a Quality, as to be incapable of any Improvement equivalent to the Expences of the Inclosure; and that the said Commons, in their present State, are well fitted for the breeding of Sheep and Support of lean Stock; and that many of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, who, by reason of their Residence and Occupation of small Tenements, have Rights of Common, are enabled, by the lawful Enjoyment of such Common Rights, to support themselves and their Families; but, as almost all the said Commons lie at the extreme Edge of the Parish, and are subject to very numerous and extensive Common Rights, any Allotments of the said Commons to the Idler Commoners mud be too small, and too distant from their Habitations, to be of any substantial Use to them, which Inconveniences are now prevented by the Use of general Herdsmen; and that the Inclosure of the said Open Fields and other Commonable Lands would be, in many other Respects, highly injurious to the Rights and Interests of the Petitioners: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the settled Estates of Robert Clutterbuck, Esquire, in Trustees, to be sold, and for applying Part of the Money arising therefrom, under the Direction of the Court of Chancery, in Manner, and for the Purposes therein mentioned: and for laying out the Residue in the Purchase of other Estates, to be settled in lieu thereof, and to the same Uses; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty, to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker, (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, being desirous of conferring a Mark of His Royal Favour on Sir James Marriott, Knight, late Judge of the High Court of Admiralty, in Consideration of his diligent and faithful Services in the Execution of that Office, recommends it to His faithful Commons to consider of enabling His Majesty to grant an Annuity of Two Thousand Pounds, clear of all Deductions whatever, to the said Sir Marriott, dur-

ing the Term of his natural Life, to be paid out of the Consolidated Fund. R.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties granted by the said Act on Raw Linen Yarn, being the Produce of any of the‘Territories or Dominions of the King of Prussia, and imported directly from thence into this Kingdom, shall cease and determine.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Journeymen Millwrights, working within the Metropolis and Twenty-five Miles round the fame, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the said Bill, if passed into a Law, would, in its Effect, be highly oppressive and injurious to the Petitioners, and all others exercising the Trade or Business of Journeymen Millwrights: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not be passed into a Law, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and tjiat the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being the Whole of the Sugar Refiners within or near the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for rendering more commodious, and for better regulating, the Port of London-, and Setting forth. That Persons carrying on the Business of Sugar Refining have, for many Years past, been subject to great Incon-4

veniencies, Delays, and Obstructions, from the Infus-ficiency of the present Legal Quays, and the Want of proper Avenues thereto, and it is highly expedient and necessary that some Means should be adopted for giving Accommodation and Dispatch to the very increased Trade of the Port of London, which will not be effected by the said Bill, but, on the contrary, lo far as respects the Petitioners, the Situation of the Warehouses thereby proposed to be erected, being so very distant from the Buildings now employed in the Refining of Sugar, will subject the Petitioners to incalculable inconveniencies. Delays, Impediments in Process, and increased Expences, together with Damage, Waste, and Depredation, which, from the Nature of the Article, and the Bulk of the Package thereof, could not poffibiy be avoided: And therefore praying, That so much of the said Bill, as relates to the exclusive landing of Raw Sugars, as being West India Produce, at the proposed Docks and Quays at the Isle of Dogs, may not be passed into a Law, but that such other Measures, for the Relief and Accommodation of the Commerce of the Port of London, may be adopted, as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Select Committee, who are appointed to consider of the Reports of the Minutes of the Evidence taken by the Committee, to whom the Bill for making Wet Docks, Batons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and also by the Committee, to whom the Bill for rendering more commodious, and for better regulating, the Port of London, were severally committed.

The Lord Hawkejbilry reported from the Select Committee, who are appointed to consider of the Reports of the Minutes of the Evidence taken by the Committee, to whom the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue within the Port of London; and also by the Committee, to whom the Bill for rendering more commodious, and for better regulating, the Port of London, were severally committed, and who were directed to report their Observations, together with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and Wholesale Dealers of the City of London and Borough of Southwark, and others interested in the Trade and Commerce of the River 'Thames, and the Improvement of the Port of London; and also, the Reports which were made from the Committees, to whom the said Bills were severally committed; and also, the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being the Whole of the Sugar Refiners within or near the City of London; and also, the Report which, upon the 13th Day of May 1796, was made from the Committee appointed to enquire into the bell Mode of providing sufficient Accommodation for the increased Trade and Shipping of the Port of London; and also, the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and other Wholesale Grocers within the City of London, and the Parts adjacent, were severally referred; and who are empowered to report their Proceedings, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had made a Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report; thereof, together with a Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followeth;

Your Committee have proceeded, in pursuance of the Order of the House, to consider the several Matters referred to them, and are desirous of Hating, in the First Place, their unanimous Opinion, that it is indif-penfably necessary, for the Accommodation of the Trade of the Port of London, that some Plan should be , forthwith adopted for the Improvement of the Port. — ' The great Increase of the Trade for some Years; the Prdspect of a Hill further Increase; the Inconvenience, and even Danger, to which Ships are exposed in navigating the River, and the Delay in loading and unloading their Cargoes from the crowded State of the Shipping $ the Advantages which several of the Out Port! have obtained from the Establishment of Docks, cannot' fail to impress on the House the Truth of this Opinion,- Your Committee regret, that though this Subjtft has been now under Consideration for several

nil. A 1799.

Years, no Measure should yet have been taken for remedying Evils so universally felt and acknowledged by the commercial Part of the Metropolis; and they trust that a Decision wiil take place, without further Delay, in favour of some one of the Plans that have been proposed.

Influenced by these Considerations, Your Committee have proceeded to examine the Three Plans submitted to them; the Plan of the Merchants for Docks at Wapping; the Plan which is called the City Plan, fot Docks in the Isle of Dogs; and the Plan recommended by the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and Wholesale Dealers of the City of London and Borough of Southwark, and others interested in the Trade and Commerce of the River Thames, and the Improvement of the Port of London, for newly construCling London Bridge, and for enabling Ships of Five Hundred Tons to lie between that and Blackfriars Bridge. Your Committee first examined the Plan recommended by the said Petition. — The Establishment of Docks appears to have so many Advantages, which a Tide River cannot, under any Circumstances, afford, independent of them, from the Security they give to Shipping at ever}' Season of the Year, and from the Convenience of lo'acting and unloading Cargoes in them, that Your Committee would consider any Plan for the Improvement of the Port imperfect, of which Wet Docks did not make a Part; but even independent of this Consideration, it appears to Your Committee, that the Part of the River above London Bridge could never be a convenient Station for large Ships; the re-building London Bridge upon a new Construction, might become a valuable Addition to any Plan that may be adopted, and afford great Con venience to that Part of the Commerce of the River which is carried on in Ships of inferior Tonnage; but Your Committee are of Opinion, that it could not answerthe Purpose of a Substitute to the Plan of Wet Docks.

Your Committee next proceeded to examine the Two Plans proposed for establishing Wet Docks at Wapping, and in the Isle of Dogs. Each of these Plans appear to Your Committee to have peculiar Advantages attending it, and the speedy Adoption of either would be a great Relief and Advantage to the whole Trade of the Port. The Contiguity of the proposed Wet Docks at flapping to the Centre of Trade, where the Merchants transact their Business; their Vicinity to the Custom House, and to the Warehouses already existing, where the Cargoes might be deposited without Delay; and, the Saving of Lighterage attendant on this Plan, are all Advantages with which Your Committee are strongly impressed, and which have recommended this Plan most ieriously to their Attention.

On the other Hand, the Situation of the Isle of Dogs is peculiarly adapted for large Ships, from being lower down the River, and in the Event of Docks being established there. Ships would enter more immediately from Sea, and would avoid the circuitous Passage of the Isle of Dogs, which is a Navigation attended both with Danger and Delay, particularly to Ships of that Description. The Rei'ult fieems to be, that the Wapping Plan would.afford the greatest Convenience to small Ships, which -comprize the far largest Proportion of Shipping and Trade. The Establishment of Docks at the Isle of Dogs would answer bell for large Ships, and particularly for those employed in th India and

East India Trades.

Your Committee have no Hesitation in delivering it as their Opinion, that it is desirable that Docks should be established in both of these Situations, and that they would be in no Respect incompatible with each other: But, considering how important it is that something should be done without further Delay, Your Committee have unanimously resolved most earnestly and decidedly to recommend the immediate Adoption of the Plan of the Isle of Dogs. They are induced to

39 Geo. III. i° Junii.

571

give the Preference to this Plan, from the very great Advantage of providing for large Ships in a Manner which would enable them to avoid the Danger and Delay of the circuitous Passage, from the conl'equent Relief it would immediately give to the Shipping in the higher Parts of the River, and from the Consideration of the comparatively small Expence at which it could be executed, and the comparatively small Space of Time in which it could be begun and completed.

Your Committee are sensible, that in the Adoption of this Plan it will be necessary, at lead in the First Instance, to require all West India Ships to make Use of the Wet Docks in the Isle of Dogs j but they are dif-inclined to the Imposition of any general and permanent Burthen on the Trade of the Port, especially as it might interfere with the Execution of other Plans for its further Improvement; they, therefore, recommend such an Alteration of the Provisions for defraying the Expence of the Canal and other Improvements proposed to be made by the City of London, as shall admit of the speediest Reduction or ExtinAion of the general Rates.

Your Committee have already dated, that this Plan for Wet Docks in the Isle of will not afford all the Accommodation to the increasing Trade of the Port of London that could be desired: They confident as a Part of a System which may afterwards be extended; but they think its Adoption in the Course of the present Setfion of l'o much Importance, that they would not delay submitting their Opinion, in this RespeA, to the House, reserving for a subsequent Report such other Matter as they may feel it their Duty to bring under the Consideration of the House.

Your Committee have subjoined to their Report, by way of Appendix, the Reports of the Elder Brethren of the Trinity House, and the Report of the Commissioners of His Majesty's Cudoms, upon the several Plans referred to their Consideration by the Committee.

In conformity to what has been dated in this Report, Your Committee have come to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Bill for rendering more commodious, and for better regulating, the Port of should be pro-

ceeded on without further Delay.

At a General Court of the Corporation of Trinity House, held on Monday the 27th of May 1799 i

The amended Plans of the City of London, and of the Merchants, which were under the Consideration of the Court on Thursday last, upon the Reference of the Committee of the Honourable House of Commons, being taken into further Consideration this Day, as te which is moil preferable for the immediate Accommodation of the Port of London j

It was Resolved,

wich, and Limehouse Reaches, would thereby be rendered unnecessary to the largest Ships, and the Navigation be more immediately relieved, this Court are of Opinion, to recommend that the Docks at the Ife of Dogs be-the First to be carried into Effect.
