We Report,

That the Order appears to us to direct our Attention to Two specific Objects, a Comparison of the Plan of the proposed London Docks with a Plan of the proposed Canal and Wet Docks for the West India Trade in the Isle of Dogs; and a Comparison of both Plans with any other Plans for the Improvement of the Port of , which have been antecedently referred to us.

Having with due Attention considered the Order and the Subject to which it relates, and in what Mode we might belt yield Obedience thereto, and fulfil the Purport thereof, we beg Leave to state, that various Plans for the Improvement of the Port of London have at different Periods been referred for our Opinion; that we have repeatedly, with all becoming Care upon so important a Subject, exerted our bell Diligence and Judgment in the Attainment of Information, and in examining and considering the several Plans proposed, according to the Principles Which it behoved us to have stedfastly in View, the Safety of Revenue, and the Welfare and Accommodation of Trade; and after very mature Deliberation have suggested in several Reports to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, what we thought most confident with, and conducive to, those great Objects. That if from any Light afforded, or Information obtained, since we had the Honour of fub-mitting the Reports alluded to, we were enabled to offer additional Observation or Suggestion, material to the more speedy or effectual Accomplishment of the Object in View or if we had found Realoh to deviate from or modify the leading Opinions therein given, it would be highly satisfkdtory to us to have the present Occasion of tendering such supplethental or corredVive Matter; but having taken into Cortsideration the Order of the Select Committee, and having carefully revised and rt-considered our Reports on the Subject, fthd the Materials whereon they were founded, we think, however strongly impressed we are with Zeal and Desire to contribute what Aid might lie in our Power in furtherance of a National Concern of such Moment as the carrying the Port of London to the highcfl practicable State of Improvement, We can in no Way more expeditiously or efficaciously gratify such our Desire, and obey the Order ehjoindd, than by transmitting to the Select Committee N" 1,2, 3. Copies of the Reports to which We allude, and which we accordingly anhex, thereby bringing into one col-lective and methodised View, the general Refill t of the extensive Investigation, at fiiccessive Periods, directed to this Subject, after every Exertion of Diligence and Consideration on our Part. Taking Leave thus to fub-mit these Reports, and particularly that of the 16th May 1796, as containing the most useful and comprchen-five Matter that occurs to us applicable to the Subject at large, we trust we shall have furnished the belt Criterion and Ground within our Province and Capacity for instituting the relative or general Comparison pointed out by the Committee, and for judging how far either of the Plans proposed accord with, or tend to the System, jn our Opinion, belt adapted to the most perfect State of Improvement of which the Port is fcapable, in the conjoined View of Commerce and Revenue *

Apprehending, however, from the Order, that the Comparison of the Merits of the Two Plans transmitted might be more especially within the Contemplation of the Committee; and that it was their Pleasure that such Information as we could procure ihovlld be had with a

?eculiar Dispatch, we immediately, upon receiving the )rder, deferred the same to the several practical Branches of the Department, which, according to the regular official Course of Proceeding, it was riccessary toconiult, and urged Returns to the References with all Expedition, and if possible within a Time limited. The consequent Returns obtained from these Departments, contain elsential Diversity Of Opinion touching the relative Merits and Expediency of the Two Plans; and we have therefore judged it most fit and proper on our Part in a Matter of fufch high and general Concern, not to fub-ttiit Extfadts therefrom, or the general Substance thereof, 4,5,6, but to transtnit Copies of all the Returns for the Inspec- yt 3, <y. tlon of the Committee.

Recutring to certain of the leading Principles which governed us, ih framing Opinions oh the Plans for the Improvement of the Port of London, heretofore submitted, we think it right to observe, that should the Syftfcm of Docks be adopted not limply as Receptacles of Ships, in Eafeliient of the crowded State of the River, or for the Purpose of unloading the Cargoes of Vessels into Lighters, to be afterwards discharged at the Legal Quays, but for ultimate Examination, Ascertainment of the Duties due to the Crown, and Delivery, the Plan of the London Docks, in the elsential Circumstance of Contiguity to the Centre and Seat of Business; has obvious Claim to Preference; and that on the other Hand the Plan of the PVeJl India Trade, though less eligible in regard of Locality, being designed for the Reception of one valuable and extensive Branch of Commerce, is more consonant with that Appropriation and Distinction which we recommended wherever It could with Propriety be introduced, as highly conducive to the mutual Accommodation iud Benefit of Trade and Revenue.

It mdy riot be immaterial to remark, that both of the Plans, as we Understand them, are confined to Imports, and tonfequentiy it does hot appear how far a Separation or Ihtermixtafe Of the Import and Export Trade maybe intended.

Regarding the Canal, coririedted with the Plan for the Docks in the Isle of Dogs, in a View to the Security of Revenue, to which our Attention is peculiarly demanded, we tlilhk this Part of the Proposition liable to Weighty Obiedtion.

Having thus submitted our former Reports, for the general Improvement of the Port, to the Attention of the Committee, we trust it will be needless to observe, that neither of the Plans how in Discussion comprize various general Objects, as well respecting the hiver as the Conduct of the Business upon Land, w'hich, clatfed and ranged under principal and leading Heads, we represented, and Hill deem to be elsential to that enlarged and comprehensive Scale of Improvement luited to the Port of London.

The Reduction of Public Expence, in railing the Revenue entrusted to our Management, is stated to be one of the beneficial Effects connected with the Dock Plan.

Upon this Aloft important Object it is impracticable for us to form at prelertt any Warranted Opinion. The Diminution of Expence, incurred for the Services of inferior Officers of Two Descriptions, denominated Tidewaiters and Cartfollowers, Would undoubtedly be occasioned by Curtailment of the Time the former Clals of Officers remain Rationed on board Ships, and by a Discontinuance of the Necdfity of employing the latter in the Custody and Conveyance of the Articles, by this Plan immediately to be lodged in WarehoUfts; but how far ah Augmentation of the Number of another Description of Officers, for the fecUre unlading and Delivery of Merchandize Under this new System, upon a Quay of large Extent and remote from the Custom House, might be requisite, and how the general Result of Saving and ofincreased Expenditure in these Respects might ultimately stand, we have no Data whereon to

§9 Geo. til. i° yuni573

toft any Calculation of sufficient Weight to be laid before the Committee.

We doubt not should the Dock Sydem take Effect, that every possible Measure of Precaution and Care to ward off the Calamity of Fire will be devised, and enforced with the most rigid Punctuality and circumspection. Whild, however, a Misfortune of so dreadful a Nature, and of such extensive Injury, in a Place where Masses of Property to very large Amount must be deposited, is in Possibility, we thought it a Duty incumbent upon us to ascertain, by the Authority of the Law Officers of our Department, how far the proposed Principle of placing Ships and their Cargoes under joint Custody of the Crown and Merchant, might expose the Crown to Loss and Responsibility in the unhappy Event of such an Evil, or in the same of Plunderage or Robbery; they have given it as their Opinion, that the Crown will not in either Instance be responsible.

The Committee will be pleased to notice, that we have avoided going into Diicuffion or Detail upon any of the Regulations annexed to or requisite for the carrying into Completion either of the Plans, and this we have designedly and out of Caution done, being of Opinion that it would be premature and unsafe to pledge ourselves in so early a Stage to their Aptitude and Propriety; and that at all Events, whatever Plan may be finally feleCled for the Improvement of the Port of London, the subordinate System of Provision and

Regulation for the Execution thereof, would, with more Safety and Fitness; be Matter of future Consideratioil.

Report of the Commissioners of the Customs to the Lords of the Treasury, on the Improvement of the Port of London. — 16th , 1796.

May it please your Lord ships: x> Mr. Long having, by his Letter of the 8th of March in Appendirt last, signified, that having laid before your Lord ships a (C.) Memorial of the Ibid.Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, representing, that the Execution of the Plan proposed in a Bill now depending in Parliament, for making Wet Docks and Wharfs in Wopping, will be an Infringement upon their Charters, and upon the Rights and Privileges of various other incorporated Societies, as well as Individuals; and submitting Plans and Surveys for the making Wet Docks, and providing such other Accommodations as the increased Trade of the Port of London may require, within the Limits of the present Legal Quays; he (Mr. Long) is commanded by your Lordships to refer the said Memorial, with the accompanying Plans and Surveys, to us, and to desire that we will report our Opinion upon the comparative Advantage of this Plan, and that which was before referred to us, in general, and particularly as far as relates to the Security of the Revenue under our Management; and further signifying your Lordships Desire, that we will enquire into the Practicability of Ships of a large . In obedience to your Lordships several Commands, thus communicated to us.

We Report,

That we are well aware of the Importance of the Subject Matter referred for our Consideration, namely, the Improvement of the Port of London. Under this Impression we have exerted our utmost Diligence and Attention to obtain such Information, and collect such Documents, as might bed enable us to form a Judgment thereon; and have, with Cate, Caution, and Deliberation, weighed the Information and Materials procured for that End.

Having Regard to the Magnitude of the Object in Contemplation, the Variety of Plans and Suggestions offered for the Attainment thereof, and the many ancj extensive Confederations, principal or subordinate, connected therewith, we have thought it most conducive to Order and Perspicuity, and indeed essentially requisite for our clear and methodical Guidance in this compre-hensive Enquiry, to select those Points and Branches of the Subject, which more direCUy appertain to our Province, and to disguised the Matter so selected under didinct and leading Heads.

Before we proceed to this Arrangement, the following preliminary Remarks may not improperly be introduced — The Necessity of this Inveitigation, and the- Utility of the Measure to which the several Proposals relate, red on the Ground that the Accommodation at present legally afforded to the Merchant in the Port of London, for the Dispatch of his Business, and the Security of his Property, is inadequate.

The Truth of this Postion is so obvious and acknowledged, that it mud be unnecessary, and it might be deemed a Wade of your Lordships Time, to enter into any Reasoning thereon.

A Companion of the Trade and Shipping of the Port of London, about the Period when the Legal Quays or Wharfs now in Exidence were set out and appointed, with the actual State thereof at this Day, presents ample Proof, not merely of the Fact in this relative View, but also incontedable Demondration of the vad Extent to which the Commerce of this Kingdom has happily attained.

The progressive Increase of that Commerce, especially within these late Vears; the Credit and mercantile Spi-

and the Situation, at this Juncture, of Countries in Europe, heretofore out Rivals, appear to justify a Con-elusion, that the Trade of Great Britain is capable of, and to warrant a rational Expectation that it will be carried to, far greater Extent. To afford the Trade of the Port of London, which constitutes a material Portion of that of the Kingdom at large, every fair and expedient Accommodation, and to provide such Convenience for the Merchant as may invite and facilitate his Plans for the Enlargement of Commerce, must, we think, be deemed an Object of high national Concern. — The public Trust committed to our Management demands it of us, as a peculiar and primary Duty, to have special Regard to, and keep a vigilant Watch over, the Collection of the Revenue derived from the Commerce of this Kingdom, and the faithful Execution of Laws framed for the Guard of that Revenue, the Prevention of illicit, and the Support and Advancement of honest Trade. — This Object must, with us, be anterior to all other Considerations; and no Plan or Proposition inconsistent therewith, or in any Way repugnant thereto, can have our Sanction or Approbation. — But whilst we lay down this as a fundamental Principle for our Government, we ate ready at the same Time to admit, that we do not apprehend a strict Adherence to this Duty on our Part will be ad-' verse. to the general Measure had in View by the Merchants and Traders of the Port of London.

The Plans offered for the Improvement of the Port are Five in Number: One by the Merchants — Two by the City of London — One by Mr. Samuel Wyatt — and One by Mr. Edward Ogle. These Plans, taken in the Aggregate, import to connect the greater Security of the Revenue, and a more effectual Safeguard against illegal and iniquitous Practices, with the better Accommodation of Trade. As far as these Two Objects are in strict Union, it behoves us to regard the Measure as beneficial and ialutary. Indeed it is a plain and self-evident Truth, that the Augmentation of the Trade of this Realm must increase the Public Revenue, and contribute to National Prosperity.

Having assumed that the Port of London labours under certain Inconveniencies, Difficulties, and Embarrassments, in the conducting its Trade, from which it ought to be and may be relieved, the natural Order of Proceeding seems to be, to ascertain the Causes of those Evils, and to apply the belt and most effectual Means for their Removal.

The Evils complained of may be referred to Four great Sources:

1 ft. The Inadequacy in Point of Extent of the Legal Quays.

2d. The crowded and obstructed State of the River.

3d. The Want of a proper Arrangement and Distribu-tion of the Business on the Quays.

4th. The Want of a well-ordered System in the Dif-position of Vessels in the River, and in the Management of Lighters and Craft.

There are other secondary and subordinate Causes, which contribute to the Grievance in question, and which will be adverted to in their proper Places.

Having stated the leading and principal Causes of the Inconvenience and Obstruction experienced by the Merchants, we shall now investigate and difeufs the several Proposals offered for their Easement and Relief, in the Order above stated.

Q_U AYS.

For the first and principal Evil, the Inadequacy of the present Legal Quays, the plain and foie Remedy is their Extension. The Quantum of that Enlargement, and the most fit and commodious Places for such Addition, are the Points in Research. A Sufficiency of Space, and Capacity within reasonable and expedient

KA

Limitations, yielding rather Amplitude for; than tend- ing to Confinement in the Transaction of Business on the Quays, ought , we think; to be provided for the Merchant. The Concerns of Revenue, we are of Opinion, would profit by such a System. The Officers, whole Duty it is to att upon the Quays, would be enabled to discharge every Branch of the Employment in a more orderly; accurate, and perfect Manner; Dispatch, alike advantageous to the Crown and the Merchant, would be promoted; dtie Examination; In-spedtion, Superiritendance, and Controul, would be facilitated thereby; Irregularity, Error, Delay, Fraud, and Plunderage, occasioned or covered by Crowd, Confofion, and Intermixture of the different Species of Goods, must necessarily be less frequent, and qbviously be more open to Detection.

The Modes proposed for the Attainment of an Extension of Quays by the Merchants we only learn by a Bill now pending in Parliament, and an engraved Plan transmitted to us. By the 41st Section of the said Bill, we observe it is provided,

" And for the more general Benefit of Shipping, and " of the Trade and Commerce of the said Port, the " said Company shall and may also build, or cause to " be bvlilt, from Time to Time, Quays and Wharfs " adjoining to the said Docks and Batons, convenient " and sufficient for the Trade and Business of the Dock; " for the landing and discharging, lading and shipping " of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize that may or " shall at any Time or Times be legally landed or shipped at the said Quays or Wharfs; and for the greater " Accommodation of the Trade of the Port of " the said Quays and Wharfs shall be deemed and taken, " and are hereby declared to be deemed and taken,.to " all Intents and Purposes whatsoever. Legal Quays and " Wharfs for the landing, re-landing, and discharging " lading and shipping of any Goods, Wares,- and Merchandizes whatsoever, within the Port of ."

A general Power is here given to the intended London Dock C.ompany for building, from Time to Time, Quays, or Wharfs, adjoining to Docks or Basons proposed to be formed, within certain Limits prescribed in the Bill; the only Conditions annexed to the Construction of such Quays arid Wharfs are, that they shall be adjoining to the said Docks and Basons, and be convenient and sufficient to the Trade and Business of the landing and discharging, lading and shipping, of any Goods, Wares, and Merchandize that may and shall at any Time or Times be legally landed or shipped at the said Quays and Wharfs.

Of the Fitness and Propriety of the Quays themselves, thus proposed to be made, we have no Materials for judging. Their Capacity, Extent, Breadth, and Openness, with other Circumstances forming essential Requisites for the right Constitution of a Legal Quay, are no ways explained or provided for. As we understand the Bill, the mere Act of constructing Wharfs and Quays, according to the Mode therein prescribed, immediately imparts to them the full Properties and Rights of Legal Quays, to all Intents and Purposes.

The Extent of Quay thus legalized, where, of consequence, the Merchant has a Right to claim the Attendance of the discharging Officer, might be carried under the Sanction of such a Law to a very great and excessive Degree, and the Number of Officers necessary for the Port be extremely and unnecessarily multiplied.

Under the Force of these Observations, if just, it is not in our Power to report with becoming Accuracy, or indeed to form any founded Opinion on the Aptitude of the Quays thus to be conftnnfted, though we have no Reason to doubt the Discretion of the Company, and proper Application of the Powers so vested in them.

But in this Place we take Occasion to introduce a Remark, applicable to the Subject in general. It is

this:

,. The Proposition of a Quay, thus covered, is, in our Opinion, altogether objectionable, as excluding Light and Operiness, as incommodious to the Officer in the Execution of his Duty; not favourable to the free Dispatch of Business; and pregnant with Danger, by affording Opportunities for Concealment, Pillage, Depredation, and Fraud, both by Night and by Day, to the Injury of the Crown and the Merchant.

kr. WYATT'S PLAN.

The great Object of this Plan does not appear to be the Extension or Enlargement of, or Addition to the Legal Quays, for the Purpose of carrying on the Merchants Business, as subject to the Interference of the Custom Department. . -

A covered Wharf within one of the intended Docks is proposed for the gauging-correctly, and ascertaining the Quality of Wine, and Spirits, and this is the only Quay or Wharf included in his-Plan. . t

The Mode of Delivery suggested by Mr. Wyatt, is by-an Application of the King's Scale immediately to the Ship's Side, by means of a floating Platform or Wharf. This Method of Delivery being in fact a Substitute for a Quay, may properly be considered under this Head. .

This System is to be confihed to Ships within , constructed and guarded according to his. Plan, whereby, in his Opinion, the real Cargoes and Duties will be much more accurately ascertained than can possibly be done on any Quays whatever. - -

It is not for us to investigate the mechanical Merits of this Invention, or the Fitness thereof for the Ule proposed, unless such System of Delivery appears to be admissible with improved Safety and Advantage to the Crown, compared with that now existing.

Without questioning either its Merit or Practicabi-lity, we think ourselves bound in Duty to observe, that such a complete and wide Departure from the ancient and approved Mode of raising the Revenue of Customs, is in our Opinion inconsistent with, and, as far as it extends, at once overturns the whole System of Examination and Controul, tried, established, and fane-tioned in this Department.

The Essence of the Check instituted for the Guard of the Revenue on the Article liable to Duty, or to the Laws-of Revenue, is, that whilst the delivering Officer, who ascertains the Duty according to the Criterion fixed, or watches the due Execution of those Laws, is discharging his Trust, controlling Officers, Rationed on the Quays for that Purpose; shall promiseuously, and as Occasion or Discretion may require, inspect, supervise, or examine the Weight, Tale, Gauge, or Measure of the Article when in the Custody of the Crown, in Correction of Error, and in Prevention of Fraud or Collusion. For this Service, Nine Landing Surveyors are appointed in the Port of London; it is their Duty to controul the whole Class of delivering Officers on the Quays, confiding of Landing and Deputy King's Waiters, and a numerous Body of inferior Officers. Indeed it is our (landing Principle, that no Officer shall

A. 1799.

London be permitted to act without Control. Upon an open Quay the Officer become also a Kind of mutual e° Check upon each other.

N j We fee no Means of preserving this tnoft important la Appendix Part of the System with equal Energy and Effect in (c,) this new Mode of Delivery. Esther a Landing Surveyor mud: attend each Landing Waiter on the Platform, or he rauft be moving from Platform to Plat form to fulfil his Trtift; The first would be a most expensive and unnecessary Increase of Officers and Charges of Management; the latter we conceive feaveely practicable with official Effect.

Whild Goods remain on the Quay, in the Cudody of the Crown, the superior Officer may have them, with little Difficulty or Inconvenience, re-examined.

In the Process of this Transit from the Vesselto the Lighter, this material Means of Check appears to be greatly lessened, if not totally lod. Should the Article be deemed dill in the Charge of the Officer when in the Lighter, the Perplexity and Trouble in disturbing the Stowage, and bringing the Goods back for Reexamination, provided there was Space on the Platform (which in numberless Cafes there could not be) would be great, and the official Process on the Platform impeded during such Operation,

As the Articles, when in the Lightef and out of the Dock, if not of that Description which are to be brought to the Legal Quays, would be free from all farther Control of the Officers, the Duties having been paid thereon, we think great Opening for Fraud upon the RivCr would be the Consequence.

The Smuggler might with Facility fubditute other' Articles in Packages corresponding in Size, Marks, and 1 Numbers, after such Discharge from the Docks, instead of those which had passed Examination, and by this, and various other Artifices, prohibited Articles might be introduced, or Evasion of Duty effected; and the Cudom House Officer would at all Events be perplexed in the Execution of his Duty, whild some Articles are to be examined in this Way in the Docks, and others delivering in the River, according to the present Mode, in order to be brought up to the Legal Quays, and on which the Duties have not been paid.

In respect to Diipatch, our practical Officers date, in the dronged Manner, the Difference of Time re-quisite for the Delivery of a Cargo from the Hold of a Ship and from Lighters, the former Mode being out of all Proportion the most tedious: Upon this Principle therefore, apart from the Remotenels of Situation, and the Difficulty incident to the Separation of Articles, which would dill remain to be examined, and delivered as at present, the Attendance of superior Officers of the Crown alongside the Ship would be an unthrifty Application of their Labour.

This Idea of discharging Goods afloat is not alto gether new; a Practice somewhat analogous thereto prevailed at Hull for many Years, but it was confined to that Port, and admitted from Necessity, there being no Legal Quays there at that Time; Goods were therefore permitted to be examined upon the Ship's Deck, and delivered immediately into the Cudody of the Merchant.

This Practice being found frotn Experience to be highly injurious to the Revenue, the same was repre-fented in the Reports of this Board, dated the 20th February 1767, and 9th April 1772, to the then Lords of the Treasury, and an immediate Stop put thereto v Aipon the Erection of Legal Quays at that Port. The Floating Platform appears to us more objectionable than the Delivery from the Deck of a Ship, particularly in point of Space, as the former will be lets and more confined than the latter.

Upon the most mature Confederation, we cannot but think that this Innovation would be hazardous, inexpedient, and tend to additional Expence of Management; indeed alt Plea jtbr the Necessity of such Change will cease when the Legal Quays are established upon an improved System, which we trud will ere long be eflefted.

Having thus stated and difeuffed the Propofols, contained in the different Plans for the Extension Of the Legal Quays, it is incumbent upon us to observe; that no one of those Plans appears to be any Way adequate to the Object in Agitation. — That by lelcfting such Parts of them as in our Opinion ougiit tb be approved of, and combining those several Propositions,-namely, the Embankment of the Thames in the Mode suggested, if it can be done without Detriment to the River; the filling up and applying certain public Staire and Landing Places, and Dice , as specified in Mr. Ogle's Plan, and adding Dock to the

But we think it our Duty also to remark, after full and mature Deliberation, that, in our Opinion, the collective Benefit thence to be derived will not be adequate to the great Object in View, and that, of consequence, considerably larger Addition to the Legal Quays becomes requisite.- — Under this Conviction, we have directed our Thoughts and Enquiries to the Selection of a Spot for such Extension and Enlargement, possessing to the greatest Degree attainable, or capable of being made to possess, Proximity, Contiguity, and the other essential Requisites for a Legal Quay before specified.

We conclude the North Side of the River to be the most convenient for the general Trade of the Merchant. The Place we have to fugged, as most fit, is a Spot in Saint Catherine's, in Front of the River, from Iron gate Stairs down to Storehouses belonging to His Majesty, called The King's Brewhouse, containing something more than Seven hundred Feet, and including a Dock called Saint Catherine's. It has occurred to us, that a Space of Ground, called Tower Wharf, and extending from the Ead End of the present Legal Quays to Irongate Stairs, would, in point of Locality, be highly definable; and provided the Whole, or a Portion thereof, and that Portion confiding in Length on the River, could be obtained, for the Good of the Trade and Revenue of the Country, without Prejudice to the public Department to which it belongs our Plan would be rendered, complete. With respect to the Tower Wharf, it appears from Papers in our Office, that in or about the Year 1762, a Commission did issue from the Court of Exchequer to make Part of the said Wharf a Legal

The Front to the Thames consists of Warehouses, Dwelling Houses, Public Stairs, a Wharf, and some Waste Ground, making for the moll Part the Southern Side of a poor narrow Street, called Saint Catherine's Street. The Space on the North of this Street, exclusive of Saint Catherine's Church and Church

The Houses on the Banks of the River are extremely prejudicial to Revenue, as affording great Opportunities for iniquitous Acts, particularly by the Means of small Vessels, usually called Short Traders, lying close to the Shore at the.Back of these Houses; a Practice which this Board have used every Effort to flop, but without Effect. — We therefore recommend that the Whole of the Site in the Front of the River, with sufficient Depth, be applied to the Object of a Legal Quay, on the North Side of which Warehouses might be constructed. — The Ground, when obtained, we are of Opinion, ought to be cleared of all improper Buildings and Incumbrances, and a Quay formed, embracing all the requisite Properties — We submit this Measure, as of l'uch great Public Utility, that it would deserve the Interference of the Legislature for the Ac-complishment thereof, if such Interference should be found requisite. — We are here likewise confirmed in the Propriety of our Suggestion, by having the concurrent Opinion of the Board of Customs in the Year 1763, when, in consequence of their Recommendation to the Lords of the Treasury, a Commission issued from the Court of Exchequer, constituting the Spot a Legal Quay.

CROWDED AND OBSTRUCTED STATE OF THE RIVER.

We now proceed to the Second Head of our general Arrangement; viz. the crowded and obstructed State of the River.

That the River Thames is frequently so crowded, as to occasion Damage to Ships, Detention, Opportunities for Plunderage, Interruption to Business, and increased Expence for Demurrage and Port Charges, is a Fast, the Truth whereof, we understand, is not to be controverted. — The increased Number and Size of the Shipping of the Country, and the Number of Foreign Vessels resorting to the Port of , are the causes

of the Evil in question; and if those Objects should be progressive, the Inconvenience and Injury to Trade in these Respects must augment therewith.

In the View of Revenue, Detriment must arise, in-as much as the more the Vessel is impeded and detained after her Arrival at Gravesend, at which Place Officers of the Customs are first stationed on board as a Guard, till her final Clearance, when the Officers are taken off, the greater Opportunity for Smuggling is given, and a greater Expence for Management incurred. — Impediment and Delay, in the Navigation of the River, are conl'cquently unfavourable to Revenue. — The direct and most effectual Remedy for this Grievance is, the taking a certain Portion of the Shipping out of the River, by Means of Docks and Basons.

MR. SAMUEL WYATT'S PLAN.

By Mr. Wyatt's Plan, Three separate Docks are proposed between Blackwall and the Ife of Dogs; one for loaded Ships, another for empty Ships, and one for Colliers, with a Bason at the Entrance at Blackwall for One hundred and Sixty Ships.

MR. EDWARD OGLE'S PLAN.

By Mr. Ogle's Plan, no Dock or Bason is proposed;

but to facilitate the Navigation of the River, Mr. Ogle suggests the mooring and classing of Ships, according to the respective Trades in which they are employed, conformably to a Mode fully explained in his Plan.

Of the Propriety of Docks as a general Measure; the moll fit Place for, and the Mode of their Construdion, we are not competent Judges.

The Depth of Water, the Course and Circumstances of the River, the Soundness of Bottom, with various Points of Consideration, many of a professional Nature, and all material in determining upon and executing this Measure, are foreign from our Department.

Viewing Docks as Places of Reception for Ships in Easement of the River, in order to unship their Cargoes on board Lighters, but not as Places for the due Examination and final Delivery of Cargoes from Foreign Parts, the few Remarks we venture to osier on the Subject are. That if a Dock or Docks are construded, their being so formed as to provide the best possible Security against Fire, lecms to be the first and most important Point; that to ward oft'this Danger, the more spacious, the more distinct and subdivided they are, the more proper; that looking to the Possibility of this dreadful Calamity, and the Extent of Mischief which might result therefrom to the Public and Individuals, we cannot help entertaining some Doubt how far it might be adviseable to admit Vessels loaded with valuable Cargoes into Docks, or those whose Cargoes may consist of Articles combustible, or liable to the greatest Injury by Fire; that if withdrawing the Colliers (a numerous Class of Vessels, and arriving in Fleets) and any' other Class of Ships that may be thought most proper to be leleded, into a Dock let apart and conveniently adapted for them, would be sufficient Relief for the crowded State of the River, it might perhaps be the most safe and eligible Mode of Easement; and that the Site of a Dock the most removed from Buildings, and the most (hut up and inclosed from the Intrusion of Persons not having Business to transact in them, demands the Preference.

want OF PROPER ARRANGEMENT AND DISTRIBUTION OF THE BUSINESS ON THE LEGAL QUAYS.

The Third general Head is, The Want of proper Arrangement and Distribution of the Business on the Legal Quays.

Allulions thereto, and Suggestions for the Removal thereof, we find to be thrown out in a general Way in the Explanation of some of the before-mentioned Plans.

We are of Opinion, that a Regulation of this Kind is much wanted, and that the Eft'etft thereof would be highly beneficial both to Trade and Revenue. — The hitherto contracted Scale of the Legal Quays has precluded the Possibility of such Improvement, upon any; Plan sufficiently large and dillindt; nor does this Board at present poll'd s legal Authority to inforce the fame, if it had been practicable. — Upon the Enlargement of the Quays, the First Impediment to the Execution of the Measure would be removed; and we should deem it an Object claiming our immediate Attention to introduce the Amendment, if so empowered by the Legislature.

The First great Outline of this Regulation would be, to keep dillindl and separate the Import and Export Trade; and to provide, that no Part of the Coasting Trade should be carried on at the Legal Quays.

The Confusion and Irregularity attending a Mixture of these several Branches of the Custom Department, and these different Concerns of Trade, would be avoided, and Openings for fraudulent Proceedings, to the Detriment of the Crown and the Merchant, thereby prevented. A considerable Acquisition of Room on the Legal Quays would accrue from the proposed Exclusion of the Coalting Trade; our practical Officers calculate this Gain in Space to be in the Proportion of One-fifth' of the whole present Amount, and of One-third in Cranage.

Another Suggestion, conducive to this beneficial Object of Space, may properly be noticed here. — Certain Foreign Vessels now come up to the Legal Quays, and discharge their Cargoes at them; they occupy the Place which might otherwise be appropriated to Lighters, and the Delivery from the former being comparatively far more dilatory, the Practice in question causes Delay, and a Waste of the Officers Time. The legal Prevention of this, therefore, appears to be worthy of Confident ion; and in this Place we cannot omit to advert to a Practice very prevalent, and highly repugnant to the common Object had in View for the Advantage of Revenue and Trade, viz. the acquiring free Space, and the avoiding unnecessary Delay in the Examination and Delivery of Goods. Certain Articles, particularly 'Wine, Spirits, Fruit, and Oil, are left upon the Quays for a considerable Time after the Duties have been latislied; other Goods remain for Want of the Duties being paid. The imposition of an additional Duty on all Articles so left beyond a reasonable Time, sufficient to correct the Practice, with proper Exemption in Relief of Cafes of Necessity, would, in our Opinion, compel the due Removal, and effectually cure this Evil.

The proper Guard of the Legal Quays being of much Importance, we cannot quit the Subject without observing, that their being ihut up at Night, and completely lighted, would, we think, materially contribute to that End.

WANT OF WELL-ORDERED SYSTEM RESPECTING VESSELS AND CRAFT.

The Want of a well-ordered System in the Disposition of Vessels in the River, and in the Management of Lighters and Craft, constitutes the Fourth and last general Head, under which we have classed the great Sources of Inconvenience to which the Trade of London is exposed. Regulation here is urgently necessary, and the Want thereof severely experienced. Should the Formation of a Dock or Docks be adopted, Obstruction and Danger in the Navigation of the River will be 4

lefTcned proportionally to the Capacity of the Docks, and the Number of Vessels received therein. A proper Degree of clear Space, and the right Distribution of Business on the "River, is little less necessary than on the Quays, to promote Dispatch, and repress Fraud; Harbour Mailers of Experience and Ability ought therefore, we think, to be appointed, with Tower to enforce the Mooring of Ships in the River, according to a well-regulated Plan, and proper Controul and Superintendance over them be provided in order to secure the Discharge of their Duty.

The rightly fixing and ordering of Mooring Chains is strictly connected with, and indeed mull form the Basis of this Improvement. Mr. Ogle has suggested and detailed at Length a Scheme for the general mooring and placing of Ships according to their respective Trades; though we cannot think this Scheme would be effectual, or produce the End he thereby proposes, yet, whatever may be the ultimate Determination respecting Docks, useful Hints for the Object now in Difculfion might be obtained therefrom, and the Parts fit for practical Application selected.

The Lighters at present employed upon the River appear to us to be under an irregular and defective System, if indeed any System at all can be said to obtain. We mean, however, to confine the Force of this Observation to the Concerns of Revenue: — The Lighters in Use arc moltly open; Plunderage, a great Source of Loss and just Caule of Complaint to the Merchant, is obviouily effected with less Difficulty in this uncovered Mode of Conveyance; Damage and Injury to the Article lb brought up are also frequently the Consequence, and Revenue in these Ways is prejudiced. Lighters, by being under no Controul or Government by Officers of the Revenue, on their Approach to the Legal Quays, often crowd and block up the Access thereto j empty ones remain to the Interruption of loaded ones, and while the latter deliver without being distributed or ranged according to any Method, the Dispatch of . Business is greatly impeded.

Certain Goods from their Bulk or Nature are less liable to Damage and Plunder than others, and do not require, or are not so well adapted for Stowage in covered Lighters.

We are of Opinion, that Goods not of this Description should be brought up in those only that are covered, and the Hatches properly secured. One or more Lighter Mailers should be appointed, to attend constantly, and manage this Department in like Manner as Harbour Mailers are proposed for the Regulation of Ships in the River, and be also made accountable to some superior Authority.

Having thus submitted to your Lordships what we have to offer under the Four General Heads laid down, we proceed to some subordinate Objects, alluded to in the early Part of our Report, which, though not so immediately within the Department of Revenue, are more or less eilentially connected therewith, and are of material Consequence } they are Three in Number:

1 ft, Warehouses.

ad, Narrowness of Streets and Avenues adjoining to the Custom House and Legal Quays.

3d, Regulation of Carts.

What.we have to submit touching these Points will be comprized in a few general Remarks.

WAREHOUSES.

Certain Articles of Commerce mull by the Laws of # Revenue be warehoused under the joint Custody of the Crown and Merchant: A Sufficiency, bf Warehouse Room, to receive Articles of this Description, the Security of such Warehouses, and their Proximity to the Custom House, are Objects of Moment to the Crown. — In Times of great Import of these Articles, and during particular Gluts of Business, the providing of Warehouses has been found difficult; should the warehousirtg

NARROWNESS OF STREETS AND AVENUES ADJOINING TO THE CUSTOM HOUSE AND LEGAL QyAYS.

The Magnitude of this Evil, and the Extent of the Inconvenience and Interruption to Bufinel's thereby occasioned, cannot be expressed in Terms too forcible. Access to, and Return from the Quays, are frequently rendered impossible. Tumult, Consulion, and Accidents in the Streets and Passages contiguous thereto, and on the Quays themselves, are often occasioned, and the commodious carrying on of Trade and Revenue, alike counteraded. The Proposals, therefore, both in the City Plans, and Mr. Ogls, which go to open and widen these Streets, Passages, and Avenues, and to substitute, in lieu thereof, large and commodious Streets, are of very useful Tendency, and ought, we think, to be speeuiiy carried into Execution. Connected therewith is t'le Attainment of additional Warehouses, by eroding them on the Spot where certain Houses, to be pulled down for the Completion of the Plan, now stand; and tuch Warehouses will, we have to observe, in point of Situation, possels the Advantages stated in the preceding Article.

REGULATION OF CARTS.

The irregular System of Carts, and the Want of Method in the Arragement of them, is another Grievance.

We lee, however, no Means of complete Remedy, while the Avenues to the Quays remain in their present contracted State, and the Approaches to them are so perpetually interrupted; but when the same are properly widened, we trust sufficient Regulation will be established; indeed, in their present State, some Relief might be afforded, if Officers were appointed to attend Daily for the Superintendance and Controul of Carmen.

Having had Occasion to recur to various Accotihts for Information in the Course of this Enquiry, we take the Liberty of annexing the same to this Report, as they are distinct from those ordered by the Committee of the Honourable House of Commons, and may serve to throw some Light upon the Subject; and we also transmit a Schedule to such Accounts, to afford your Lordships the Means of more easy Reference thereto.

We cannot close our Report without requesting Indulgence for having trespassed so much upon your Lordships Time, but we hope to stand excused, in Consideration of the Extent and Magnitude of the Matters referred.

Report of the Commissioners of the Customs, to T the Lords of the Treasury, on the Improvement In of the Port of London. — 2ill April I'jtgj.

May it please your Lord ships,

Mr. Long having by his Letter of the ill December

last, signified that, having laid before your Lordships »

Memorial of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled; inclosing Mr. Dance's, Report on the proposed Improvements of the Legal Quays, and Estimates of the Expence thereof; he (Mr. Long.) is commanded to transmit the said Memorial and Report to this Board, and to desire we will call upon Mr. Dance for any Explanation we may require upon the Subject of the Plan alluded to by him, and report our Opinion thereupon to.youf Lordships with as little Delay as possible.

We Report,

That in obedience to your Lordships Commands thus signified, we have attentively considered the Me morial and Report referred to us, and procured such Information as we found necessary, in order to warrant an Opinion thereon.

Having in our Report to your Lordships of the t 6th. of May last, entered fully into the Difcufiion of various Proposals then offered for the Improvement of the Port ot London, send lelecled such Parts of those respective Plans, as upon mature Enquiry and Deliberation we thought might with Safety anti Efficacy be adopted for the Attainment of the great ObjciSt in View, and having further suggested fiuch additional Measures to the same End, as according to our best Judgment appeared to be requisite and adequate, we think a Reference to that Report will tend much to supersede the Necessity of troubling your Lordships with a Repetition of Matter already luggefted, and at the same Time draw your Lordships Attention to what we deem a Sort of Ground or Criterion forjudging upon the Pro posal now before us; and such Reference seems to be the more apposite, because, upon Examinations wo find that this Plan, in the general and leading Principle and Outline thereof, has great Conformity with the System we thought ourselves justified in recommending for the mutual Accommodation and Benefit of Commerce and Revenue in the Port of London.

Under the Force of these Remarks, we shall proceed to investigate the Propositions contained in Mr. Dance's, Re port, expressing simply a Concurrence in Sentiment where they accord with our Opinion antecedently given, or appear to be eligible; and where we think the Suggestion ought not to be adopted, or that it should be modified in the Execution, or the Determination on the Expediency thereof suspended, explaining, as may be needful the lieafons on which our Opinion is founded.

FIRST PROPOSITION.

* To purchase a sufficient Quantity of Ground " on the East Side of the upon the Site

This Proposition, as far as it goes to the Construiftion. of an open Legal Quay at Saint Catharine's, is in perfect Consonance with our Opinion, and we think highly fit to be adopted.

We are not, however, prepared to offer any determinate Opinion upon the Confinement or App^cation thereof, in the Manner proposed by Mr. *

the Port to that Spot, are Matters of considerable Importance both in Magnitude and Nature. Due Examination and Enquiry, with a View to the common Benefit of Trade and Revenue, ought, we think, to precede and Fully evince the general Utility of the Measure, before so material an Alteration should be established.

In the Report alluded to we proposed a suitable Arrangement and Distribution of Business on the Legal Quays, as an elsential Requisite to the Improvement of the Port, and suggested that a Distinction and Separation of the Import and Export Trade, and the Removal of the Coast Trade from those Quays, ought to be made the Balls of the Measure.

The practical Institution of such a System, in the most beneficial Mode, mud necessarily involve a Variety of Commercial and Official Concerns and Tran factions, and demand many Regulations. Any final Judgment or Decision thereon, at present, would, we think, be premature and unadvised.

Thus impressed we submit to your LordshipsWifdom, whether the most expedient and safe Order of Proceeding would not be to legalize an additional Extent of Quay Room, fully sufficient for the Improvement of the Port; to sanction, by the Authority of the Legislature, the general Principle of a Separation and Appropriation of the great Branches of Inward and Outward Trade, to certain Parts of the Legal Quays, in such Manner as might be found most secure and advantageous for Commerce and Revenue; and proper Authority being delegated for that Purpose, to commit the executive Part of the Plan to subsequent Accomplishment, under an Injunction of all the Dispatch compatible with the Right and orderly Completion of so extensive an Object. A System thus introduced would not only have the Benefit of proper antecedent Enquiry and Deliberation, but it might be matured, and from Time to Time perfected, under the Aid of Experience.

In the explanatory Part of Mr. Dance's Report, touching this Proposition, we find a Suggestion for forming Two ample Docks behind the Quay at Saint Catharine's, for the sole Purpose of receiving Lighters . for the Export Trade, with covered Sheds, Cartways, Buildings, and an Inclosure; these Docks to communicate with the 'Thames by Two Openings, with Gates, according to a Description in his Report, and a Delineation in a printed Plan transmitted to us by him. Our Recommendation of a Legal Quay at Saint Catharine's, had no View to any Plan of this Kind. Under a Conviction that an adequate lineal Extent of spacious open Quay Room, unincumbered, and of free Access, is the primary Desideratum, and must be the Groundwork of solid and permanent Improvement of the Port, we deem it incumbent upon us to object to this Proposal. An Interruption of the Line of Wharf in Two Places, for the Passage of Lighters to and from the River, would destroy the Continuity and diminish the Quantity of spacious connected Quay Room, and in both Ways we think be incommodious toTrade and Revenue.

Apart from this Consideration, of sufficient Weight in itieif, we think the Plan of these Lighter Docks objectionable, as tending rather to delay and embarrass than to facilitate Business, as likely to occasion Confu-fion from the Compression and Intermixture of Property; and as affording increased Opportunity for Concealment, Plunderage, and Fraud, to the Injury of the Crown and the Merchant.

The Landing and Shipping by Means of Lighters di-rectly along a free open Line of Wharf, appears to us of obvious comparative Superiority.

SECOND PROPOSITION.

{‘ To improve the Site of the Bridge Yard, so as " to render it perfectly adequate to the convenient Dispatch of all the Coasting Trade, and " also to the landing of all Wines and Spirits, " Fruit, and such other Articles as may be " found proper to relieve the present Legal " Quays."

The Designation of a proper Space of Ground at Bridge Yard, for the Erection of a commodious Legal Quay, coincides with our Opinion already offered, and is, we think, requisite to the Amendment of the Port. Touching the Removal from the Legal Quays to the Quay at Bridge Yard, when constructed, of the Articles of Foreign Commerce enumerated in this Proposal, or the like exclusive Selection of any other Articles, we do not deem ourselves warranted to submit any conclusive Opinion; but think in this Instance also, the ultimate Application of that Quay, and Distribution of Business thereon, ought to be postponed; possibly that Situation, if proper Warehouses were erected contiguous to the Quay, might be found peculiarly adapted to the landing of Articles of Import Trade intended for Exportation.

The Relief of the Legal Quays, by taking away from thence all the Coasting Trade, as we have Rated, appears to us a most material Regulation, both for the Attainment of Space and the Prevention of Confusion and Disorder in the carrying on of Business. To that Branch of the Proposition we fully accede; but any Confinement of the Coasting Trade to Bridge Yard, or to any other Spot or Wharf, would, it strikes us, be injurious. That Trade is of the utmost Importance to the Country, as such it deserves every practicable Encouragement, and an Exemption from all Restraint and Burthen not essentially necessary. In conformity with this Principle, we think the Freedom of Choice as to the Place of landing or taking in his Goods, which the Master of the Coast Vessel at present enjoys, ought, with the proposed Exclusion from the Legal Quays (by which we trust this Trade will in fact benefit) still to be maintained.

When the Apportionment of Foreign Trade to Bridge Yard has been digested and settled, if without commercial Inconvenience and practical Objection on the Part of the Revenue, there should remain suitable Space to be set apart for the Coasting Trade, we do not foresee any Impediment to such Partition and Application.

No doubt, the Coasting Trade will be attracted to those Wharfs, where, in point of Locality, Convenience, and Expence, it can be belt accommodated.

Having in this Report had Occasion to express our Objections to Docks for receiving Lighters, we think the general Remarks thereon submitted, coupled with wjjiat we have just observed respecting the Propriety of suspending the Decision in what Way the Legal Quay at Bridge Yard should be applied, and the Expediency of leaving the Coasting Trade unfettered, will justify us in disapproving this Dock Plan at Bridge Yard, whether meant, as Rated in the Proposition, for the Lighters employed in lading or unlading Coasters, or in Mr. Dance's Explanation by Letter, for the Admission of the Coasting Vessels themselves.

The Proposal of covered Quays, with Warehouses over the fame, in Front of the River, militates direCUy against the Opinion delivered in the Report which we had the Honour to make to your Lordships, on which Occasion the Grounds of our Objection to any Measure of the Sort were detailed; we have only therefore to observe, that we deem this Proposal unfit to be adopted.

THIRD PROPOSITION.

Respecting a Proposition thus general and extenfivC, we mult again beg Leave to reter your Lordships to the Report, to which we have so frequently had Occa-fiori to allude, wherein will be found the Opinion and Matter we have to offer upon the various Parts and Objects ranging under or connected with this Head.

We think it, however, right to mark our Agreement in Opinion with Mr. Dance, as to the Order in which he hereby proposes to complete his Plan. The Acquisition of Quay Room at Catharine' % and at

Bridge Tard, in Easement of the present Legal Quays, crowded, obstructed, and overloaded as they now are, before the projected Improvement of those Quays is carried into Execution, appears to us to be highly judicious and proper. The Transactions of the Port, as well in regard to Commerce as Revenue, will, by that Method of Proceeding, be the less incommoded or disturbed, and in all Probability the Work will advance with greater Facility and Dispatch.

Observing that in these Propositions no direct Mention is made of a Dock or Docks for the Relief of the River, though, in the printed Plan accompanying them, the Design of a Floating Dock for Ships at the Isle of Dogs is laid down, we thought it behoved us not to leave the Intention respecting an Object so material to the improved State of the Port to Implication or Surmise, we accordingly applied to Mr. Dance for Information on this Particular; his Letter in return clears up this Matter; and on that Account, as well as that it makes a Kind of farther Explanation or Supplement to the Propositions themselves, we have annexed a Copy thereof to our Report; it there appears that Floating Docks for Shipping at the Isle of Dogs without Wharfs, forms a decided Branch of the Plan of the City of London.

Our Opinion, as to the general Expediency of a Dock . or Docks for the Advantage of the Navigation of the River, and the collateral Benefit to Revenue, under Conditions and Qualifications, and with the Remarks and Suggestions which we thought we were competent, and1 it behoved us to offer, are already before your Lordships, and w-e have nothing to add on the Subject except a Recurrence to a Principle, which has been a governing one in this Report, namely, that the Application of a Dock or Docks to any particular Description of Vessels be delayed, until the Fitness of their being so used lb all have been ascertained.

Mr. Dance's Plan does not, we find, include some Matters fuggelled in our former Report, which, though comparatively of a subordinate Nature, we regard as in-diipcnfably conducive to the grand Object in Contemplation; — we allude to well-ordered and properly enforced Systems for mooring Vessels in the River, regulating Lighters employed in the Conveyance of Merchandize to and from the Quays, and also the Carts frequenting the Quays, or waiting thereon or in their Vicinity for Hire.

There is, we are persuaded, urgent Want of good and effectual Regulation touching these different Objedfs, and we think any Plan for carrying the Port of London to a proper State of Perfedfion would be incomplete without due Interposition to that Effcdf.

We have forborne from entering at all into the Calculations Hated in Mr. Dance's Plan j we do not regard

Respecting the Third and lad Object contained in your Lord ships Reference, Whether there would be Room on the present Free Quays to land the Goods which may be imported in such other Ships as are not employed in the West India Trade, we have to represent, that we have taken the Opinion of those Officers usually consulted, and from their Situations in the Department Left qualified to give Information upon Subjects of this Kind; they (late, that if the Plan of Delivery of the India produce at a Dock in the Isle if , as proposed by the Planters and Merchants, should be carried into Effect, in their Opinion the present Free Quays would be sufficient to land all other Goods which may be imported, without Delay or Inconvenience.

This being a Consideration highly material and important in itself, and involving not merely the present and near, but the future and distant Well-being and Prosperity of the Commerce and Revenue of the Port, We deemed it incumbent upon us to have very peculiar Regard thereto, and to tevifeand exaniine, with great Circumspection, the Returns of our Officers, and the Documents which were before us when we framed the Report to your Lordships, which we have so frequently found it requisite to mention.

The most urgent and indispensable Necessity was then Rated for the immediate Completion of divers Plans for the Enlargement of, Alteration in, and Addition to, the Legal Quays; which, with various other Matters, we at that Time submitted to your Lordships.

Comparing the Opinions of our Officers given on that Ocealion with those offered on the Plan under Difcussion, we do not find that relative Confidency and Uniformity which would, we think, justify us in reding with sufficient Confidence upon the Reasons or Result now submitted on their Part. And bringing into Compa-rifon the Magnitude of the Inconveniencies, Embarrassments, and Difficulties of the Trade of the Port of London, and the concomitant Injury and Peril to Revenue occasioned by the contracted, crowded, and incommodious State of the Legal Quays, so universally, so strongly, and, in our Opinion, so judly complained of, with the- Degree and Extent of the Relief and Ealement comprehended in these Propositions, we cannot, in the Exercise of our bed and most impartial Judgment, regard this Plan as adequate to, or commensurate with, the Attainment of the great Objects in View, a Sufficiency of ample, convenient, apposite Quay Room, and of free unobdrufted Space in the River for the Trade and Navigation of the Port. Impressed with this Conviction, we think it may not be improper, before we dole our Report, to submit to'your Lordships, that without entering into the comparative Aptitude or Merit of the different proposed Plans for Docks, as far as the same are to be applied to the Purpose of Legal Quays for the Examination and Delivery of Articles of Commerce, and having due Regard to those momentous Objects the Welfare and Convenience of Trade and Revenue, we think we should be wanting in our Duty if we omitted, with becoming Deference, to repeat our Opinion, that the most solid and perfect Plan for the Amendment of the Port of J, as well to meet the present as what we trust wiU become hereafter the in-creasing and progressive State of the Commerce thereof, will be by the Adoption of some such aggregate Principles of Improvement as we have had the Honour to Jay before your Lordships in our before-mentioned Report of the 16 th May 1796.

Report of the Landing Surveyors. (C.)

Honourable Sirs,

In a Matter of such serious Importance to the Revenue as the Plan now under Reference, we considered ourselves as called upon to take a Personal Survey of the Whole of the Premises contained in the Two Plans, the better to enable us to submit to yo.ur Honours our Observations upon the same; Which having done, we have the Honour to report.

Fird, upon the proposed Dock at the of Dogs. —

This Dock from Situation appears to us as yery defir-able, as Ships will enter it from Blackwell immediately upon their Arrival from Sea. Upon Ships entering this Dock, it is proposed that the Crews and Revenue Officers shall be discharged, and the Ships jpfeced under the King's Lock. The Ships then to be moored in the Center of the Dock, as Bulk is not to be broken nor the Hatchways opened, until the whole Contents of every Ship's Cargo shall be firstentered for the Duties.

This done, the Ships arp to be laid alpng-fide the Wharfs (hngly) for the Purpose of unloading, when the Hatchways are only to be opened during the Hour» of working, and that in the Landing Waiter's Pxefence.

Coffee and Cocoa are proposed to be . landed at the

Quay close to the Coffee Warehouse. Rums are pro-poled to be gauged upon landing, and immediately secured in the Bonded Cellars; and no Sample ever to be allowed to be drawn but upon the open Quays, and that after the Calks shall have been gauged. Sugars to be weighed immediately upon landing, and as immediately to be secured in the Warehouses. Ships, when discharged of their Cargoes, to be rummaged by the Tide Surveyors, and then to be removed into the Dock. marked B. intended for light Ships only, as the unloading Dock marked A. is to be devoted wholly to the Import Branch of West India Produce.

The Warehouses proposed to be built, appear to us as fully adequate to the Reception of the Whole of the West India Produce imported.

The Sixty Feet allotted in Front of the Warehouses next the Quays will be ample for the Dispatch of Business, and the Restriction that no Cart6 shall ever be allowed upon those Quays is, in our Opinion, truly desirable.

By this Plan great and material Saving will be made to the Revenue in Tidesmen, Cart Followers, and Weighers, as the Dock Company undertake to perform the Whole of the weighing Duty to the Exception of one Weigher at each Scale; and so far as die Revenue is concerned, we mud admit, that under a System so very Ample and apparently so easy to be carried into Effect,

the Revenue must (land fully protected from the immediate Arrival of Ships within this Dock until their final Discharge. The Danger from Fire on board Ships, alone excepted, which in all Situations is more or less hazardous; but it does appear to us, from the Regulation of preventing Persons from remaining on board Ships within this Dock, prohibiting the Use of Fire and Candle on board Ships, together with the Limitation that no Building shall be erected within 500 Feet of the Shipping alongside the Quays, that the Danger is not to be considered as forming any material Objection to the Plan.

The only remaining Point is the Distance, and this to us does not appear objectionable on the Part of the Revenue. It is an Inconvenience that can alone be felt by the Merchants, in any Delay it may occasion to their receiving your Honour's Orders, upon such Papers as may be submitted by them to the Board.

Having, we humbly conceive, answered your Honour's Refetence as far as relates to the Plan for Docks at the Iste of Dogs, it is incumbent on us to give a circumstantial Detail of the Wapping Plan.

We therefore have to observe, that Ships destined for this Dock will have to pass through the Whole of the ' Lower Pool and a great Part of the Upper Pool, and such Ships as are not able to enter the Dock before High Water must lay at least Two Tides out of the Dock, and Ships of great Draught of Water so circumstanced, must be removed a considerable Distance down the River to find a convenient Depth of Water to ride in Safety, till the returning. Tide enables them to get into Dock, -during which Passage through the Pools, and the Delay occasioned by not laving the Tide, the Revenue, we are humbly of Opinion, must be exposed to great Danger, as it will afford an Opportunity for running the private Adventures of the Officers ancj Crews. It is here necessary to remark, that these Docks are proposed for the promiscuous Reception of the Trade of the Port, the same Regulations therefore, so essentially necessary for the Safety of the Revenue which are proposed to be adopted in the Dock at the Iste of Dogs, cannot possibly be carried into Execution in these Docks; namely, the discharging the Revenue Officers and Crews from the Ships immediately upon their entering the Docks, placing the Ships under the Locks of the King and Merchants, and also the Ships Hatchways not to be opened but in the Presente of the Landing Waiters; . the whole Contents of every Ship's Cargo to be entered for the Duties before Bulk shall be broken, and without

which it would be incompatible with our Duty tore- Do k°nj!0 commend any Docks whatever; for in such Docks the Ships lying alongside the Quays, the Crews and Revenue >

Officers remaining on board, and the Resort of Persons N° 5. to the Docks, beyond Description numerous, the Reve- In APpen<l1 nue must be infinitely more exposed than when Ships deliver their Cargoes in the Stream; and it is easy to conceive that the Articles of Cambricks, Lawns, Threads, and Crapes, &c. &c. which are pretty generally Objects of illicit Trade, would be easily run, and without that Rilk which at present the Smuggler has to contend with between the Ship and the Shore.

There is also another Objection, and which we conceive is of the first Importance to the Revenue, the Danger of Fire arising from the Proximity of building to these Docks,'it appearing to us, upon our Survey, that Mell'rs.

Allen's Brewery is to constitute a Part of the Dock Wall, which is not at the Distance of Thirty Feet from the Dock itself, and in various other Parts Houses are within as small a Distance from the Docks; indeed the Whole of the Walls surrounding these Docks have Buildings too contiguous for the Safety of the Revenue, and in case of Fire at any such Building the Shipping must be endangered; this we presume must operate as a serious Objection against these Docks, as the Crown must sustain the Loss of its Duties upon all Goods so destroyed on board Ships, from the Impofiibility of ascertaining the Nature, Quality, and Quantity of Goods so destroyed.

Respectully submitted,

Report of the Surveyor for Sloops and Boats, alluded to in his Report of the 20th 1799.

Honourable Sirs,

1 have carefully examined Mr Walker's Plans

for erecting Wet Docks, and attentively read and con-lidered his Explanation and Reference thereto, and pray Leave to report,

The Plans for Docks, A. and B. are similar to the Merchants Plans for making Wet Docks in Wapping.

The Plan for making a Wet Dock at Saint Catherine's is, in my Opinion, the moR eligible, from its Locality to the City, CuRom House, and Tobacco Warehouses on Tower Hill. Here the Whole of the West , Wine, and Tobacco Ships might deliver their Cargoes; the Two former might be warchoulbd on the Quays or-taken to the Merchants, and the latter conveyed immediately to the King's Warehouse on Tower Hill, by which Means, there would be sufficient Room at the present Legal Quays for the Accommodation of every other Kind of Foreign Trade. This Dock may be made at Saint Catherine's at much less Expence than

any other which has been proposed by any other Person. 1

The Plan for making a Cut through the Isle of Dogs, if carried into Execution, would be very injurious to Vo l. 54.

the Revenue and fair Trader, because -in that Transit, Ships muR be near the Shore on each Side, and there fore would, be open to the Plunderer and Smuggler, as was more fully Rated in my Report on the Merchants Plan for making a Cut from to Wapping.

Mr. Walker's Plan for building a new Bridge in lieu of the present, would be of great Service to the River, for by a free Admission of the Flood there would be a greater Quantity of Water.to return by the Ebb, and thereby cleanse and deepen the Channel; the Water, would flow much higher up the River, and improve the Navigation; it would likewise remove the Dangers which now occur in pafEng through the present Bridge on th£ Ebb Tide.

Mr. Walker's Suggestion of putting the Thames Na-. vigation under the National Prete&ion, which, if adopted, I am satisfied would be the Means of increasing the Trade and Commerce of this Port, the River would be relieved of the present Number of Shoals, Banks, and ObRructions; Ships would be properly moored, and with the proposed Dock at Saint Catherine's there would be sufficient Room to deposit the whole Trade with Safety, without any Embankments, or making use of the Bridge Tard on the South. Side of the River, as has been proposed by the City.

Upon the Whole, I am decidedly of Opinion Mr. Walker'sPlan, for making a Wet Dock and Legal Quays at Saint Catherine's, is by far the moR eligible of any which have been presented to the Honpurable Committee of the House of Commons, and are the beR adapted to prevent Smuggling and Plunderage, and Security of the Revenue.

Humbly submitted.

(c>) Report of the Inspectors of the River.

Honourable Sirs,

In obedience to your Reference of the 17th Instant herewith annexed, to consider the Two Plans for making Docks at Wapping, and the Isle of , we respectfully report. That in our former Reports from the Inspector's Office, we have fully entered into, and given our humble Opinions upon all the Plans that have been referred to the Inspectors of the River. Two of these Plans have engaged the Attention of Parliament j the Merchants Plan for making Wet Docks at and the Corporation's Plan for Docks for the West India Ships at the Iste of Dogs. In our First Report, j6th November 1795, on the Merchants Plan, we gave our impartial Opinion in Favour of the Utility and Prac« ticability of this Plan. And in a Report,- 26th March 1796, also from the Inspe<flor's Office, on the Corporation's Plan for erecting Wet Docks for the West India Ships at the ljleof Dogs, we humbly ftibmitted our Objections to that Plan. To these Two Reports we beg Leave to refer your Honours.

In this present Report we therefore conceive it will be necessary only to state some general Observations.

By the Iste of Dogs Plan it is proposed to take into that Dock only West India Ships. This we are of Opinion will be far from effectually remedying the Defects of the River arising from its crowded State, for wc have frequently remarked, that the River has been extremely crowded and confuted even when no India Ships have been in the River. Moreover we conceive, that the Distance from the Center and Seat of Business in the River is too great, and will be found very inconvenient. And with respect to those Ships, it has been said that few West India Ships come up above Deptford; but this is erroneous; for it is an undeniable Fact, that Four-Fifths of these Ships, the greatest Part of them of large Size, came up into the Pool last Year (dangerous as it was) where they discharged Inwards and loaded Outwards, and Ships of all other Trades do the fame, except East India Ships.

By the Merchants Plan (which is the original) for Docks at Wapping, not only West India Ships, but Ships

It being Rated in the Explanation of the Plan for Docks at the Isle of Dogs, that 46 Ships may discharge singly in the Dock at the same Time, without one lying alongside of another;

The Landing Surveyors are to report upon the Practicability of nrch Discharge, and what Number of Officers, and of what Descriptions, will be necessary to attend at the same Time, in order to the Safety of Revenue during the Discharge.

They are also to explain, as far as they are enabled, what they understand is to be the Nature of the proposed Building in the Center of the North Side, for the Accommodation of the Revenue and Dock Officers; to what Description of Officers, at what Times, and in what Way to be applied; referring to any Document or Authority they may have for making a Return to this Reference.

The Landing Surveyors are also to report, whether they have considered that Part of the India Trade Plan, which proposes that upon Ships entering the Docks, the Tide Waiters lfiall immediately be discharged therefrom, and the Vessels put under the joint Locks of the King and Merchants; and if so, in what Mode they apprehend this Business is to be conducted with Safety and Dispatch, and by what Officers, lb as not to interfere with the current Business of Discharge, &c. then conducing within the Docks.

They are also to Rate, what they understand by the Proposition for weighing Goods upon Landing, to be performed by the Servants of the Dock Company, except a Revenue Officer at each Scale, £sV. how far this is confident with the Practice of Weighing for the Ascertainment of Duties now and heretofore in Ule, or reconcileable with the System of due Guard on the Part of the Crown.

alongside the Lending Wharf in the Dock in the Isle of Dogs, we have not understood that so many are in-

tended to be discharged at one and the same Time, nor do we conceive that it would be necessary for the Dil-patch of Business, One Landing Waiter only will be i'ufficient for the Security of the Revenue to attend each Ship at the Time of her Discharge.

With respect to the Building intended to be erected in the Center of the North Side, for the Accommodation of the Revenue and Dock Officers, we understand it is to answer the Purpose of the Landing Waiter's Office at the Custom House, namely, to keep their Books in, and to tranlaft such official Duty as cannot at Times be performed at the Waterside.

We have maturely considered that Part of the India Trade Plan, which proposes that upon Ships entering the Docks the Tide Waiters shall be immediately discharged therefrom, and the Vessels put under the joint Locks of the King and Merchant; and the Mode we apprehend for conducting this Business with Safety and Dispatch is, that when the Ships are discharged of the Revenue Officers and their Crews, they are to be hauled into the Dock by the Servants of the Dock Company, who are to be und^r Oath and Security, which we humbly conceive will not interfere with the current Business of Discharge, then conducting within the Docks.

We understand the Proposition for weighing Goods upon Landing to be, that One Weigher is to Hand at each Scale to see the laborious Part of the Duty performed, namely, the placing the heavy Weights in the Scales by the Dock Servants, and he then weighing and calling the Weights to the Landing Waiter, as is the Practice at the Sufferance Wharfs, for the Ascertainment of the Duties, and which we deem consistent with the Safety of the Revenue.

Respectfully submitted,

L. Leitch.
