A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, interested in an intended Inilitution, to be called The Globe Insurance , was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners and others are desirous of forming a new InRitution, to be called The Globe Itifurance Office, for granting Insurances on Lives, and for securing Annuities and Sums payable at future Periods, and for granting Insurances, against Loss or Damage by Fire; and that, in order to afford Solidity and Permanency to Friendly Societies established for railing, by voluntary Subscriptions from the Members thereof, separate Funds for the mutual Relief and Maintenance of the Members in Sickness, old Age, and Infirmity, and in order to assist other charitable and benevolent Institutions and Societies, formed for the Purpose of relieving, by voluntary Subscriptions and Benefactions, Widows, Orphans, and the Families of the Clergy and others, in distrelled Circumstances, the Petitioners are desirous that the said Establishtnent, to be called The Globe Itifurance , should be intrulled with the Disposition, Management, and Custody of the Monies, Effects, and Funds of such Friendly Societies and other charitable Institutions above mentioned, as shall be willing to appoint the intended Office to be their Treasurer, and to intrull their Monies, Effects, and Funds to the Disposal, Management, and Custody of the said Office, upon Condition that the Office shall allow Interest thereon, and shall become bound with sufficient Sureties for the just and faithful Execution of such Trull, and for rendering a true and just Account of such Trull, according to the Rules, Orders, and Regulations of such respective Friendly Societies and other charitable Institutions aforesaid, and shall, upon Demand made by the Society or other Inilitution to which the Office' is Treasurer, pay over all the Monies and Funds, or any Part thereof, intrulled to the said Office, and assign and transfer-or deliver all Securities, Effects, or Funds, to i'uch Person or Persons as any such Society or Institution shall appoint; and that the Petitioners are also desirous of affording Assistance to such Friendly Societies and other charitable Institutions as shall con-nest themselves with the said Insurance Office, by receiving from such Societies and Institutions Insurances for the Relief of the Members in the following Exigencies; viz. Funeral Expences Maintenance for Children, and Provision for old Age, and for Widows, according to the Rates and Tables of Insurances, which shall be adopted by the said Insurance Office; and that, for the Encouragement of Frugality among the labouring Clafl'es, and in order to promote the Happiness of Individuals, and at the same Time to diminish the Public Burthens occasioned by the Poor Rates, the Petitioners are desirous that a Branch of the said In-iurance Office should be appropriated to the Receipt of Deposits in Money from the industrious Clalfes, and that on such Deposits Interests should be allowed; and that, for these Purposes, the Petitioners are desirous that His Majesty should be empowered, by an Act of the Legislature, to grant a Charter of In-Vo l. 54.

corporation to the Petitioners, and others interested in the intended Office, for enabling them to raise a Capital Stock of £.500,000, within such Time, and by such Proportions, at a Time, and in I'uch Manner, as by the said Act or Charter shall be appointed, and that they should be authorized to grant Assurances on Lives, and Insurances against Fire, and to grant Annuities, and Sums payable at a future Period, at such Rates as may be agreed on between the Insurer and the Allured; and that, in order to render the intended Insurance Office beneficial to the Public, the Petitioners are willing that £.300,000, or Three-Fifths of the Capital Stock intended to be raised, shall be inverted in the Purchase of Land Tax ppon Houses, and that One Half of the net Profits (after paying the Annual Dividend of Five Pounds per Centum to the Proprietors, and all Expences attending the said Insurance Office) shall also be laid out in the Purchase of Land Tax on Houses, provided that when One Million (viz.' £. 300,000 Capital, and £.700,000 Profits) shall have been laid out in this Manner, no further Purchase of Land Tax shall be required, and provided that the Interest arising from Land Tax so purchased shall not be deemed to be Profits applicable to the future Purchase of Land Tax; and that the Petitioners have been unable, as well from the Want of certain Information with respect to the Arrangements respecting the Sale of the Land Tax, as from other unavoidable Delays, to complete the Formation of their Plan, and the Adjustment of such Tables and Calculations as were essential for the Establishment of the intended Insurance Office, so as to render it of Public Utility, before the Time limited by the House for receiving Petitions for Private Bills was expired: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to exhibit a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for enabling His Majesty to grant a Charter of Incorporation to the Petitioners and others for establishing an Inilitution, to be called The Globe Insurance Office, for Insurance against Fire, for Life Assurances, for granting Annuities and Sums payable at a future Period, for providing for the Widows and Children of the Clergy, and for old or superannuated Clergymen, for affilling Friendly Societies, and for receiving Deposits in Money from industrious Clalfes and Individuals, and allowing Interest on such Deposits, in such Manner, and under such Rules, Orders, and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said several Persons.

Then a Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, interested in an intended Inilitution, to be called The Globe Insurance Office, was presented to the House, and read; Containing the same Allegations as the preceding Petition; and Praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling His Majesty to grant a Charter of Incorporation to the Petitioners and others for establishing an Inilitution, to be called The Globe Insurance Office, for Insurances against Fire, for Life Assurances, for granting Annuities and Sums payable at a future Period, for providing for the Widows and Children of the Clergy, and for old or superannuated Clergymen, for affilling Friendly Societies, and for receiving Deposits in Money from industrious ClalTes and Individuals, and allowing Interest on such Deposits, in such Manner, and under such Rules, Orders, and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Kino's Mcf- Mr. Secretary Dundas acquainted the House, That he lagtMeiative had a Meflligc from His Majesty to this House, signed Rulfaat&<rith ky His Majesty j and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followed); viz.

GEORGE R.

I lis Majesty thinks proper to acquaint this House, that He had, some Time ficce, concluded an eventual Engagement with His Good Brother and Ally the Emperor of Rnffia, for employing Forty-five Thousand Men against the Common Enemy, in such Manner as the State of Affairs in Europe at that Period appeared to render moll advantageous. The Change of Circumstances which has sincearifen having rendered a different Application of that Force more desirable, His Majesty has recently had the Satisfaction to learn that the Views of the Emperor of Russia, in that Respect, are entirely conformable to His own. But His Majesty has not yet received any Account that the formal Engagements to that Effect have been regularly concluded: He has, however, the Satisfaction of knowing that the same Promptityde and Zeal in Support of the Common Cause, which His Ally has already manifested in a Manner so honourable to himself, and l'o signally beneficial to Europe, have, induced him already to put this Army in Motion towards the Place of its Destination, as now ' settled by mutual Consent. His Majesty therefore thinks it right to acquaint the House of Commons, that the pecuniary Conditions of this Treaty will oblige H is Majesty to pay the Sum of Two Hundred and Twenty-five Thousand Pounds, in stipulated Instalments, as Preparation Money, and to pay a Monthly Subsidy of Seventy-five Thousand Pounds, as well as to engage for a farther Payment at the Rate of Thirty-seven Thousand Five Hundred Pounds per Month, which Payment is not to take place till after the Con-elusion of a Peace made by common Chnfent.

His Majesty relies on the Zeal and Public Spirit of His faithful Commons, to enable Him to make good these Engagements: And His Majesty, being desirous of continuing to afford the necessary Succours to His Ally the Queen of Portugal, as well as to give timely and effectual Assistance at this important Conjuncture to the Swiss Cantons, for the Recovery of their ancient 'Liberty and Independence, and to make every other Exertion for improving, to the utmost, the signal Advantages which, by the Blessing of God, have attended the Operations of the Combined Arms on the Continent since the Commencement of the present Campaign j recommends it also to the House of Commons, to enable His Majesty to enter into such farther En-

Theri the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have laid4before the ' House an Account of the Money granted for the Year 1797, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act 23 Geo. II. intituled, "An Act for extending and improving the Trade to " Africa and that they have inverted the Money, granted in the last Session of Parliament for the Support and Maintenance of the F^orts and Settlements on the said Coast: And that Parliament, taking into its serious Confederation the various increased Expences to which the Establishments in Africa were subject, as well from the defective Condition of the Forts and Settlements, as "From unavoidable Alterations in the Nature of the Service of the Petitioners, and from a very great Increase of ‘ their Charges in consequence of the War, was pleased ‘ to grant the Sum of £.20,000. for the Service of the Year 1795, and a like Sum for the Service of the Year 1796, but, notwithstanding the Continuance of the said increased Expences, and though it has been humbly represented that most of the Articles of Supply have been further very greatly advanced, inso much that the same Grant will not now produce a Supply of much more than the Half of what it yielded before the Commencement of the War, yet Parliament was pleased to grant Ho more than the usual Peace Supply of £. 13,000. for Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements for the Years 1797 and 1798, the Consequence of which is, that the Petitioners are utterly unable to keep up the Establishments at the said Forts and Settlements necessary for their Defence, and their Officers are getting To much in Advance for the Public Service, that it is altogether impossible to answer for the Security of the same without a more adequate Provision: And that the Petitioners, being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House, for the Preservtion, Extension, and Im-, provement of the Trade to Africa, and for the Defence

and Maintenance of the Britisji Forts and Settlements on that Coast necessary thereto, therefore pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum as may be sufficient, as well for the Expences already incurred and not provided for, as for the extra Expences in consequence of the War, and likewise for the effectual permanent Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Matter of the Rolls reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees of the British Museum, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Probate of the Will of the late Reverend Clayton Mordaunt Cracherode, dated 9th A 1792, was produced to Yout Committee, and read; Wherein he bequeathed to the Trustees of the British Museum sundry Books, Drawings, and Prints, and also various Gems, Coins, Medals, and Specimens of Natural History, together with the Cabinets in which the same are contained: And,

Mr. 'Thomas Payne, of the Gate, Bookseller,

being examined, laid. That he has icen the Collection of the Books left to the Museum by the Testator and is of Opinion, that the same is one of the most curious and valuable Collection that has ever been made; and estimates the Worth of them at about £..10,000: And,

Mr. John Thane, a Printfeller, being also examined, said, He has leen the Drawings and Prints be- questhed by the said Testator to the said Museum, and is bf Opinion, that the least Value that can be put upon them is £. 5,000: Then,

Mr. Richard Miles, Dealer in Medals, being also examined, laid. He has inspected the Coins and Medak bequeathed by the said Will, And is of Opinion that the same are worth at least £.6,000. And it appeared by an Estimate produced and proved to Your Committee, that the Getris bequeathed by the said Will to the said Museum are of the Value of £. 534. 7 s.Then, Mr. George Humphrey, Dealer in Subjects of Natural History, being alftrexamined, said. That he has inspected the Specimens of Natural History bequeathed by the said Will, and is of Opinion the least Value that can be put upon them, including the Cabinets in which, they are contained, is £. 2,000.

Then an Act, passed in the Thirty-sixth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, for repealing certain Duties on Legacies and Shares of Personal Estates, and granting other Duties thereon in certain Cales, was read: An<| Mr. Miles, who is Accountant to the said Museum, being again examined, informed Your Committee, That there is no Fund to enable the Trustees to discharge the Tax impol'ed by the said Act, the Funds appropriated for the Support of the said Museum being inadequate to the necessary Expences thereof, inso much that the Trustees have, from Time to Time, been under the NecelTity of applying for the Aid of Parliament, in order to discharge the said Trull.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Bragge, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Twenty-seventh Report, relating to Courts of Justice, which, upon the 26th Day of June, in the last Session of Parliament, was made from the Select Committee, who were appointed to examine and state the Total Amount of the Public Debts, and other Matters relating to the Public Revenue and Expenditure, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which lie read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty be enabled to grant, out of the Con-solidated Fund, such Annuities, in Augmentation of the present Salaries and Profits of the Offices of Master of the Rolls, Chief Baron of the Court of Exchequer, the Puisne Justices of the Courts of King's Bench and Common Pleas, and Barons of the Coif of the said Court of Exchequer, for the Time being, as will make up their respective Salaries and Profits to the Annual Sums herein after mentioned; that is to say, the Master of the Rolls, Four Thousand Pounds; the Chief Baron of the Court of Exchequer, Four Thousand Pounds; and to each of the said Puisne Justices and Barons, Three Thousand Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty be enabled to grant unto any Person holding the Office of Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, or Keeper of the Great Seal of Great Britain, for the Time being, a contingent Annuity of Four Thousand Pounds a Year, to take Effect on the Refig-nai ion or Removal of such Person from such Office.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty be enabled to grant, under certain Conditions to be limited, unto any Person who shall have held the Office of Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench, an Annuity of Three Thousand Pounds; and to any Person who shall have held the Office of Master of the Rolls, an Annuity of Two Thousand Five Hundred Pounds; anti to any Person who shall have held the Office of Chief Justice of the Court of Common Pleas, or Chief Baron of the Court of Exchequer, an Annuity of Two Thousand Five Hundred Pounds, to each of such Persons; and to any Person who shall have held the Office of Puisne Justice of the Courts of King's Bench or Common Pleas, or Baron of the Coif of the Court of Exchequer, an Annuity of Two Thousand Pounds, to each of such Persons; such Annuities to be granted to them respectively, after their Resignation of such Offices respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty be enabled to grant, out of the Monies that shall arise from any the Duties and Revenues payable to LI is Majesty in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, the several Annuities herein after mentioned, in Augmentation of the present Salaries and Profits of the Offices of the Lords of Session, Justices and Barons of the Courts in Scotland; that is to say, the Lord President of the Court of Session, for the Time being. One Thousand Pounds; the Lord Justice Clerk, Five Hundred Pounds; such of the other Lords of Session, being also Lords Commissioners of Justiciary, for the Time being. Four Hundred and Eighty Pounds; and such of the other Lords of Session, not being also Lords Commissioners of Justiciary, for the Time being. Two Hundred and Eighty Pounds; the Lord Chief Baron of the Court of Exchequer, for the Time being. One Thousand Pounds; and for each of the other Barons of the said Court, Two Hundred and Eighty Pounds.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill or Bills be brought in, upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Bragge, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. TovcnjhenMr. John Smyth, Mr. Douglas, Mr. Pybus, Mr. Attorney General, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr. Roje, and Mr. Long, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

And Mr. Bragge moved the House accordingly.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Spranger and Mr. Smith:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to repeal the Duty granted by an Act of the last Session of Parliament on Raw Linen Yarn, the Produce of the Territories of the King of P, and imported directly from thence into this Kingdom, and for charging another Duty in lieu thereof; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing a Moor or Common, called Knayton Moor, and other Wafts Lands, within the Town-ship of Knayton, and Parish of Leek, in the North R d-

ing of the County of York without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing the Open Arable Fields, Open Meadows, Common Pastures, Common Grounds, and Waste Grounds, in the Township of Grajlhorpe, in the County of Nottingham , without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing several Open Fields and Stinted Failures, within the Township of Long Preston, in the Parish of Long Preston, in the West Riding of the County of York, and for embanking and draining several Parcels of Ground within the same Township, called Long Preston Ings; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Commons, and Waste Lands, within the Parishes of Houghton and South , in the County of Sujex; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting the Inheritance in Fee Simple of Part of the settled Estates of Sir Henry Every, Baronet, in Trustees, in Trust to make Sale thereof, and to apply the Money produced by such Sale, or a competent Part thereof, in Payment and Discharge of divers Debts, Charges, and Incumbrances affecting the fame, and to invest the Surplus of such Money, if any such shall be, in the Purchase of other Lands or Hereditaments to be settled to the same Uses; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The House was all'o moved. That an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for " the better Protection of the Trade of this Kingdom; " and for granting new a ad additional Duties of Customs on Goods imported and exported, and on the " Tonnage of certain Ships entering outwards or inwards " to or from Foreign Parts, until the signing the Preliminary Articles of Peace," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Com-jnittee. That they do consider of the said Act.

An ingrossed Bill to enlarge the Term, and alter and enlarge the Powers of several Acts, relating to the Harbour of Liverpool, and for making Two additional Wet Docks and Piers in or near the Port of Liverpool, and for rendering more safe and commodious the said Port and Docks, was read the Third Time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, for making One entire Compensation to Persons interested.

And the said Clause was Thrice rqacl; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, declaring. That no Release by One of the Plaintiff's shall assess the rest.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Then the Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 5. 1. 1. To leave out " hereafter," and insert " thereafter" inllead thereof.

Fr. 9. 1. 2. To leave out " hereafter," and insert " thereafter" inllead thereof.

Pr. 39. 1. 9. After " for" to insert " and, " and to leave out " and applied."

Pr. 40. 1. 36. After " River," to insert, " or haling " into or out of any of the Docks " of the said Port."

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act to enlarge the Term, and alter and enlarge the Powers of several Acts, relating to the Harbour of Liverpool, and for making Two additional Wet Docks and Piers in or near the Port of Liverpool, and for rendering more safe and commodious the said Port and Docks.

And the Witness added, That the Sums advanced by the Petitioners, appeared to have been entirely expended by the said Robert Reeves; and upon the fullelt Investigation it appeared, that he had no other Property whatever, out of which he could have purchased the said Receipts; and, previous to his Execution, he admitted, that the Receipts found in his House had been purchased out of the Petitioners Money, and that he committed those Forgeries, in hopes, by Speculation in Stock, to enable him to repay it.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer presented to the House, by His Majesty's Command,

The Memorial of Sir Charles Grey and Earl Vincent, praying. That the Claims for American Ships, taken in the West Indies in 1794, may be paid by Government, on their paying£.29,682,. ior. 4

And the Title of the said Memorial was read.

The said Memorial is as followeth;

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

The Memorial of the Right honourable Sir Charles Grey, K. B. and the Right honourable Earl Vincent, K. B. Commanders in Chief of His Majesty's Fjeet and Army employed in the Reduction of the French 111 and s of Martinique, Guadaloupe, and Saint Lucia, in the Year 1794, on Behalf of themselves, and the Officers, Seamen, Soldiers, and Marines, serving under their rei'pebtive Commands,

Sheweth,

That when Your Memorialists, in the Beginning of February 1794, proceeded to the Attack of the French Islands, in obedience to His Majesty's Orders, they found the principal Ports crowded with small Vessels under American Colours, all, or moll, of which had brought Provisions for the Enemy, and many of them arrived after Your Memorialists had ifl'ucd the Proclamation directed by His Majesty's Ministers, calling upon the Inhabitants of the French Islands to surrender those Poflessions to His Majesty's Arms; and under l'uch Circumstances, and particularly under the Orders of November 1793, the Admiral thought it his Duty to take Possession of, and "bring all the Vessels to Adjudication.

That at this Time the Americans were very much attached to the French, and unfriendly to the Government, and for this Reason Your Memorialists judged it necessary to take Measures to prevent the American Vessels, taken at Martinique, from giving Assistance to the Enemy in the other Islands, and those Measures unavoidably subjectecl the Crews of those Vessels to Restraint that they would not otherwise have experienced; and, upon the Application of a considerable Number of the Persons detained, Vessels were given up to them to remove them to America.

That from these and various other Causes, produced by the ablive and arduous Service in which the Fleet and Army were engaged, the usual Measures were not in general taken by the Agents for the Navy, to obtain the regular Examinations of the Persons found on board the Ships captured, so as to proceed to a legal Adjudication. These Irregularities were increased by Your Memorialists being advised. that, as Commanders in Chief, they had Authority to erebl a Court of Admiralty; and, agreeably to that Advice, appointing a Judge, Register, and other Officers, to abt as such: Proceedings were commenced in the Court, so constituted, against all the Vessels captured and their Cargoes; and, either for Want of proper Claims, or upon EVidence of their belonging to the Enemy, they were condemned as Prize, and afterwards fold.

That upon Your Memorialists' Return to this Country, they were, for the first Time, informed that the Court of Admiralty erected by them was not legally constituted, and that all the Proceedings carried on in it 7 were

were null and void; and they were called upon by the American Claimants to ii.flitute Proceedings in the High Court of Admiralty here, and to proceed to the Adjudication of all the captured Ships and Cargoes.

That Proceedings were accordingly instituted in the High Court of Admiralty again!I each Ship, and in the Month of December last, most of the Claims were heard before Sir William 6 icqjtand Your Mcmoriaiitls have annexed a List of the Claims, and a Minute of the D^cilion upon each.

That the Agents, employed by the Navy and Army in the Indies, fold the Vessels and Cargoes, in consequence of their being condemned by the Court of Admiralty in; but, unfortunately, they did not

keep 1'eparate Accounts of the Species and Quantities of Goods of which each Cargo was composed; and the Claimants have taken Advantage of this Irregularity, by claiming Property that never came to the Hands of the Captors, and Your Memorialists have no Means of checking these Claims.

That, independent of this Inconvenience (as the Authority of the Court of Admiralty in Martinique is denied) the Claimants are not bound by the Sales made as before dated, and have fixed Values and Prices upon their Ships and Goods far beyond what they fold for; and the Sums to be paid them, under the Decrees of Restitution, are ascertained by the proper Officer, without Regard to what has been received by the Captors. Under these Circumstances, Your Memorialists (who are considered by the Court as responsible for the Sums awarded to the Claimants) will be called upon to pay conllderable Sums, which they are totally unprovided with the Means of doing; for, except what was paid by Government for the Ordnance and other Public Stores taken from the Enemy, Your Memorialists have not, to this Hour, received One Shilling for Prize Property, taken either on Shore or afloat at the Capture of the French Islands.

That the Money received from the Sale of the Property, restored as American, was inverted, in Your Memorialists Names, in the Purchase of Stock, and, since the Investment, the Reduction in the Price has exceeded the Dividends received upon it.

That, upon a very careful Examination of the Agents Accounts, it appears that the Sum received for the Ships and Cargoes, claimed as American (after deducting the Expences of Sale) was

only ----- ----..... - £. 30,996 18 —

Out of this Sum, £. 1,314. 7 s.8 d.has been paid in Discharge of a Claim allowed - - 1,314 7 8

Net Sum inverted - -£.29,682 10 4

That by the Decisions of the Court of Admiralty, some Cargoes, and Parts of Cargoes, have been condemned, the Value of which cannot be exactly ascertained; but if Your Lordships should be pleased to afford Your Memorialists the Protection they solicit, they do not mean to claim any Advantage from those partial Condemnations, but to give up to Government the above Sum of £.29,682. ioj. 4J. upon being relieved from the Payment of the Claims.

That, under the very peculiar Circumstances of the Cafe, Your Memorialists trust Your Lordships will think them entitled to this Protection. The Court of Admiralty has decided in every Cafe, except in one very trifling Capture, that Your Memorialists were warranted in detaining the Ships, and bringing them to Adjudication, and on that Ground refused to give Colts and Damages to the Claimants.

That considering the very arduous Service Your Memorialists were engaged in, and the Mischiefs that might 1 have resulted from dismissing a Number of American Provision Vessels from Martinique, at a Time Your Memorialists were proceeding to attack the other Islands, they trust Your Lordships will be of Opinion that what they alk is reasonable. And, independent of these Considerations, Your Memorialists beg leave to observe, that Estates of great Value, belonging to the Enemy in the captured Islands, were taken Possession of, and placed under the Management of Agents for Government, and yet remain under their Care, from which the Captors have received no Advantage whatever, which Your Memorialists submit to Your Lordships Confklcration, as an additional Circumstance to entitle them to the Protection they solicit.

That Your Memorialists have no Means of stating correctly the Amount of the Claims made by Americans, as the Claimants have yet only proceeded to ascertain the Value of One or Two Vessels and Cargoes; but, upon an Examination of all the Claims, it appears that the estimated Value put by the Claimants upon the Property claimed, is about - -- £.140,000 ——

Deduct the estimated Value of Ships and Cargoes taken by the French at which the High Court of Admiralty has pronounced the Captors not liable for - - - 35,000 ——

£. 105,000 ——

That by the annexed Minutes of the Decrees of the Court of Admiralty, Your Lordships will find that Parts of Cargoes are condemned in some Instances; and there are several Claims now waiting for further Proof, some of which, at Icaft, are likely to experience a similar Decision.

Your Memorialists are informed by their Agents, that there is great Reason to believe that at least One-Third of the Sums claimed will be deducted, upon a Reference to the Register and Merchants; and that Your Memorialists may, with a considerable Degree of Confidence, represent to Your Lordships that £.60,000. to £.65,000. will be the utmost probable Amount of the American Claims that have been, or may be established; and consequently the probable Loss to Government, by taking the Responsibility thereof, and protecting the Captors, will not exceed £.30,000. to£.35,000.

Your Memorialists therefore submit their same to Your Lordships Consideration; and, upon Payme nt by Your Memorialists of the before-mentioned Sum of £.29,682. iox. 4 to such Person as shall be appointed to receive the same, Your Memorialists entreat Your Lordships to give the requisite Directions for Payment of the American Claimants, when, and as the Amount of their Claims shall be ascertained by the proper Officers, so as to entitle them to call for Payment; and that Your Memorialists may be protected from all Liability to answer the fame.

For Admiral Lord Saint Vincent and Self,

Charles "John Jervis.

Letters, and of charging certain Rates of Postage thereon, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to ,the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's \

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That His Majesty's Postmaster General be authorized to collect Letters and Packets directed to Places within His Majesty's Dominions, and to Countries beyond the Seas, and to forward the same by any Ships he shall think fit, and to take for every Letter and Packet so forwarded, One Half of the Rates arid Duties of Postage that would be payable for such Letters and Packets if conveyed by Packet Boats; and where no Rate of Postage is already established, then to take One Half of the Rates paid for Letters sent beyond the Seas.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That H is Majesty's Postmaster General be authorized to take, for every Letter and Packet brought by Ships (other than Packet Boats) from Places within His Majesty's Dominions, and from Countries beyond the Seas, in Addition to any Inland Postage, the Sum of Four Pence for every single Letter, and so in Proportion for Packets.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Mr. Braggereported from the Committee, who were

appointed to consider of the Expediency of requiring Notices to be given of any intended Application to Parliament for Leave to bring in a Bill for the making of Ways or Roads, usually called Railways or Dram Roads, or for the Renewal or Alteration of any Act passed for that Purpose, and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred, and had come to a Resolution thereupon, which they had directed him to Teport to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolution of the Committee was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standing Orderis of the House, of the 7th of May 1794, relating to Bills for making Navigable Canals, Aqueducts, and the Navigation of Rivers, or for altering any Act of Parliament for any or either of those Purposes, be extended to Bills for making any Ways or Roads, commonly called Railways or Dram Roads, except so much of the said Standing Orders as requires an Interval of Seven Days between the First and Second Reading of such Bills, and also between the Day on which such Bills are reported, and the Day on which the Reports shall be taken into Consideration, and also with respect to the printing of such Reports.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Friday Morning next.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Holford and Mr. Graves:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for regulating the Rates of Porterage to be taken by Innkeepers and other Persons, within the Cities of London and Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, and

Places adjacent; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to amend an Act, made in the Thirty-f^venth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, and Two Acts made in the last Session of Parliament, for raising a Militia Force in that Part of the Kingdom of Great Britain called Scotland; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for authorizing the Company of Proprietors of the Stratford upon Avon Canal Navigation to vary the Course of certain Parts of the said Canal, directed to be made by an Act, passed in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, and also to make a Branch out of the said Canal, and also to vary the Course of a navigable Cut directed to be made from the said Stratford upon Avon Canal, in the Parish of Lapworth, into the Warwick and Birmingham Canal, in the Manor of Kings-wood, in the County of Warwick, by another Act, passed in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, and for amending the said Acts; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing the Common Fields, Undivided inclosures, Commons, Waste Grounds, and Commonable Places, within the Townships of San-dall Magna, Walton, and Cin the Parish of Sandall Magna, in the West Riding of the County of York-, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, Common Meadow's, Common Pastures, and other Commonable and Waste Lands, Grounds, and Places, within the Hamlet of in the Parish

of Aylesbury, in the County of Buckingham; without any Amendment: And also.

Mr. Bragge accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had considered the Matter . to them referred, and had come to several Resolutions thereupon, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Refo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standing Order of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, which directs that, before any Petition is presented to the House for inclosing, draining, or improving any Lands, Fens, or Commons, a printed or written Notice of such intended Application to Parliament be affixed on the Church Door of the Parish or Parishes in which such Lands, Fens, or Commons do lie, for Three Sundays, in the Months of August and September, or either of them, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be presented, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, before any Petition is presented to the House for inclosing, draining, or improving any Lands, Fens, or Commons, a printed or written Notice, signed by at least One Fourth Part of the Proprietors in Number and Value, of such intended Application to Parliament, be affixed on the Church Door of the Parish or Parishes in which such Lands, Fens, or Commons do lie, for Three Sundays in the Months of August and September, or either of them, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be presented.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standing Order of the House, of the 27th of April 1774, which directs that, in all Bills for Inclosures th^re be inserted a Clause compelling the Commissioners to account for all Monies by them laid out, and affetfed on the Parties concerned in the said Inclosures, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Bills for Inclosures there be inserted a Clause, compelling the Commissioners to keep, at the Office of their Clerk, a Book of Accounts open, at all reasonable Times, during the Progress of the Inclosure, and till the Accounts are finally settled, for the Inspection/of any of the Proprietors, which Book shall contain an Entry of the Particulars of all Sums of Money raised or expended by virtue of any Powers granted by the Act, under a Penalty on such Commissioners, or their Clerk, for ne-gledting or refuting the fame; and all'o a Clause, pro-, viding that all Monies, to be raised under and by virtue of the Powers contained in such Act, shall, as often as the same shall amount to the Sum of Fifty Pounds, be paid into the Hands of some Banker, or of such other Person or Persons as shall be approved by a Majority of such Proprietors, and that no Monies be issued out of the Hands of such Banker, or other Person or Persons, without an Order of the Commissioners, specifying the . Person to whom the same are payable, and the Service for which the same are due, and that the Balance, if any, upon the final Settlement of Accounts, shall be immediately repaid to the Land Owners, in propprtion to the Sums respectively paid by them; and also a Clause, providing that the final Award shall be read and signed by the Commissioners, in the Presence of the Proprietors, at a Special General Meeting called for that Purpose, of which Ten Days Notice at least shall be given in some Newspaper to hp named, circulating within the County,

and that such Award shall be proclaimed the next Sunday in the Parish Church, from the Time of which Proclamation the same shall be considered as complete for the Purpose of Appeal.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Friday Morning next.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty recommends it to the House of Commons, to consider of enabling His Majesty to make Remittances, from Time to Time, to be applied to His Service in Ireland, in such Manner as shall be approved by the Parliament of that Kingdom, to an Amount nqt exceeding Three Millions, on Provision being made by the Parliament of Ireland, for defraying the Interest and Charges of a Loan to that Amount.

G. R.

Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Joseph Kaye, Esquire, Agent for Sir Charles Grey and Earl Saint Vincent, produced to Your Committee, an Account Sales, verified by Oath in the High Court of Admiralty here, of the Ships and Goods captured by the Memorialists, and sold by their Agents in the Island of Martinique, in the Year 1794, and which had been condemned by a Court of Admiralty erected by the Memorialists in that Island, amounting to the Sum of ,£.52,523 Currency, which (after deduding the Expences of Sale and other Charges, being 10 Cent.) is equal to £.27,012 Sterling. And being examined, he -said. That the said Court of Admiralty, lo erected by the Memorialists as aforesakl, being held not to be legally constituted, and that the Proceedings carried on in it were null and void, they were called upon, by the American Claimants, to institute Proceedings in the High Court of Admiralty here, and to proceed to the Adjudication of all the captured Ships and Cargoes; and he produced to Your Committee, a Minute of the Sentences of the High Court of Admiralty upon each Ship and Cargo: And further said. That it appears, from the Account

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of assembled, by Public Advertisement, at the London Tavern, on the 20th June 1799, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have been long since convinced of the Neccftity of adopting some Measures for the Improvement of the Port of London, and have, with Pleasure, found several Plans proposed for that Purpose, by making Wet Docks, and other Works, in different Parts of the River;

and that the Petitioners have perceived, by the Report of the Select Committee of the House of Commons, to whom different Plans have been referred, that the Plans for making W et Docks in the of Dogs and Wagping, were each of them reported to be attended with peculiar Advantages, and that the speedy Adoption of either would be a great Relief and Advantage to the whole Trade of the Port, but that the immediate Prosecution of that in the Isle of Dogs was recommended; and it appears by a Bill, now before the House, that the Use of those Docks was to be confined to the West India Trade, and that the Ships in that Trade were to be compelled to load and unload in those Docks only; and that the adopting this Measure of Compulsion, instead of being beneficial, will be highly injurious to every Branch of Commerce; and that the Monopoly of so extensive a Branch of Commerce as the India, obviously tends to prevent any further Improvement by other Plans, the Propos'ers of which, while they have had the Benefit of the General Trade of the Port in View, must have looked for Compensation for the Hazard and Expence of their Undertakings, to the Advantages which would arise from the Resort of Shipping to such Docks as might offer the most convenient Accommodation, and, precluded from the A Hi fiance of a Trade exten-V r,. 54.

five as the West India, may be discouraged from those Undertakings which would afford Relief from the various Inconveniencies now experienced; and that the Petitioners have been led to expect, that a laudable Competition, between different Plans, aiming at the most effectual Means of answering every Purpose, by insuring the Protection and Security of Property and Revenue, by lessening the Expences, and adding to the Accommodation of the Port, and founding their Hopes upon their respective Merits only, would have placed the Port of London in such a State as to insure its Convenience, under every supposed Increase of Commerce: And therefore praying, That the Clause, compelling Ships in the West India Trade to resort to the Docks in the Iste of Dogs, may not pais into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That, among other Provisions contained therein, is One, That the Whole of the West India Trade shall load and unload in or near certain Wet Docks which are proposed to be made in the lfte of Dogs -, and that the Ward of is principally situ-

Gaily s, Wool's, Custom House, Porter's, Bear's, Sab's, Wig-gin's, Young's, Ralph's, and Dice's and that the Inhabitants of the Ward principally consist of Persons who get their Living by the Business of the Water Side, anti upon whom is levied the greater Part of the Ward and Parochial Taxes and Assessments of the said Ward; and that the Removal of so considerable a Proportion of the Trade of the Port as the West India Trade from its present Station, must inevitably and considerably lefl'en the Amount of the Ward and Parochial Taxes and Assessments of the said Ward: And therefore praying, That there may be introduced into the said Bill, a Clause for the Indemnification of the Petitioners against such Defalcation in the said Ward and Parochial Taxes and Assessments as they may experience in consequence of the Removal of the said West India Trade, pursuant to the Enactments contained in the said Bill, and that they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, Agents, or Witnesses, at the Bar of the House, in Support of the said Clause, and of the Allegations contained in their Petition.

redeeming the National Debt; reducing the actual Amount of the Debt, existing on 5th January 1 793, to

£. 209,553,559, and the Annuities to £. 1,253,670;

Ordered, That the said Debate be further adjourned till Tomorrow Scvennight, the 11th Day of this Instant July.

Resolved, That this House will, immediately, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to con- COmcandEx-fuler of the Income, Expenditure, and Commerce, of penUiture. the Country, and oi the Progress which has been made, and may be expected to be made, in the Reduction of the National Debt, and the preventing the Accumulation thereof in future.

Ordered, That the several Accounts and Papers, which &c"

have been presented to the House in this present Session „ of Parliament, relating to the Public Income and Expenditure, be referred, to the said Committee.

Resolved, That, in case it shall be thought expedient by the Petitioners to renew their Application to this House, in the next Session of Parliament, for the specific Purposes stated in their said Petition, and no other, this House will deem general Notices of such intended Application, inserted in the London Gazette, and the adjacent County Newspapers (as directed by the First Standing Order of the 7th of May 1794) and given at the different Quarter Sessions of the Peace, in the Manner therein directed, to be sufficient Notice to all Persons concerned; and that the Maps or Plans, with the fooks V o l. 54.

of Reference, which have been delivered to the several Clerks of the Peace (in pursuance of the Third Standing Order of the 7th of May 1794) shall be deemed sufficient, without again delivering such Maps and Books.'

Resolved, That, all Persons concerned in Interest, who have been applied to, and have given their Consent to the Bill, which was depending in this House in the Session of Parliament of the Years 1795-6, for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks in Wapping, shall be considered as consentingto such Bill as may be brought in upon the like Petition, for the Purposes mentioned in the last Resolution, and no other, unless they shall personally attend the Committee, to whom such Bill may be committed, and express their Diflent, or shall give Certificates in Writing, or other Evidence, of their Dilfent, to be proved to the Satisfaction of such Committee.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, supposing the Price of Three Cent. Stock, to be on an Average, after the Year 1800, £.90 in Time of Peace, and £. 75 in Time of War, and the Proportion of Peace and War to be nearly the same as in the Course of the last One Hundred Years, the Average Price of Peace, and War would be about £.85. The Fund applicable to the Reduction of Debt, existing previous to 1793, will have reached its greatest Amount in 1808: The Whole of the Capital of Debt created in each Year of the present War will be redeemed in about Forty Years from such Year respectively; and the Whole of the Capital Debt, existing previous to 1793, will be redeemed , in about Forty-seven Years from the present Time.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from the Year 1808 to 1833 (at which Time the Capital Debt created in the First Year of the present War would be redeemed, and the Taxes applicable to the Charges thereof would become disposeable) Taxes would be set free in the Course of each Year of Peace (on the JSupposition of the Price of Stocks before stated) to the Amount of £.133,000, and in each Year of War . to the Amount of £.168,000; making (on the Proportion of Peace and War above stated} the Total Amount of Taxes let free during that Period £.4,284,000: — That the Amount of the Sum Annually applicable to the Reduction of Debt would, in the Course of the same Period, gradually rife from £.5,000,000 to about £. 10,400,000, and may, at a Medium, be computed at £.7,700,000: — That the Permanent Loan to be borrowed in each Year of War during the same Period, would, according to the System now adopted, amount to the same Sum: — That the Interest, and One per Cent, on the Capital, of such Loan, may, for every such Year of War, be computed at about £.410,000; and the Total Charge thereof would, on the Supposition above stated, amount to £.5,300,000; exceeding the Amount of the Taxes, which would be set free in the same Period, by about £. 1,000,000.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, supposing the Charges occasioned by each Year of War during the Period before stated, and the Sums raised within the Year, to remain as computed for the Year 1800, the total Amount of that Part of the Loan necessary for the Service of every such Year (which, according to the Plan now adopted, will be to be raised on the Credit of the Tax on Income) will be gradually decreasing during the Whole of the Period, in proportion as the Sums, applicable in each Year to the Reduction of Debt, increase; and that the Period for which the Tax on Income must afterwards continue in Time of Peace, on Account of each Year of War, will decrease in like Manner.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That (on the Suppositions before stated) Taxes equal to 3

the Amount of the Charge created during each Year of the present WTar will be successively set free from the Year 1833 to 1840 inclusive, to the Amount, in the Whole, of about £.8,500,000: — That Taxes to the Amount of nearly £.2,000,000 will also be set free from the Year 1833 to 1846, inclusive, and farther Taxes, to the Amount of £.4,200,000 (being the Sum applicable from 1808 to the Reduction of Debt existing previous to 1793) will be set free about 1846, when the Whole of the said Debt is estimated to be redeemed; making, in the Whole (together with the Taxes before stated to be set free from 1808 to 1833)near£. 19,000,000 of Taxes set free up to 1846.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, supposing the same Number of Years of , War to 1846, at the same Rate of Expence, the Sums necessary to be raised by Loans for defraying the same (if the System for raising a Portion of the Supplies within the Year, as stated, should not be adopted) would amount, in each Year of the War, to about £.25,000,000, the Whole to about £.450,000,000 Sterling; which (supposing the Price of Three per Cents, to be £.50 on an Average of War) would amount to £.900,000,000 Capital Stock, and the Interest and Charges of One per Cent.to £.36,000,000 per Annum-, which, after deducting about £.19,900,000 Taxes, estimated to be set free within the same Period, would require an Increase of £. 17,000,000 of Permanent Taxes beyond those now existing.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second < .

Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to Address for His Majesty, That He will be graciously pleased to con- ^j"yntothe fer some Dignity in the Church upon the Reverend Mr. P William Busby, Chaplain to this House.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Afient to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission 'read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, at the Desire of the Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Afient to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of , His Royal High-

Mr. Douglas reported from the Committee, who were appointed to consider of the present State of the Distillery of Spirits in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and of the Laws relative thereto, and the Duties payable in respect thereof, and to report the fame, together with their Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had considered the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof, together with several Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Laws concerning the Prevention and Prosecution and Punishment of Offences committed in respect of the Distillery of Spirits in Scotland, and the Duties payable thereon, as a Branch of the Revenue of Excil'e, require Revision, and will admit of considerable Amendment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there are very considerable Defects incident to the System of Survey, and also to that of Licence, if taken separately, which, from their Nature, appear to be incapable of being cured by any further Improvement which can be real'onably foreseen as applicable to either.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Plan may be formed, whereby the Two Svftems of Licence and Survey shall be combined together, in a Manner calculated, on the one Hand, on the Knowledge which has already (and which may (till be obtained by farther Investigation) been acquired with respect to the Art of Distillationj and, on the other Hand, with a just Regard to the real Interests of the Country, of the Distiller, and of the Revenue, as connected therewith, and which shall possess many of the Advantages, without being liable to many of the Objections inherent in the one and the other System, when considered as exclusive Modes of Taxation on the Distillery of Spirits in Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, on a Comparison of the different Computations, made on various Grounds, which have been dated to them, That the Numbej of Gallons of Spirits annually

consumed

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee That the dilicrent Computations, made on various Grounds, which have been Hated to this Committee, of the Rate per Gallon of Spirits the Distiller could afford to pay to the Revenue, give, on the Average thereof, the Sum of Two Shillings and Six Pence Gallon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, according to the Two Average Computations of the Quantum of Consumption and Rate of Duty, mentioned in the Two foregoing Resolutions, the Annual Sum which might be expected to be raised on Spirits distilled from Grain in Scotland, for the Consumption of that Country, if an effectual Scheme of Assessment and Collection could be deviled, from the above-mentioned Statements, would appear to be £.460,767, on the Supposition that the Strength of Spirits, with regard to which the said Computations of Consumption and Rate of Duty have been made, was taken to be One to Ten over Hydrometer Proof.

't After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a most Gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The favourable Appearances which I announced to you, at the Commencement of the present Session, have since been followed by Successes beyond My most fan-guine Expectations.

By the Progress of the Imperial Arms, under the Command of the Archduke Charles of , a great Part

of Switzerland has already recovered its ancient Religion, Laws, and Liberties; and the uninterrupted and brilliant Victories of the Combined Armies, under the Command of Field Marshal , have, in the short

Period which has elapsed since the Opening of the Campaign, nearly accomplished the Deliverance of rom the degrading Yoke of the French Republic.

The Decision and Energy which distinguish the Councils of My Ally the Emperor of , and the intimate Union and Concert happily established between Us, will enable Me to employ, to the greatest Advantage, the powerful Means which you have entrusted to Me, for establishing, on permanent Grounds, the Security and Honour of this Country, and the Liberty and Independence of Europe.

I have the Satisfaction of seeing, that internal Tranquillity is in some Degree restored in My Kingdom of Ireland.

The Removal of the only remaining Naval Force of the Enemy to a distant Quarter, mult nearly extinguish even the precarious Hope which the Traitorous and Dif-affected have entertained of Foreign Assistance.

But Our great Reliance for the immediate Safety of that Country, must still rest on the experienced Zeal and Bravery of My Troops of all Descriptions, and on the unshaken Loyalty and voluntary Exertions of My faithful Subjects in both Kingdoms.

Its ultimate Security can alone be ensured by its intimate and entire Union with Great; and I am

happy to observe, that the Sentiments manifested by numerous and respectable Descriptions of My Irish Subjects justify the Hope, that the Accomplishment of this 8

great and salutary Work will be proved to be as much the joint With, as it unquestionably is the common Interest, of both My Kingdoms.

The Provisions which you have made for suppressing those dangerous and seditious Societies, which had been formed for the Purpose of dilleminating the destructive Principles of the French Resolution, are peculiarly adapted to the Circumstances of the Times, and have furnished additional Security to the established Constitution.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The unusual Sacrifices which you have made in the present Moment, on Behalf of My Subjects, are wifely calculated to meet effectually the Exigencies of this great Crisis. They have, at the same Time, given additional Security to Public Credit, by establishing a Syl-tem of Finance, beneficial alike to yourselves and to Posterity; and the Chearfulness with which these heavy Burthens are supported, evince at once the good Sense, the Loyalty, and the Public Spirit of My People.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is impossible to compare the Events of the present Year with the State and Prospects of Europe at the Distance of but a few Months, without acknowledging, in humble Thankfulness, the visible Interposition of Divine Providence, in averting those Dangers which so long threatened the Overthrow of all the Establishments of the civilized World.

It may be permitted to Us to hope, that the same protecting Providence will continue to Us its Guidance through the Remainder of this eventful Contest; and will conduct it finally to such an Ifl'ue as shall transmit to future Ages a memorable Example of the Instability of all Power founded on Injustice, Usurpation, and Impiety; and shall prove the Impossibility of ultimately dissolving the Connection between Public Prosperity and Public Virtue.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Ma- Parliament jesty's Command, said, r>gued.

By the KIN G.

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

Whereas by an Act, passed in the Thirty-seventh Year of Our Reign, intituled, An Act to shorten the Time now required for giving Notice of the Royal Intention of His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, that the Parliament shall meet and be holden for the Difoatch of Business, and more effectually to provide for the Meeting of Parliament in the same of a Demise of the Crown, it is enacted. That, whenever We shall be pleated, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to issue Our Royal Proclamation, giving Notice of Our Royal Intention that Parliament shall meet and be holden for the Dispatch of Business, on any Day, being not lets than Fourteen Days from the Date of such Proclamation, the same shall be a full and sufficient Notice, to all Pei Ions whatever, of such Our Royal Intention; and the Parliament shall thereby stand prorogued to the Day and Place therein declared, notwithstanding any previous Prorogation of the Parliament to any longer Day, and; notwithstanding any former Law, Usage, or Practice, to the contrary. And whereas Our Parliament now Rands prorogued to Tuesdaythe Twenty-ninth Day of October next; and forasmuch as for certain Causes We are desirous that Our Parliament should meet on an earlier Day, for the Dispatch of Business, We, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, do, by this Our Royal Proclamation, publish and declare Our Royal Will and Intention, That Our said Parliament shall meet, and be holden on Tuesday the Twenty-fourth Day of this Instant September, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs of the House of Commons, are hereby required to give Attendance accordingly, at on the said Twenty-

fourth Day of September.

Given at Our Court at Weymouth, the Ninth Day of September One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-nine, and in the Thirty-ninth Year of Our Reign.

God lave the KING.
